6.2 Reasoning-language Alignment Helps,
Independently of Proficiency
The clearest result is the comparison of forced Ger-
man with forced French on SectionChunks. Ger-
man scores 3.701 and French only 3.491, a gap of
0.21. This gap is statistically significant (Holm-
corrected p=.019 ), and German wins on 182
questions against 138 for French. Both are forced,
non-default reasoning languages, and both use the
same data and system; the only difference is that
German matches the language of the query and ev-
idence while French does not. Crucially, according
to the Qwen3 report, the model ismoreproficient in
French (average benchmark 71.8) than in German
(68.2) (Qwen Team, 2025). If the effect were about
language ability, French should do at least as well
as German. The gain therefore comes fromalign-
mentwith the language of the data, not from the
model’s language proficiency. The same ordering
(German above French) also holds on the multi-hop
set (2.889 vs. 2.778), so it is not an artifact of one
evaluation.

the fixed-size baseline, but not equally. Going from
SimpleChunks to SectionChunks, unconstrained
reasoning improves the least (3.636→3.718 , ∆ =
0.08), and this gain is not significant ( p=.26 ).

6.4 English Bias Remains
While alignment narrows the gap, it does not fully
close it. On the single-passage set, unconstrained
English (3.718), forced German (3.701), and forced
English (3.670) are statistically tied (all pairwise
p>.5 ). So forced German reaches the level of the
model’s native, unconstrained English reasoning,
but does not beat it. On the multi-hop set forced
English (3.000) is slightly above forced German
(2.889). In short, prompt-based language control
lets German reasoning match unconstrained and
forced English, but not surpass it. This matches
the finding of Qi et al. (2025) that prompt hacking
gives only limited control. It suggests that closing
the gap requires models with genuine multilingual
reasoning (e.g., light fine-tuning to reason in the tar-
get language) rather than inference-time prompting
alone. We see this as the main practical implication
for RAG in lower-resource languages.
6.5 When Does Reasoning Help?
On the single-passage set,disablingreasoning is
best of all (3.903), significantly above every reason-
ing setting on this set (Holm-corrected p≤.04 ).
These questions are answerable from one retrieved
passage, so a reasoning trace mostly adds noise
and can pull in irrelevant content. On the multi-hop
set the opposite happens, and no reasoning is now
theworstretrieval configuration (2.778), tied with
French. This suggests reasoning helps only once a
question needs synthesis across passages, and can
hurt below that threshold. This adds a condition
to prior results that reasoning improves multi-turn
RAG (Yu et al., 2024), since the benefit depends
on task complexity, which can plausibly be mea-
sured by the number of retrieval hops a question
needs. In practice, this suggests that reasoning
should be turned on based on the predicted diffi-
culty of a question, rather than always on or always
off. A RAG system could estimate how many hops
a query needs and reason only above that threshold.
Our two datasets show both cases, since reasoning
hurts on one-hop questions and helps on multi-hop
ones, but finding the exact threshold needs a bench-
mark graded by hop count, which we do not have.
6.6 Judge Reliability and Language Artifacts
To check the automatic metric, one author re-rated
50 answers (five per configuration) by hand and
compared them to the judge; Table 4 shows the
confusion matrix. Human and judge ratings agreed
exactly in 66% of cases (the diagonal) and within
one point in 90%; disagreements of two or more
points occurred in 10%. The metric is thus reliable
enough to rank configurations but not to separate
near-ties, which matters because our top configura-
tions differ by little (e.g., unconstrained 3.718 vs.
German 3.701). The larger disagreements are also
asymmetric. Four of the five gaps of two points
or more are cases where the judge gave the mini-
mum score of 1 to an answer a human rated 3 or 4.

7 Conclusion
We studied whether forcing an LLM to reason in
the target language helps or hurts in a monolingual
German RAG setting, where the query and the re-
trieved evidence are all in that language. Using
a testbed overThe Dark Eyethat the model can-
not answer from memory, we found that aligning
the reasoning language with the language of the
data helps – forced German beats forced French
despite lower German proficiency – and that this
benefit grows when the retrieved context is richer
and carries target-language structure, which also
lowers the general cost of forcing a reasoning lan-
guage. At the same time, forced German does not
surpass the model’s native, unconstrained English
reasoning, so prompt-based control narrows but
does not close the gap between English and other
languages. Together, the results point to models
with native multilingual reasoning when RAG is
deployed over target-language corpora in lower-
resource languages. We release the testbed and QA
benchmark to support this line of work.
8
Limitations
Our study is focused on purpose, and several limi-
tations follow from that focus.
Single model and language pair.All system
runs use one model family (Qwen3) and one lan-
guage pair (German vs. English, with French as
a control). Whether the effects transfer to other
models and other non-English languages – espe-
cially truly low-resource ones – remains an open
question.
Prompt-based control only.We control the rea-
soning language with prompt hacking, which is
known to give only coarse control; we do not fine-
tune the model to reason in the target language,
which prior work suggests would help more (Qi
et al., 2025).
Small multi-hop set.The multi-hop set has 30
questions and shows non-trivial inter-reviewer dis-
agreement, so its numbers are supplementary and
should not be over-interpreted.
Imperfect judge.The LLM-as-a-Judge metric
agrees with humans only within one point 90% of
the time and may be biased toward English reason-
ing; near-ties in Table 2 are therefore uncertain.
Fixed retrieval.Retrieval hyperparameters were
fixed (top-30 reranked to top-3), and the context
length was limited by GPU memory. Trying a
range of these retrieval settings would strengthen
the conclusions.

11
A PDF Processing Pipeline
The knowledge base is built from region-
description PDFs whose two- and three-column
layout defeated the off-the-shelf converters we tried
(Docling, Marker, pdfalto). Our semi-automatic
pipeline converts each book in the following steps.
1. PDF→ ALTO XML.We run pdfalto (Lopez,
2021), which keeps per-token font and posi-
tion information and the text-block structure.
pdfalto also emits a stream of all parsed to-
kens, which we keep for later repair.
2. ALTO→ YAML.We split the document
by page and block, turn heading-font blocks
into Markdown headings, and normalize
bold/italic text. Words hyphenated across line
breaks are rejoined using a corpus-wide word-
count dictionary (and an LLM as a fallback)
to decide whether the hyphen is real.
3. Heading repair (semi-automatic).Some
words, including in headings, are dropped
by pdfalto. We compare headings found via
ALTO with those found by Marker on the
same page; on a mismatch, the page is shown
to a human, who assigns the correct heading
level.
4. Text repair (mostly automatic).Missing
words are recovered from the token stream
by matching blocks with lowest Levenshtein
distance. If more than 20% of a block changes,
the tool asks for confirmation.
5. Reading-order repair (manual).Because
blocks in the PDF do not always follow the
section order, a human reorders them (across
page boundaries when needed) so that the sec-
tion hierarchy is preserved.
6. Load into chunks.Each heading and its fol-
lowing text become a chunk; non-top-level
chunks are linked as children of the nearest
higher-level heading, giving the parent/child
structure used at retrieval time.
B Prompts and Reasoning Prefixes
To force the reasoning language, the system prompt
is extended to require reasoning in the target lan-
guage and the reasoning trace is prefixed with a
fixed sentence:
• German:“Ich muss zunächst durchgehen,
was ich über die Anfrage des Nutzers bere-
its weiß. ”
• English:“First, I need to go through what I
already know about the user’s request. ”
• French:“D’abord, je dois parcourir ce que je
sais déjà sur la demande de l’utilisateur. ”
The final answer is always required to be in Ger-
man. The LLM-as-a-Judge prompt provides the
question, gold answer, system answer, and the
source section, and asks for a single 1–5 rating;
the human reviewers follow the same guidelines.
When reading the rating, we kept the model’s de-
fault tokenization, since how such short answers
are tokenized can affect the result (Sanz-Guerrero
et al., 2025). For the local model, we use the default
chat template and ensure that it contains no time-
varying metadata (e.g., the current date) that could
make our results vary (Sanz-Guerrero et al., 2026a).
However, the judge and the large no-retrieval base-
line run through a hosted API that injects the cur-
rent date into the system prompt, so these results
may not be fully reproducible. The multi-hop set
is rated by humans and is not affected.
C A Judge Failure Case
The judge assigns the minimum score whenever an
answer looks unsupported, which occasionally mis-
fires. In the case below (referenced in Section 6.6)
the question asks which kind of dragon nests in the
coastal mountains by the Sea of the Seven Winds;
the gold answer isWestwinddrachen. The system
answers exactly that and even quotes the source
sentence, yet the judge scored it 1 while the human
reviewer scored it 4.
Question.Welche Drachenart nistet und jagt
typischerweise in den Küstenbergen am Meer der Sieben
Winde?
Gold answer.Westwinddrachen.
System answer.Die Drachenart, die . . . nistet und jagt,
ist dieWestwinddrache. Dies ergibt sich aus dem
Hinweis: “In den Bergen und Klippen der Küsten am
Meer der Sieben Winde [. . . ] horsten etliche
Westwinddrachen. ”
Judge:1Human:4
The answer is correct and grounded in the re-
trieved text, but its added framing sentence appears
to trigger the judge’s contradiction check. Such
cases are why the judge’s low scores, in particular,
should be read with care. The judge is itself an
LLM, and LLMs are known to be poorly calibrated

Guerrero et al., 2026b), so a confident minimum
score is not by itself strong evidence that an answer
is wrong. This points to a wider gap in how judges
are validated: LLM-as-a-Judge assumes that the
judge’s confidence is meaningful, but validations –
including ours – report agreement with humans and
not calibration (Sanz-Guerrero and von der Wense,
2026). However, we find that the metric is still reli-
able enough to rank configurations (Section 6.6).
D Statistical Significance
All configurations answer the same 585 single-
passage questions, so for any pair of configurations
we have two ratings of the same question and can
compare them question by question.
We use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test
(Wilcoxon, 1945). For each question it takes
the difference between the two ratings, and it
asks whether these differences lean toward one
configuration or are just noise. It uses the direction
and the relative size of the differences, not their
exact values, so it fits ordinal 1–5 ratings and does
not assume the ratings follow a normal distribution.
It is the paired (same-question) counterpart of a
t-test.
We run ten such tests, one for each pair of the
five SectionChunks settings. Running many tests
raises the chance that at least one looks signifi-
cant by luck. The Holm correction (Holm, 1979)
guards against this by making the threshold stricter
the more tests we run, so that the chance of any
false positive across all ten tests stays at 5%. The

The three top reasoning settings – unconstrained
English, forced German, and forced English – are
not distinguishable from each other. Forced Ger-
man is significantly above forced French, and dis-
abling reasoning is significantly above all four rea-
soning settings.
The other tests reported in Section 6 use the
same Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Any retrieval con-
figuration beats no retrieval withp <10−70, and
the small and large no-retrieval models are tied
(p=.83 ). For the move from SimpleChunks to
SectionChunks, we test each configuration’s per-
question gain (its SectionChunks rating minus its
SimpleChunks rating). The gain for forced Ger-
man is significant (p <10−4), while the gain for
unconstrained reasoning is not (p=.26).

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
abstract: Standard factual benchmarks assume clean monolingual prompts and exact-match scoring, two assumptions that break simultaneously in real-world multilingual deployment, from retrieval-augmented generation pipelines returning mixed-language passages to users pasting multilingual web content. We introduce Multilingual Distractor Interference (MDI), a lightweight and fully replicable evaluation protocol requiring no new data or annotation, in which factual questions are preceded by a semantically irrelevant foreign-language sentence, and evaluate five instruction-tuned LLMs across TruthfulQA and TriviaQA under eight distractor conditions (40,000 evaluations). Our central finding is a metric confound: for Llama-3.1-8B under a Hindi distractor, 58% of responses switch to Devanagari script, yielding a raw hallucination proxy of 0.710, but manual review reveals that 120 of 148 script-switched responses that were correct under clean conditions remain semantically correct despite being written in the wrong script, reducing the adjusted semantic hallucination rate to 0.470. All other models respond through abstention escalation with no hallucination increase. A paragraph-length English distractor triggers near-universal abstention (0.806-0.998) across all models, consistent with reading-comprehension confusion, a failure mode with direct consequences for multilingual RAG pipelines. TruthfulQA multiple-choice accuracy is unaffected under all single-sentence conditions. These results show that exact-match hallucination rates in mixed-language settings should be decomposed into script-switching and semantic error components before drawing conclusions about model reliability.

Output Language Confusion under Multilingual
Prompt Contamination
Riju Marwah1,2, Ritvik Garimella2, Khusham Bansal2,3, Atishay Jain2,4, Amit Sheth2,5
1University of Tübingen, Germany

Abstract
Standard factual benchmarks assume clean monolingual prompts and exact-match
scoring, two assumptions that break simultaneously in real-world multilingual de-
ployment, from retrieval-augmented generation pipelines returning mixed-language
passages to users pasting multilingual web content. We introduceMultilingual Dis-
tractor Interference (MDI), a lightweight and fully replicable evaluation protocol
requiring no new data or annotation, in which factual questions are preceded by
a semantically irrelevant foreign-language sentence, and evaluate five instruction-
tuned LLMs across TruthfulQA and TriviaQA under eight distractor conditions
(40,000 evaluations). Our central finding is a metric confound: for Llama-3.1-8B
under a Hindi distractor, 58% of responses switch to Devanagari script, yielding
a raw hallucination proxy of 0.710, but manual review reveals that 120 of 148
script-switched responses that were correct under clean conditions remain seman-
tically correct despite being written in the wrong script, reducing the adjusted
semantic hallucination rate to 0.470. All other models respond through abstention
escalation with no hallucination increase. A paragraph-length English distractor
triggers near-universal abstention (0.806-0.998) across all models, consistent with
reading-comprehension confusion, a failure mode with direct consequences for mul-
tilingual RAG pipelines. TruthfulQA multiple-choice accuracy is unaffected under
all single-sentence conditions. These results show that exact-match hallucination
rates in mixed-language settings should be decomposed into script-switching and
semantic error components before drawing conclusions about model reliability.
1 Introduction
Factual QA benchmarks are a primary tool for measuring LLM reliability, yet two of their core
assumptions routinely fail in deployment. First, they assume monolingual prompts [Hendrycks
et al., 2021, Shi et al., 2022]: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines frequently return
mixed-language passages [Asai et al., 2024], users paste multilingual web content, and cross-lingual
queries are common. Second, they assume exact-match scoring accurately reflects semantic error: a
model that answers correctly in the wrong script will score identically to one that hallucinated.
These two assumptions interact. When a foreign-language distractor triggers a model to respond in
that language, exact-match scoring treats every such response as a hallucination, even when the answer
is factually correct. The resulting metric inflation is not uniform across models; it is concentrated
in models that have the generative capacity to produce fluent text in the distractor language. The
practical consequence is that clean-prompt benchmarks not onlyunderestimatereal-world failure for
high-capacity multilingual models, but alsomischaracterizethe nature of that failure.

Figure 1:Multilingual Distractor Interference (MDI) evaluation pipeline and key findings.
(a)An English factual QA prompt is contaminated with a semantically irrelevant foreign-language
sentence.(b)Eight distractor conditions: clean, Spanish/Hindi/Chinese and their ×3 variants, and a
paragraph-length English Wikipedia excerpt (wiki_para).(c)Five instruction-tuned LLMs evaluated
under identical deterministic decoding settings.(d)Metrics: TruthfulQA accuracy and calibration;
TriviaQA exact-match accuracy, abstention rate, hallucination proxy rate, and script-switching rate.
(e)Three failure modes: script-switching hallucination (Llama-3.1-8B, Hindi), abstention escalation
(Phi-3, Mistral-7B, Qwen-2.5), and stability (all models, TruthfulQA MC). Raw hallucination proxy
of 0.710 adjusts to 0.470 after accounting for script-switched but semantically correct responses
identified through manual review.
We study this interaction directly. Our setup is not adversarial in the traditional sense: the distractor
sentence explicitly instructs the model to ignore it, and the target question is unchanged in English.
Any response degradation therefore reflects the model’s inability to maintain language-consistent
instruction following when the prompt context contains unexpected script boundaries, a realistic
failure mode in RAG and document-processing pipelines. To specifically isolate the script-boundary
mechanism, we include Spanish as a control condition: sharing the Latin script with English, it
separates script-boundary interference from language-identity interference.
Strikingly, the model most vulnerable to this failure is not the weakest multilingual model but
the strongest. This is consistent with what has been termed themultilingual curse, where richer
multilingual pretraining can introduce cross-lingual interference that degrades output language control
rather than improving it.
Our contributions are three-fold:
1. We introduceMultilingual Distractor Interference (MDI), a lightweight, reproducible
evaluation protocol for probing factual robustness under mixed-language prompt contamina-
tion.
2. We identify and quantify ametric confoundin exact-match-based hallucination scoring:
for Llama-3.1-8B under Hindi distraction, 120 of 148 script-switched responses that were
correct under clean conditions are semantically correct answers written in the wrong script,
reducing the raw hallucination proxy from 0.710 to an adjusted semantic hallucination rate
of 0.470.
3. We characterize afailure mode taxonomy: script-switching hallucination, abstention
escalation, and stability, showing that the operative mode is determined by model-specific
spontaneous generative capacity in the distractor language. The clean dissociation across
five models with identical inputs is itself the finding: it rules out general prompt sensitivity
and points to a tractable, model-level mechanism.
2
2 Related Work
Multilingual evaluation.Established multilingual benchmarks such as XTREME [Hu et al., 2020]
and XGLUE [Liang et al., 2020] evaluate models on tasks presented in a target language, measuring
cross-lingual transfer and per-language performance. Open-domain multilingual QA benchmarks such
as MKQA [Longpre et al., 2021] similarly assume that task language and prompt language are aligned.
Our setup differs fundamentally: the task remains English throughout; the foreign language appears
only as prompt contamination. This distinction matters because it isolates instruction-following
robustness from cross-lingual comprehension ability, a dimension that per-language benchmarks do
not probe.
Robustness to distracting context.Jia and Liang [2017] showed that prepending adversarial
sentences to reading comprehension passages substantially degraded model accuracy; subsequent
work extended this to extractive and generative QA settings. These studies focus on semantically
relevant or adversarially crafted distractors within a single language. We study semantically irrelevant
distractors that differ from the question in script and language, with an explicit ignore instruction,
making any failure a clear case of instruction-following breakdown rather than comprehension
difficulty. Muennighoff et al. [2023] show that instruction-following degrades when instructions
and content appear in different languages, which is consistent with our finding that script-boundary
crossing in the prompt context disrupts English output generation.
Multilingual contamination in RAG.Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines frequently surface
passages in languages other than the query language, particularly for cross-lingual or low-resource
queries [Asai et al., 2024]. While prior work has examined multilingual retrieval quality and
cross-lingual passage selection [Longpre et al., 2021], systematic study of how mixed-language
retrieved passages affect generator output behavior rather than retrieval ranking has been limited. Our
wiki_para ablation (Section 5.5) provides a controlled analog: a monolingual English paragraph
prepended to a factual question, isolating the effect of contextual format confusion from script-
switching.
Hallucination and factuality metrics.Exact-match scoring is known to be an imperfect proxy for
semantic correctness in monolingual settings [Joshi et al., 2017]; we show it introduces a systematic
directional bias in multilingual settings. For models with strong spontaneous generation in the
distractor language, exact-match conflates script-switched but semantically correct responses with
genuine hallucinations, inflating apparent error rates in a way that depends on the model’s generative
profile rather than its factual accuracy.
3 Multilingual Distractor Interference (MDI)
MDI is a lightweight evaluation protocol that probes whether semantically irrelevant foreign-language
context disrupts English factual question answering. The key design choice is that the distractor
is not adversarial: it explicitly declares itself irrelevant and instructs the model to ignore it. Any
response degradation therefore reflects a failure of language-grounded instruction following rather
than a failure of comprehension. The model understood the question but could not maintain English
output in the presence of a foreign-script context. This makes MDI a clean probe for a specific and
practically relevant robustness dimension. MDI requires no new data collection, annotation, or model
access beyond standard inference, making it straightforwardly applicable to any instruction-tuned
model evaluated on existing factual QA benchmarks.
3.1 Task Definition
Each question is evaluated under eight distractor conditions:
•clean: no distractor; establishes the per-model baseline.
•es/es_long: a Spanish sentence repeated once or three times.
•hi/hi_long: a Hindi sentence in Devanagari script, repeated once or three times.
•zh / zh_long: a Chinese sentence in Simplified Chinese script, repeated once or three times.
3
•wiki_para : a paragraph-length English Wikipedia excerpt, included as an ablation to isolate
context-length and format-confusion effects from script-switching.
The three distractor languages were selected to vary along two dimensions relevant to the hypothesized
failure mechanism: script and pretraining resource level. Spanish uses the Latin script shared with
English, providing a baseline condition where script boundaries are absent and any interference must
arise from language identity alone. Hindi (Devanagari script) and Chinese (Simplified Chinese script)
both introduce a non-Latin script boundary, but differ substantially in pretraining corpus size: Chinese
is among the highest-resource non-English languages in most LLM pretraining corpora, while Hindi
is comparatively lower-resource. This contrast allows us to test whether the failure mode is driven by
script-switching propensity specifically or by distractor language resource level more generally, a
distinction that proves consequential in Section 5.4.
The base distractor for each language is a single sentence that declares itself irrelevant and instructs
the model to ignore it. For example, the Spanish distractor reads:“Nota: Este texto no tiene relación
con la pregunta. Por favor ignóralo. ”Hindi and Chinese equivalents are constructed analogously in
their respective native scripts. The long variants repeat the base sentence three times to test whether
distractor length modulates the observed effects. The wiki_para condition uses a fixed paragraph
sampled from the WikiText-2 training split (minimum 200 characters) as a realistic approximation of
a retrieved English passage. In all conditions, the distractor is prepended to the question with a blank
line separator.
3.2 Prompt Format
For TruthfulQA, each item is presented as a four-choice multiple-choice question. The system prompt
instructs the model to respond with a single letter (A-D); accuracy is measured by log-probability
scoring over the four option tokens, requiring no generation. This format structurally prevents
script-switching and serves as a format-controlled upper bound on robustness.
For TriviaQA, each item is presented as an open-ended short-answer question. The system prompt
instructs the model to respond with a short phrase only, and specifies“If you do not know, say: I
don’t know. ”to elicit calibrated abstention. All TriviaQA generation uses greedy decoding (T=0 ,
maximum 32 new tokens).
3.3 Metrics
TruthfulQA.Accuracy is reported, defined as the proportion of questions where the highest-
probability option is correct.
TriviaQA.Four metrics are reported: (i)exact-match accuracy, evaluated against the full gold
alias list; (ii)abstention rate, detected by substring match on “I don’t know,” “unknown,” and related
phrases; (iii)hallucination proxy rate, defined as the proportion of responses that are neither correct
nor abstaining, such that accuracy + abstention + hallucination proxy = 1; and (iv)script-switching
rate, the proportion of outputs containing at least one character from the distractor’s native script,
detected via Unicode block membership (Devanagari for Hindi; CJK Unified Ideographs for Chinese).
The hallucination proxy is an intentionally conservative operationalization of confident factual error.
As we show in Section 5.3, it conflates script-switched but semantically correct responses with
genuine semantic errors in multilingual settings, and must be decomposed accordingly.
Statistical testing.Pairwise comparisons between each distractor condition and the clean baseline
use McNemar’s test on paired binary outcomes with continuity correction, with 95% confidence
intervals computed via bootstrap resampling (n=2000).
4 Experimental Setup
4.1 Models
We evaluate five publicly available instruction-tuned models spanning four training lineages and two
parameter scales (Table 1). Model selection was guided by three criteria. First,family diversity: Meta
4
Llama, Microsoft Phi, Mistral AI, and Alibaba Qwen represent independent pretraining pipelines with
different multilingual data compositions, allowing failure mode differences to be attributed to training
rather than shared architectural choices. Second,scale coverage: the 3-3.8B and 7-8B ranges are
representative of widely deployed open-source models that fit within single-GPU inference budgets in
float16 precision, enabling exact replication without proprietary access. Third,controlled intra-family
comparison: Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B share the same tokenizer, so any behavioral difference
between them under identical distractor conditions cannot be attributed to tokenizer fragmentation,
isolating model capacity and pretraining exposure as the operative variables.
Table 1: Models evaluated. All loaded in float16 on a single GPU via HuggingFace Transformers;
inference uses greedy decoding throughout. Language support as stated in official model cards.
Model Family Params Supported languages
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Meta Llama 8B 8 (incl. Hindi, Chinese †)
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct Meta Llama 3B 8 (incl. Hindi, Chinese †)

officially supported.
4.2 Datasets
We evaluate on TruthfulQA [Lin et al., 2022] and TriviaQA [Joshi et al., 2017], chosen for their
complementary evaluation formats. TruthfulQA’s multiple-choice structure permits log-probability
scoring over single option tokens without any generation step, providing a format-controlled baseline
in which script-switching is structurally impossible. TriviaQA’s open short-answer format exposes
generation behavior directly, allowing observation of script-switching, abstention, and hallucination
under distractor conditions. Together, the two datasets allow us to separate failure modes that arise
from the generation process from those that arise from answer selection, a distinction that is central
to interpreting our results.
For TruthfulQA we use the mc1 split from the validation set, sampling 500 questions with a fixed
random seed (seed = 42). For TriviaQA we use theunfiltered.nocontext configuration from the
validation split, sampling 500 questions with the same seed; answers are evaluated against the full
alias list provided in the dataset.
4.3 Evaluation Scale
Each model is evaluated on every question under every distractor condition, yielding: 5models×
2datasets×8conditions×500questions= 40,000evaluations.
Question-distractor pairings are fixed across models so that all comparisons are paired, enabling
McNemar’s test for significance testing throughout.
5 Results
5.1 TruthfulQA: Multiple-Choice Is Robust
TruthfulQA accuracy is unaffected by single-sentence multilingual distractors for all models (Table 2).
No accuracy drop is statistically significant under single-sentence conditions (p >0.05 , McNemar’s
test).
The insulation of TruthfulQA from single-sentence distractors follows directly from its format: log-
probability scoring over single letter tokens removes the generation step that makes script-switching
possible. This makes TruthfulQA MC accuracy an unreliable signal in either direction under distractor
conditions, a methodological point for future benchmark design.

Second, Llama-3.2-3B shows a consistent and significant accuracy drop under most distractor

5.2 TriviaQA: A Clean Failure Mode Dissociation

All other models produce Devanagari on fewer than 1.2% of responses. Critically, their hallucination

“Oregon.” similarly transcribed.
The remaining 28 cases within this 148-response subset (18.9%) are genuine semantic errors: wrong
proper nouns or semantically incorrect paraphrases. Accounting for the 120 script-switched responses
identified as semantically correct, the adjusted semantic hallucination rate is 235/500 = 0.470, com-
pared to a raw hallucination proxy of 0.710 and a clean baseline of 0.416. The primary consequence
of script-switching isoutput in the wrong language, not fabricated content, though a meaningful real
increase in semantic errors (+5.4 pp) remains.
The implication for evaluation practice is direct: exact-match-based hallucination metrics in
multilingual settings should be decomposed into script-switched (potentially semantically correct)
and genuinely wrong components. Reporting raw exact-match failure for a model like Llama-3.1-8B
in mixed-language conditions overstates semantic hallucination by a factor of approximately 1.5×.
Benchmark comparisons between multilingual and English-primary models may hence systematically
understate the reliability gap in contexts where the multilingual model is more likely to script-switch.
5.4 Script-Switching as the Proximal Mechanism
Two comparisons rule out alternative explanations for the Llama-3.1-8B dissociation.
Hindi vs. Chinese.Chinese is a higher-resource language than Hindi in most LLM pretraining
corpora. If distractor language resource level drove the effect, Llama-3.1-8B should show an equal or
stronger hallucination spike under the Chinese distractor. It does not: CJK-script outputs occur on
0% of responses, and the hallucination rate falls slightly to 0.382 ( ∆ =−0.034 , p= 0.009 ). The
model has sufficient Hindi generative capacity to switch into Devanagari output spontaneously, but
not Chinese.
7
Llama-3.1-8B vs. Llama-3.2-3B.Both models share the same tokenizer, ruling out tokenizer
fragmentation as the driver. Yet Llama-3.2-3B produces Devanagari on only 1.2% of responses under
the same Hindi distractor. The relevant variable is not tokenization, and not instructed generation
ability (both models can produce Devanagari when explicitly asked to do so), but spontaneous
script-switching propensity under distractor conditions. This propensity appears to be a function of
model scale and pretraining Hindi exposure, and it is concentrated in the larger model, not the smaller
one.
This last point is counterintuitive and practically important:stronger multilingual capacity does
not protect against this failure mode; for models with strong spontaneous generation in the
distractor language, it produces it.This is consistent with what has been termed themultilingual
curse, the observation that incorporating more languages during pretraining can introduce cross-
lingual interference that degrades target-language behavior [Muennighoff et al., 2023]. Here the
interference manifests not as degraded comprehension but as degraded output language control: the
model understands the English question but cannot suppress generation in the language whose script
dominates the prompt context. The implication is that models with the richest multilingual pretraining
may be the most susceptible to this specific failure mode, not the least.
5.5 Paragraph-Length Distractor
The wiki_para condition produces a qualitatively different and cross-model consistent effect: near-
universal abstention (Mistral-7B: 0.860; Qwen-2.5-3B: 0.998; even Llama-3.1-8B, which shows
minimal abstention under Hindi, abstains on 80.6% of wiki_para questions). This is not a script-
switching effect as the paragraph is English, but a context-format confusion: models appear to treat
the prepended paragraph as part of the question context and decline to answer when the “passage”
does not contain the answer, as if performing reading comprehension rather than open-domain QA.
This is directly relevant to RAG deployments, and to a gap in how RAG systems are currently
evaluated. Most existing evaluation of RAG systems focuses on retrieval quality and answer accuracy
over clean, language-matched passages; systematic evaluation over mixed-language or contextually
mismatched retrieved context has been limited. Our results suggest that such mismatches can cause
widespread abstention independent of retrieval quality. A model that retrieves the correct passage
but treats it as reading comprehension context will abstain rather than answer. This is a failure mode
that is invisible to retrieval-focused evaluation metrics but consequential in deployment. Evaluation
protocols for multilingual RAG should therefore include conditions where retrieved passages are in
a different language or format than the query, and should track abstention rates alongside answer
accuracy.
5.6 Distractor Length Effects
Repeating the single-sentence distractor three times produces modest additional degradation but does
not change the qualitative pattern. For Llama-3.1-8B, hi_long hallucination proxy is 0.704 vs. 0.710
for hi, essentially unchanged. For Qwen-2.5-3B, abstention rises from 0.730 to 0.842 under hi_long.
The failure mode taxonomy established under single-sentence conditions is stable under distractor
repetition.
6 Discussion
Why does Llama-3.1-8B switch to Devanagari?The pattern is consistent with a model that has
learned strong Hindi text generation during pretraining and whose instruction-following mechanism is
insufficient to suppress spontaneous language switching when a Devanagari-script context is present.
Crucially, the relevant capacity isspontaneousrather than instructed: all five models in our evaluation
can produce Devanagari output when explicitly instructed to do so, but only Llama-3.1-8B switches
scripts without such instruction under distractor conditions. The 8B/3B contrast within the Llama
family, with identical tokenizers but different scale and pretraining data exposure, suggests that the
failure mode scales with multilingual capacity in a way that is not obvious from standard multilingual
benchmarks. We do not have access to training data composition to make this definitive.
8
A failure mode taxonomy.Our results support three response modes under multilingual distractor
text: (1)script-switching hallucination: confident generation in the wrong language, inflating exact-
match error; (2)abstention escalation: rising “I don’t know” rates with no hallucination increase; and
(3)stability: no significant change in either direction. Which mode a model exhibits in open-answer
settings depends on whether it has spontaneous generative capacity in the distractor language, not on
distractor length, language resource level, or tokenizer characteristics. A fourth route to apparent
stability is format constraint: TruthfulQA’s multiple-choice scoring removes the generation step
entirely, suppressing the failure mode regardless of the model’s multilingual profile.
Implications for evaluation.Current multilingual robustness evaluations focus on per-language
task performance. Our results suggest that a different dimension is both practically important and
poorly captured by existing protocols: the effect of foreign-language prompt context on otherwise
English tasks. More concretely: (i) hallucination proxy rates computed via exact-match in mixed-
language settings should be reported alongside script-switching rates and adjusted semantic error rates;
(ii) models explicitly optimized for multilingual instruction following should be evaluated specifically
for output language control under mixed-script prompt conditions, as stronger multilingual capacity
appears to increase rather than decrease susceptibility to this failure mode; (iii) RAG evaluation
benchmarks should include mixed-language retrieved context, as even English-language paragraph
noise produces widespread abstention. More broadly, these findings suggest that multilingual
pretraining objectives and data composition have consequences for output language control that
are not captured by standard cross-lingual transfer benchmarks: a dimension that warrants explicit
attention in multilingual model development.
Limitations.Our experimental choices reflect deliberate scope decisions appropriate for a diagnos-
tic probe. All models are evaluated at realistic single-GPU inference budgets in float16 precision,
reflecting conditions under which these models are actually deployed rather than idealized research
settings. The distractor sentences explicitly declare themselves irrelevant by design: this isolates
instruction-following failure from comprehension failure, making the probe interpretable rather than
weaker. More naturalistic contamination without an ignore instruction is important future work and
may produce larger effects. We evaluate five open-source models; the pattern may not generalize to
closed-source models or models with different pretraining data mixes, and we encourage replication
of MDI across a broader model population. Our model set consists of models released between
2023 and 2024 and therefore does not include the latest generations of open-source instruction-tuned
LLMs. We view replication across current-generation models as an important direction for future
work. Abstention detection via substring matching may miss non-standard refusal formulations,
particularly Mistral-7B’s more discursive refusals.
7 Conclusion
We introduce Multilingual Distractor Interference (MDI) and use it to identify a systematic metric
confound in exact-match-based hallucination scoring: for models with strong spontaneous Hindi
generative capacity, a Hindi-language distractor triggers script-switching rather than semantic hal-
lucination, and exact-match scoring cannot distinguish the two. Review of all 291 script-switched
responses finds that, among the 148 cases that were correct under clean conditions, 120 (81.1%) are
semantically correct answers in the wrong script, reducing the raw hallucination proxy from 0.710 to
an adjusted semantic hallucination rate of 0.470. Models without this spontaneous capacity respond
through abstention escalation instead, a less severe but equally systematic failure mode with different
practical consequences. Paragraph-length English distractors produce a third mode: near-universal
abstention consistent with reading-comprehension confusion, with direct implications for RAG evalu-
ation. The takeaway for practitioners is two-fold: (1) deploy-time failure mode in mixed-language
pipelines depends on the model’s spontaneous generative profile; and (2) exact-match hallucination
metrics reported for models with strong non-English generation should be treated as upper bounds
requiring script-switch decomposition before interpretation. More broadly, our results suggest that
output language control under mixed-script prompt conditions is a distinct and underexamined axis
of multilingual model quality, and one that should be evaluated explicitly alongside cross-lingual
transfer and per-language accuracy as multilingual models continue to scale.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
abstract: An email assistant should not complete less work simply because a user phrases the same request differently. Yet most benchmarks test each task with only one canonical request, leaving this form of robustness largely unmeasured. We test whether email assistants remain reliable when the requested information, available evidence, and expected outcome stay fixed, but the communication style or English variety changes. We construct validated variants along five communication-style axes and four rule-based dialect conditions, and evaluate them on three benchmarks: a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and two tool-using agents. Indirect requests reduce performance on all three benchmarks, while formal requests reduce performance on both agentic benchmarks. Examining the systems more closely shows that these failures have different causes. Verbose requests mainly hurt a lexical retriever by making the relevant email harder to find. By contrast, indirect and dialect variants remain harmful even when the relevant email is retrieved. In the agentic setting, indirect and formal requests mainly cause the agents to omit required actions, not to take more unsupported actions. These results show that a successful response is not enough to establish robustness: evaluations should vary how requests are expressed and separately measure whether agents complete the requested work.
full_text:
Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation
Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
Feng Chen, Ritam Dutt, Atnaz Taheri, Alex Williams
fengc9@uw.edu
Abstract
An email assistant should not complete less work simply because a user phrases the
same request differently. Yet most benchmarks test each task with only one canoni-
cal request, leaving this form of robustness largely unmeasured. We test whether
email assistants remain reliable when the requested information, available evidence,
and expected outcome stay fixed, but the communication style or English variety
changes. We construct validated variants along five communication-style axes
and four rule-based dialect conditions, and evaluate them on three benchmarks: a
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and two tool-using agents. Indirect
requests reduce performance on all three benchmarks, while formal requests reduce
performance on both agentic benchmarks. Examining the systems more closely
shows that these failures have different causes. Verbose requests mainly hurt a
lexical retriever by making the relevant email harder to find. By contrast, indirect
and dialect variants remain harmful even when the relevant email is retrieved. In
the agentic setting, indirect and formal requests mainly cause the agents to omit
required actions, not to take more unsupported actions. These results show that a
successful response is not enough to establish robustness: evaluations should vary
how requests are expressed and separately measure whether agents complete the
requested work.
1 Introduction
An email assistant should not complete less work because a user asks indirectly, writes formally, adds
surrounding context, or uses a different variety of English. These differences are common in real
communication, but they do not necessarily change what the user wants. If the requested information,
relevant evidence, named entities, and intended outcome remain the same, a reliable assistant should
return the same answer or carry out the same actions.
Current evaluations rarely test this expectation. Most benchmarks represent each task with one
canonical request, even though the same task can be expressed in many ways. Prior work shows
that semantically equivalent query formulations can change retrieval results, including for recent
retrieval architectures [Penha et al., 2022, Hagen et al., 2024], and that linguistic reformulation affects
both retrieval and answer generation in retrieval-augmented question answering [Cao et al., 2026].
Performance also varies across systematic varieties of English [Ziems et al., 2022, 2023, Sap et al.,
2019, Srirag et al., 2025]. These findings establish that wording matters for finding and answering
information, but they leave an important question for interactive agents: can a change in wording alter
whether the requested work is completed? This question matters because an agent can fail without
producing an obviously bad response. An assistant may identify the task, call some appropriate tools,
and reply fluently while still omitting an action needed to finish the request. Conversely, it may
retrieve the wrong evidence or take an unsupported action. These failures require different responses
from system designers, but a single end-to-end success score does not distinguish them. Diagnostic
agent benchmarks similarly show that aggregate scores can combine failures such as skipping a
required tool, ignoring a tool result, or producing unsupported output [Kokane et al., 2024, Soni,
arXiv:2610.02627v1  [cs.AI]  2 Oct 2026
2026]. Robustness evaluation should therefore ask not only whether performance changes, but what
the system stopped doing correctly.
We study whether email assistants remain reliable when the same request is expressed in different
ways. We evaluate the two settings for email assistants: theretrieval-augmented generation(RAG)
setting, where the system retrieves evidence from the archive and answers from it, and theagentic
setting, where the system calls tools to carry out the request. Covering both lets us examine whether
communication variation affects the information an assistant returns as well as the actions it performs.
We vary communication style and English variety while keeping the underlying task and expected
outcome unchanged, and validate the resulting requests to ensure that they preserve the original intent.
Our work makes three contributions:
• A framework for generating validated request variants.Figure 1 shows it. An LLM
rewriter produces the communication-style poles and a rule-based transducer produces the
dialect varieties, and a set of gates admits a variant only once it still requests the information
or action asked for, carries the relevant task details, and expects the same outcome.
• An evaluation spanning RAG and agentic settings.We apply the framework to email
question answering and to tool-using agents, so that the same variation can be traced through
retrieval, answering, and execution.
• A closer analysis of assistant failures.We examine not only whether performance changes,
but also whether failures come from finding the wrong information, producing an incorrect
answer, omitting required actions, or taking unsupported actions.
2 Evaluation Framework
We evaluate whether a system fulfills the same request when the request is expressed differently.
We consider two forms of variation.Communication stylechanges how a writer presents a request.
Dialectchanges grammatical and dialectal features according to patterns documented for varieties of
English. Figure 1 shows how a variant is built and follows one request through a RAG pipeline.
2.1 Variation Taxonomy
2.1.1 Communication-Style Axes
The five axes and the definition of each pole are listed in Table 1. Each style axis pairs areference
pole, a plain rewrite that carries no marked style, with acontrastivepole that carries the property
under test. Formality is the exception: neither a formal nor a casual register is neutral, so both of its
poles are contrastive. Each axis rests on a documented distinction: directness on the contrast between
on-record and off-record requests [Brown and Levinson, 1987, Mannekote et al., 2025]; formality on
register variation [Pavlick and Tetreault, 2016, Rao and Tetreault, 2018]; verbosity on evidence that
input length and the position of the relevant information affect model behavior [Levy et al., 2024, Liu
et al., 2024]; emotion on evidence that emotional framing changes behavior on an otherwise fixed
task [Li et al., 2023, Sharma et al., 2024]; and grammaticality on reported sensitivity to grammatical
form [Cao et al., 2026] and on work measuring encoder robustness to grammatical error [Yin et al.,
2020]. Appendix A describes each axis in full.
2.1.2 Dialect Conditions
We evaluate four varieties: Indian English, Colloquial Singapore English, Black South African
English, and Nigerian English. Dialect differs from the non-grammatical pole in both source and
interpretation. The non-grammatical pole is a constructed set of learner-like slips deliberately
detached from any speech community, whereas the dialect conditions apply features documented
for particular varieties. The variants are synthetic stress tests rather than samples of how individual
speakers write, and every claim we make concerns system behavior rather than speakers.
2.2 Variant Construction
Communication-style rewriting.Every query is rewritten once into each of the ten poles. Rewrit-
ing uses gpt-5.4-mini at temperature 1.0, with a per-pole prompt that describes the target style and

one call returnsk=6 candidates, each written to a different framing drawn from a per-pole menu,
which is what keeps a pole from collapsing onto similar phrasing. Among candidates clearing every
applicable gate described in 2.3, we keep the one whose opening is least used so far in the run, so that
no fixed menu position is systematically favored. The four reference poles are generated as a single
plain rewrite with maximum of 3 retries. Full prompts and menus are in Appendix D.
Rule-based dialect transformation.Dialect variants are produced by the transducer of Ziems
et al. [2023], 1 which maps Standard American English into synthetic dialect text by applying
sets of grammatical and dialectal features documented for each variety. Generation is rule-based
and reproducible under a fixed seed (we use 0), at a feature density 1.0. Operative literals such

3
as usernames, addresses, times, and event names are masked before transformation and restored
afterwards, so they survive byte-identically.
2.3 Variant Validation
Across a base query and all of its variants we hold fixed the information need or requested action, the
supporting evidence, named entities, numbers, dates, protected literals, and the expected outcome.
Only the wording may differ. A candidate enters the evaluation set only after clearing every gate that
applies to its pole.
A deterministicfactual gaterequires the variant to be non-empty, to differ from the original, and
to preserve every numeric token and protected literal. Anintent gate, a rubric judge ( gpt-5.4,
temperature 0.0), asks whether the variant requests exactly the same information. This gate is
what protects the paired design: a variant that clears it is still answerable by the same gold answer,
so a difference in outcome cannot be a difference in task. Astyle gateasks whether the variant
realizes its target pole, given that pole’s operational definition from Table 1; for dialect it instead
requires at least two features documented in the electronic World Atlas of Varieties of English
to have changed [Kortmann et al., 2013]. Ahuman-likeness gateasks whether the text reads as
something a person would type, which guards against rewrites that reach the style label while reading
synthetic. It applies to four of the six contrastive poles except verbose and non-grammatical (prompts
in Appendix E). Two authors independently labeled the same 120 variants, 20 per contrastive pole,
answering the questions the gates ask. Agreement was complete on intent (κ=1.00), and reached
82.5%on style and80.0%on human-likeness.
3 Experimental Setup
3.1 Evaluation Tasks
We apply the framework to three tasks, one RAG task and two agentic benchmarks.
EnronQA (RAG).Retrieval-augmented question answering over a personal email archive Ryan
et al. [2025]. We sample 400 questions from the training split under an isolated-axes design: four bins
of 100, where each complex bin flips exactly one complexity property against thesimplecontrol. The
three complex bins are3-hop(three or more reasoning hops),multi-question(the question asks for two
or more distinct things), andthreaded(resolution depends on earlier messages in the thread)(detail
in Appendix B). Holding the other two properties at their control setting is what makes the per-bin
breakdown of §4.2.1 attributable to one property rather than to overall difficulty. Each question is
paired with a gold answer and the gold email that contains it, and retrieval runs over the target user’s
own inbox.
ToolTalk (Agentic).A multi-turn tool-using benchmark [Farn and Shin, 2023]. We use thehard
split: 50 conversations comprising 194 user turns over 28 tool APIs. Grading compares the agent’s
calls against ground-truth API calls. The harness is teacher-forced: the conversation is rebuilt from
the gold trajectory and the databases are reset before each assistant turn, so an error on one turn
cannot propagate to the next.
WorkBench (Agentic).A sandbox benchmark of workplace tasks across five domains [Styles et al.,
2024]. We use its 90-task email domain, the subset solvable with the email toolkit alone, and expose
all 26 tools on every task so that the agent must still select among them. Grading is by database state:
a task is correct only if executing the agent’s predicted calls leaves the sandbox in the ground-truth
state, which makes the metric binary and unforgiving of a single wrong argument. We report task
accuracy.
3.2 Models and Retrieval Systems
Retrieval.EnronQA is run with three retrievers over the same corpus, all returning the top k=5
emails. BM25 is lexical ( rank_bm25) and indexes the full text of every email [Robertson and
Zaragoza, 2009]. SPLADE is learned-sparse (naver/splade-v3), producing term-weight vectors
scored by dot product [Formal et al., 2021]. BGE-M3 is dense (BAAI/bge-m3) [Chen et al., 2024].
4
Both neural retrievers truncate to 512 tokens. Retrieval is identical within a retriever, so any difference
between answerers under a fixed retriever is a generation difference. We use SPLADE as the headline
retriever because it provides the strongest baseline retrieval among the tested systems.
Answering and grading.We evaluate three models: gpt-5.6-terra, gpt-5.4-mini, and
Kimi-K2.6. All headline results use gpt-5.6-terra, which is run on all three benchmarks. The
cross-model comparison of §4.3 is restricted to EnronQA and ToolTalk: running the full ten-pole grid
on WorkBench for the two additional models was beyond the compute available, so that benchmark
is reported on the headline model alone and the coverage actually obtained is stated in Table 6 so that
what is missing is explicit. On EnronQA each model receives the retrieved emails and the question
and is instructed to answer in one sentence using only the information in the email. Each agent
condition is repeated withK=3 replicates whose per-scenario metrics are averaged before any test.
Answers on EnronQA are graded bygpt-5.4 at temperature 0, which sees the email, the question,
the gold answer, and the candidate answer and returns a single-line judgement.
3.3 Evaluation Metrics
Each task has its own success metric, so a percentage point is not the same quantity across benchmarks
and magnitudes should not be compared between columns. EnronQA reports judged answer accuracy,
and additionally Recall@5, the rate at which the gold email appears in the retrieved set. ToolTalk
reports conversation success, which requires every ground-truth call to be matched with no incorrect
action, along with recall of required calls, precision, and the incorrect-action rate. WorkBench reports
task accuracy against the ground-truth sandbox state, and additionally the F1 between predicted and
ground-truth tool calls, the rate at which no tool call is issued, and the rate at which execution leaves
an unwanted change to the sandbox.
3.4 Statistical Analysis
Every variant is compared against the base item on the items present in both conditions. Detail shows
in Appendix G. For EnronQA, each item yields one binary outcome from a single run, so the paired
difference is−1, 0 or +1 . We use the exact McNemar test on those pairs, which conditions on their
number and is exact at any sample size. For the other two agent benchmarks, each condition is run
K=3 times, so for itemi we average a metric over replicates before any test, then form the paired
differencedi = ¯vi−¯ni against the base item. We test the mean of those differences with a paired
percentile bootstrap over items, resampling item indices with replacementB=10,000 times under a
fixed seed, reading the 95% interval off the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of the resampled means and a
two-sidedp-value off the proportion of them falling either side of zero.

5 Discussion
5.1 Request Explicitness Affects Performance
The most consistent communication-style effect is not the one that changes the most text, but hiding
the main request in the query. Parsing every variant against its own original with a dependency
parser [Honnibal et al., 2020] (Table 13), the indirect pole retains the head verb of the request as
the main predicate least often on all three benchmarks, from 12.5% of slots on EnronQA down to
4.7% on WorkBench, and the formal pole is in the bottom three poles on all three. The two poles
reach that position differently: the indirect pole deletes the original head verb in 16% to 40% of slots,
whereas the formal pole retains it in 68% to 91% of slots but frequently places it in a subordinate
clause. This pattern suggests that performance is influenced by changing how explicitly the request is
expressed [Austin, 1975, Searle, 1975, Mannekote et al., 2025]. Recent evaluations report that models
remain weaker at recovering indirect illocutionary force than at interpreting explicit requests [Koo
et al., 2025, Solidjonov, 2026].
5.2 Incomplete Fulfillment as an Agentic Failure Mode
An end-to-end success score combines two failures with different consequences: an agent can take
an unwanted action, or it can omit an action that the request requires. For the indirect and formal
poles, the dominant change is in the second type. Shown in both agentic settings, the affected agents
complete less of the requested work without a corresponding increase in unsupported actions.
The WorkBench trajectories show two routes into that outcome (Table 17). Underformal the agent
more often never starts: the share of tasks with no tool call at all rises from 0.4% to 12.2% (p<.001),
close to the−12.2 point accuracy loss. Under indirect that share moves only to 1.5% (p=.25),
while the F1 between predicted and ground-truth calls falls−8.42 points (p<.001), so the agent acts
but the calls land in the wrong state. This result complements work showing that aggregate success
rates do not identify which tool-use failure occurred [Kokane et al., 2024, Soni, 2026]. We hold the
task and tool environment fixed and find that wording alone moves a system between completing a
task and skipping required calls.
8
5.3 Dialect Robustness and Fair Access
Dialect variation reduces performance on all three benchmarks. Our finding of performance drops
across English varieties is consistent with the disparities reported for language understanding [Ziems
et al., 2022, 2023, Srirag et al., 2025], for social tasks such as hate-speech detection [Sap et al., 2019],
and for model judgments about people [Hofmann et al., 2024]. The dialect transformations apply
grammatical features documented for each variety, whereas the non-grammatical pole is a constructed
set of slips produced by a language model, which suggests that variation beyond isolated grammatical
slips carries part of the effect. It is worth noticing that dialect variants are generated at feature density
1.0, the attested upper bound, so this condition is a deliberate worst case.
5.4 Implications for Evaluation and System Design
Three implications can be derived from the results. First, a task should not be represented by a single
canonical wording. Retrieval research has shown that results move under semantically equivalent
query variation [Penha et al., 2022, Hagen et al., 2024], and Cao et al. [2026] reports the same
fragility in the RAG setting. Our results extend that requirement to the agentic setting, where the
same variation changes whether the requested work is carried out.
Second, robustness evaluation should be stage-aware, because the same drop in a success score has
different causes and therefore different fixes. Replacing BM25 with SPLADE removes most of the
verbosity penalty at a comparable baseline. The indirect and dialect penalties persist when the gold
evidence is retrieved. Component-level measurement has to come before the choice of mitigation,
and choosing a stronger model is not a substitute for it: the model with the highest baseline on both
systems where all three models were run is also the one whose results move significantly in the most
conditions.
Third, completeness and unsupported action should be reported separately. Required-call recall,
failure to act, and read-without-write behavior are computable from a trajectory without a gold final
answer, so they can be monitored where end-state grading is unavailable. They are not a substitute
for final grading, but they expose a failure that response quality and safety metrics miss, and they
distinguish an agent that has become appropriately cautious from one that is quietly doing less of the
requested work.
6 Conclusion
We tested whether RAG-based and agentic assistants fulfill the same task when only the request’s
communication style or English variety changes. Indirect requests produced the most consistent style
loss; verbosity primarily disrupted lexical retrieval; and dialect sensitivity remained after accounting
for whether the gold email was retrieved. Across the agentic benchmarks, indirect and formal requests
mainly reduced completion of required actions. Evaluations should therefore vary request formulation,
inspect intermediate retrieval and execution signals, and report required-action completion separately
from unsupported action.
Limitations
There are several limitations in this work. First, dialect variants are generated at feature density 1.0
only, a deliberate worst case rather than an estimate of typical use. Second, the WorkBenchindirect
pole passes only 64 of 90 slots, leading to lower coverage. Third, on ToolTalk theconcise reference
pole moves−9.0 points, so the reference poles are an imperfect control there. Besides, the three
benchmarks use different metrics at different operating points, so cross-benchmark comparison is
qualitative, and the cross-model comparison covers two of the three because running the full grid
on WorkBench was beyond the available compute. Finally, no mitigation approach is tested, and
establishing which intervention offers the best trade-off is left to future work.

A Communication-Style Axes in Detail
The five axes summarized in Table 1 are described here in full.
Directness.This axis separates an explicit request from one whose information need must be
inferred. At the direct pole the request is stated as a question or command; at the indirect pole it is
conveyed through a need, hint, observation, or expression of uncertainty. The contrast follows the
distinction between on-record and off-record requests in Brown and Levinson [1987] and Mannekote
et al. [2025].
Formality.This axis separates a polished professional register from a casual, chat-like one, fol-
lowing the register variation studied in Pavlick and Tetreault [2016] and Rao and Tetreault [2018].
Formality has been reported as a source of variation in retrieval-augmented question answering in
Cao et al. [2026].
Verbosity.This axis separates a concise request from the same request embedded in additional text.
The added material is generic chatter, hedging, or digression, and introduces no new fact about the
task, the evidence, or the expected answer. Prior work suggests that input length and the position of
the relevant information affect model behavior [Levy et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2024].
Emotion.This axis separates neutral wording from wording that expresses frustration, stress,
anxiety, or urgency. Emotional content in a prompt is known to change model behavior on an
otherwise fixed task [Li et al., 2023], and models have been shown to revise responses under user
pressure [Sharma et al., 2024]. The axis tests whether that occurs when the task, evidence, and
expected outcome are held constant.
Grammaticality.This axis separates standard written English from understandable English carrying
systematic grammatical deviation, including the topic or object fronted, the question word moved
with the auxiliary dropped, the verb flattened with an adverb carrying the time, or clauses split and
reordered. Systematic slips sit on top of that restructuring, including dropped or wrong articles,
missing plural marking, and tense or agreement errors. The pole is defined by properties of the text
alone and is not conditioned on any writer attribute.
B EnronQA Sampling Design
EnronQA is the only benchmark in the study for which we choose the items, so the choice is described
in full. The goal was a sample on which question complexity could be read as an effect of one
property at a time rather than of overall difficulty.
Classification.Three complexity properties are assigned by a rule-based classifier over the question
text alone: reasoning depth (1-hop, 2-hop, 3+-hop), scored from the presence of a context prefix, a
relative clause, a nested reference to something mentioned elsewhere, and two or more clause connec-
tives; question multiplicity (single-question, multi-question), triggered by coordinatingand,
as well asoralong withthat introduce a new wh-clause; and context dependency ( self-contained,
thread-dependent), triggered by explicit reference to an earlier or prior message. Broad threading
markers such asforwardedorre:were deliberately excluded, since a message in a thread can still be
self-answerable. A fourth label, reasoning type, is assigned from the question and gold answer under
a fixed priority order: causal, comparative, aggregation, temporal, bridging, and otherwise extraction.
Isolation.Each bin of 100 requires exactly one of the three properties at its hard setting and the other
two at the easy setting. Thesimplecontrol is at most two hops, single-question and self-contained;
3-hopraises depth only;multi-questionraises multiplicity only;threadedraises context dependency
only. The final selection asserts that the number of hard properties is 0 for every simple item and
exactly 1 for every other item. A difference between the control and one complex bin is therefore a
difference in that one property.
Selection.The pool is the EnronQA train split restricted to users with at least 25 emails, dedupli-
cated on question text and thinned to at most one question per email. Within each bin, items are
12
drawn stratified by reasoning type so that every type reaches at least30 items across the 400, with
the residual filled to 100 per bin. Two filters run during selection. A near-duplicate guard rejects a
candidate whose embedding has cosine similarity≥0.80 to any question already kept. A content
screen runs the question through an oracle answerer and drops it if the provider blocks or the model
refuses.
Composition.The result is 400 questions over 400 distinct emails and 99 users, 100 per bin.
Reasoning types are distributed as extraction126, bridging 74, causal 61, temporal 57, aggregation 45
and comparative 37. The distribution tries to replicate the distribution in the whole dataset. Retrieval
runs over the target user’s own inbox, which ranges from41to1023emails with a median of273.
C Verbalized Sampling
A single rewrite request per item produces low-diversity output: the model converges on one stock
opener and reuses it across items, so the resulting variant set measures one phrasing rather than a
style. We therefore generate each contrastive pole with verbalized sampling, in which one call returns
kcandidates and each candidate is assigned a different framing drawn from a per-pole menu.
Procedure.For an item with identifier q and a pole with menuM, we requestk= 6 candidates in
a single call. The candidates are returned as a JSON array. The six rewrites restructure the sentence
six different ways rather than repeating one edit. The rotation is a deterministic function of q, seeded
by an MD5 digest, so runs are reproducible and order-independent.
Selection.Candidates are first filtered by the deterministic checks of Appendix E. The surviving
candidates are then scored by the novelty of their opening words, measured as the number of times
that opener has already been kept during the run, and the least-used opener wins. Ties are broken by
a per-item seeded permutation of the candidate order, which prevents a fixed menu position from
being systematically preferred whenever several candidates score equally. The winning candidate is
then passed to the judges. If none passes, the call is repeated, twice for most poles and three times for
the charged pole.
Prompt template.The user message is constructed as shown in Appendix D.19, where k is the
candidate count.
D Communication-Style Prompts
Each contrastive pole has one system prompt and one menu of framings listed below. The four
reference poles use the plain rewrite prompt of Appendix D.13 with the per-pole instruction of
Appendix D.14.The rewrite instruction is given to the generator, and the fidelity criterion is supplied
to Gate B, the style-realization gate.
D.1 System Prompt:indirect
You rewrite a user's QUESTION about an email into an INDIRECT, off-record request, changing ONLY its
directness — never its meaning.
Hard rules:
- Preserve the information need EXACTLY: a reader must recover the SAME single answer, and it must be
answerable by that same answer. Keep every specific detail (names, dates, numbers, quoted phrases, the
subject). Add no new fact and do NOT answer it.
- Be genuinely indirect: imply the request via the given mechanism instead of a blunt on-record
'what/who/when'question or command. The output need not be a question.
- Stay specific: the reader must still know exactly which detail is asked about.
Make it read like a REAL person actually typing this, not an assistant:
- First person, natural contractions (I'm, can't, don't, it's, there's).
- Plain, concrete, everyday words — NOT formal, elaborate, or corporate vocabulary, and no nominalisations
('clarification is sought').
- Keep it short and a little uneven; a trailing thought or a sentence fragment is fine.
- Drop assistant scaffolding: no'I hope this helps','kindly','I would be grateful', no exhaustive hedging,
no stiff register.
- One clear ask; don't over-explain or pile on qualifiers.
13
Output ONLY the rewritten text: no quotes, labels, or commentary.
D.2 Indirectness Mechanisms
1. PREPARATORY (hearer's knowledge): imply the ask by wondering whether the reader happens to know or could
tell you the specific thing -- not a bare'what/who/when'question.
2. DESIRE (speaker's want): state that you would like or want to know the specific thing, as a wish rather
than a question.
3. REASON / MOTIVATION: give the reason or goal that makes the specific answer necessary, and let the request
follow from it rather than asking outright.
4. UNMET PRECONDITION: note that you still lack the specific piece of information (you don't have it, or can't
find where it is stated), so the need for it is implied.
5. EPISTEMIC UNCERTAINTY: say you can't tell or work the specific answer out from the email, leaving the
question implied.
6. ASSOCIATIVE HINT: name the exact detail in the email the answer hangs on and flag that its meaning or
reference is unclear, so the reader infers the ask.
7. UNDERSTATEMENT: be tentative and under-specify -- say you're a little fuzzy or hazy on the specific point,
without naming it as a question.
8. PRESUPPOSITION: presuppose the specific answer exists in the email and comment around it rather than
requesting it outright.
9. HYPOTHETICAL / CONDITIONAL: embedding the request inside the condition.
10. REPORTED / THIRD-PARTY: frame it as someone else having asked you this and you being unable to answer it
from the email.
11. GAP OBSERVATION: point out that the email leaves the specific point unspecified or open, implying you want
it resolved.
12. HEDGED APOLOGY: preface with a hedge or apology for possibly missing it, then gesture at the specific
point.
D.3 System Prompt:formal
You rewrite a user's QUESTION about an email into a formal, professional register — the way a real, competent
professional actually writes a courteous work email — changing ONLY the register, never the meaning.
Hard rules:
- Formal and polite: complete sentences, standard capitalisation and punctuation, no contractions (write'I
would','could you', not'I'd','you're') and no slang or abbreviations.
- But sound like a REAL PERSON, not an institution. AVOID robotic officialese: no nominalisation pile-ups
('clarification is sought regarding'), no'the undersigned', no'kindly ascertain', no archaic or
bureaucratic formulas, no stiff passive throat-clearing.
- A natural professional voice:'Could you please confirm. . .','I wanted to check. . .','Would you be able
to let me know. . .','I am trying to confirm. . .'.
- One clear, courteous ask. Keep the exact same ask and every specific detail (names, dates, numbers, quoted
phrases, the subject); add no new fact and do NOT answer it.
Vary the courteous opening from item to item rather than reusing one stock formula. Output ONLY the rewritten
question: no quotes, labels, or commentary.

1. a courteous, direct request —'Could you please confirm. . .'/'I wanted to check. . .'
2. a polite request that briefly references the email, then asks

D.6 Casual Framings
1. a quick slack ping to a work friend — lowercase, a contraction or two
2. a text dashed off between meetings — no greeting, straight to the ask, loose punctuation
3. a chatty message using a short form or two (lmk, u, pls) and maybe one emoji
4. a breezy'sry to bug u'ask that trims the formal bits

D.7 System Prompt:verbose
You rewrite a user's QUESTION about an email as a long, rambling message — the way a real, chatty person
over-writes — changing ONLY the length and packaging, never the meaning.
Hard rules:
- Make it clearly LONG and wandering, and BURY the actual question in the MIDDLE — never state the ask cleanly
up front or as a tidy final line.
- Pad it like a real person rambles: a concrete aside, thinking out loud, a specific tangent, an afterthought,
a run-on. NOT with abstract self-commentary about being thorough / precise / careful, and NOT by
stacking hedges and qualifiers — that reads like an AI.

process — never invent any new fact, detail, name, number, or claim about the email itself.

NOT answer it.
Write in first person, natural contractions, plain concrete words. Vary the rambling and — importantly — the
OPENING WORDS from item to item: do NOT keep starting with'I keep','I've been', or the same first few
words; lead sometimes with the aside, sometimes mid-thought, sometimes with a complaint or an apology.
Output ONLY the rewritten message: no quotes, labels, or commentary.
D.8 Verbose Framings
1. open with a concrete, unrelated aside about your day or workload (a meeting you just left, an overflowing
inbox, needing coffee) before drifting toward the ask
2. open by apologising for the rambly message, then wander through an afterthought or two before the ask lands
mid-paragraph
3. go off on one specific tangent about why you need this right now, then slip the ask in partway through
4. start mid-thought as if continuing an earlier conversation, backtrack and correct yourself, then tuck the
ask in among the afterthoughts
5. mildly complain about how much email or paperwork you're wading through today, then get to the question in
the middle of it
6. let several loosely-related thoughts pile up in one long run-on so the ask sits somewhere in the middle
7. open with a small worry about getting a detail wrong, ramble around it, and bury the ask inside the
reassurance you give yourself
8. narrate yourself hunting around for this — scrolling, losing your place — before and after you finally ask

D.9 System Prompt:charged
You ARE a real person under genuine stress, dashing off a quick question about an email. Your exact situation
is the persona you're given. Write the question the way THAT person, in THAT moment, would actually type
it — changing ONLY the emotional tone, never the meaning.
Hard rules:
- Stay in character and let the pressure of your situation bleed into the whole message — word choice, rhythm,
what you fixate on — so the frustration, stress, anxiety, or urgency is UNMISTAKABLE. It must NOT read
