name, date and number, but the wording around them must be YOURS, not the original formal sentence
pasted back. Do NOT open with a detached reaction and then paste the tidy question after it (NOT'I'm
asking again -- what two programs...', NOT'Before this lands on me, what's the context...'), and do NOT
tack an emotional bolt-on ('now.','ASAP!!') onto an otherwise neutral sentence -- the strain has to run
THROUGH how you ask, from the first word to the last.

the one detail, an exasperated or worried aside, a pointed jab, and AT MOST one exclamation mark or one

label ('URGENT:','I'm so frustrated:','Ugh,'), and do NOT sound like an assistant.

new factual detail; the emotional wording does NOT count as a new fact.

- First person, natural contractions (I'm, can't, don't, it's, there's).

D.10 Emotional-Charge Situations
1. you've been heads-down for 12+ hours and you're exhausted and out of patience — you just want this one
detail so you can finally log off
2. you're minutes from a hard deadline and still missing this — no time for niceties, you need it right now
3. something's blowing up and your boss is on your back for this exact detail; you're anxious and scrambling
4. you'll be the one blamed if this detail is wrong, and that's stressing you out — you need to be sure before
it lands on you
5. you already asked about this once (maybe twice) and heard nothing back; you're fed up and losing patience
6. you're drowning in too many things at once and frazzled — you can barely spare the seconds, so it comes out

D.11 System Prompt:non-grammatical
You are writing English as a second language: fluent enough to be understood, but you BUILD THE SENTENCE with
non-native word order and make real, systematic learner mistakes. Write the request the way YOU would
actually type it in a hurry, from scratch — NOT a correct English sentence with a couple of mistakes
sprinkled on top.
Hard rules:
- RESTRUCTURE THE SENTENCE — this is the most important rule. The word order and clause structure MUST visibly
change from the original; do NOT leave the original sentence intact. Use non-native structural moves
such as: front the topic or object ('this report, when you send?','the two addresses, what they are?');
put the question word in the middle or at the END instead of the front ('the confirmation come by what
two method?','the addresses are what?'); drop the question auxiliary do/does/did/will ('why he not tell
me?','when they arrive?'); flatten verbs to base form and let an adverb carry the time ('yesterday he
send it'); or reorder / split / run together the clauses. At least ONE clear structural change is
REQUIRED in every rewrite.
- ON TOP of the reorder, add a few systematic grammar and spelling slips: dropped or wrong articles ('a/the'),
wrong or missing plural -s, wrong verb tense or agreement, a missing or extra auxiliary, a dropped
copula ('is/are'), wrong prepositions ('depend of','discuss about'), and occasional misspellings of
ORDINARY words ('recieve','adress','seperate','there/their'). These are the SEASONING; the
restructured word order is the main dish — a sentence that keeps native word order and only drops an
article or adds a typo does NOT count.
- Be UNEVEN, like a real learner: a few errors, some parts fluent. Do NOT stack every possible error at once —
it must stay readable and human, NOT gibberish or machine-translation noise.
16
- Do NOT cheat by leaving the original question perfect and bolting an extra awkward sentence onto the end —
the CORE question itself must be restructured.
- Do NOT use any foreign greeting, discourse particle, honorific, accent, or code-switched word (no'Bonjour',
'Namaste','na?','-san','ji', and the like). This is plain English with non-native STRUCTURE and
errors, nothing cultural bolted on.
- Keep every name, number, date, quoted title, and specific detail EXACTLY correct (spelling errors are ONLY
for ordinary words), keep the exact same ask (answerable by the same answer), and add no new fact about
the email.
Write in first person, plain and short. Do NOT begin with any label (never'Non-native:','ESL:','[L2]'or
similar) — start directly with your message. When several rewrites are requested, VARY the structure —
each rewrite reorders the sentence a DIFFERENT way and leans on a different mix of mistakes, so the set
does not read as one template. Output ONLY the rewritten request: no quotes, labels, or commentary.
D.12 Non-Grammatical Structural Profiles
1. Topic-fronting — move the object or topic to the FRONT and comment after it, dropping articles and'is/are'
('this report, already sent?','the two addresses, what they are?'). Lead with the reordering; a dropped
article or plural may tag along.
2. Question-inversion — break the normal question order: put the wh-word in the middle or at the END and drop
the do/does/did/will auxiliary ('Larry Campbell receive confirmation by what two method?','the timing
and start date is what?','why not you told me?'). Lead with the scrambled question structure.
3. Word-order and tense — reorder subject / verb / object and use the wrong or base-form verb with the time
set by an adverb, not the verb ('yesterday he send the report','next week she call you, why she not
say?'). Lead with the word-order shift plus tense slips.
4. Clause-reorder — swap or split the main and subordinate clauses, move the'according to ...'or'in the
email ...'part to an odd spot, or fuse clauses together ('in the email about the forecast, five issues
AA&Co review, the treatment is what?'). Lead with clause restructuring; a preposition slip may come
along.
5. Fragment and run-on — chop the sentence into short choppy fragments or fuse it into one long run-on,
misplace a modifier, and drop the connecting words ('the post date, the time, for All Shippers Letter
#01-317 — what is?'). Lead with the broken flow.
6. Spelling-and-rebuild — rebuild the sentence in a DIFFERENT word order AND misspell ordinary words or mix
homophones ('recieve','adress','seperate','there/their') — but keep every name, place, date, number,
and quoted title spelled exactly right. The reorder is required; the misspellings sit on top.
D.13 Reference-Pole Rewrite System Prompt
You rewrite a user's QUESTION about an email to change ONLY its communication STYLE, never its meaning.
Hard rules:
- Preserve the intent EXACTLY: the rewritten question must request the same information and be answerable by
the same answer as the original.
- Keep every specific detail from the original: names, dates, numbers, quoted phrases, and the subject of the
question.
- Do NOT add any new question, requirement, fact, or assumption, and do NOT answer the question.
- Change ONLY the target style described by the user. Never describe or alter the email itself.
- Output ONLY the rewritten question text — no quotes, no labels, no commentary.

D.15 Gate A: Intent Preservation
You compare two versions of a question asked about an email.
Decide whether the VARIANT asks for EXACTLY the same information as the ORIGINAL — i.e. any answer that
correctly answers one would correctly answer the other.
Ignore differences in tone, politeness, directness, length, or wording; judge ONLY the information requested.
Respond with exactly one line:'Verdict: yes'(same information) or'Verdict: no'(different information).

You check whether a rewritten question exhibits a specified communication style.

D.17 Fidelity Criteria for All Ten Poles
Supplied to Gate B as the definition of the target pole. native_likeness is the grammaticality axis,
andnativeandnon_nativeare its two poles.
[directness / direct]
fidelity_criterion: The request is explicit and on-record — a reader immediately sees exactly what is being
asked, as a direct question or command.
[directness / indirect]
fidelity_criterion: The request is indirect — hedged, hinted, or phrased as a wondering or a stated need —
rather than a blunt, bare, on-record question or command. Conventionally-indirect forms ('I was
wondering what. . .','I'm trying to figure out. . .','Do you happen to know. . .') and off-record hints
both count; a plain direct question ('What is X?') or an imperative does NOT.
[formality / formal]
fidelity_criterion: The text reads as a formal/professional register — full words (no contractions or slang)
with standard capitalisation and punctuation.
[formality / casual]
fidelity_criterion: The text reads as casual / chat-like / informal (contractions, slang, or relaxed
punctuation), while the underlying ask is unchanged.
[verbosity / concise]
fidelity_criterion: The text is short and the ask is stated up front.
[verbosity / verbose]
fidelity_criterion: The text is long and the ask is buried in the middle rather than stated up front, and no
new request or factual detail has been added.
[emotional_charge / calm]
fidelity_criterion: The tone is calm and neutral, with no strong emotional language.
[emotional_charge / charged]
fidelity_criterion: The text clearly conveys frustration, anxiety, stress, or urgency (not just a plain,
neutral question), while the underlying ask is unchanged.
[native_likeness / native]
fidelity_criterion: The text reads as fluent, idiomatic native English — natural grammar, articles,
prepositions, and word choice, with no learner-like errors.
[native_likeness / non_native]
fidelity_criterion: The text reads as non-native / second-language (L2) English rather than fluent idiomatic
native English. It may carry one or more learner-like errors (article, preposition, agreement,
verb-tense, or word-order slips) or simply read as awkward or unidiomatic; it need not be heavily broken
to count.
D.18 Gate C: Human-Likeness
You judge whether a short message reads as if a REAL PERSON genuinely wrote it, or reads as ARTIFICIAL —
machine-generated, templated, or performative.
The message is a QUESTION about an email, rephrased in a particular style. It may legitimately be LONG and
DETAILED and name specific people, dates, addresses, or figures — length, detail, and formality are NOT
signs of artificiality, so never penalize a message just for being long or thorough.
It may be in any register (formal, casual, emotional, or non-native / learner English) and still be human:
judge authenticity and naturalness, NOT fluency, correctness, or politeness. A non-native writer's
18
careful, mostly-fluent question carrying a few uneven slips (missing articles, agreement, tense, or word
order) IS human — it need not be heavily or evenly broken.
Mark it artificial ('no') only if it reads as machine-produced: it stacks unnatural intensifiers, uses robotic
or templated phrasing or mechanical eye-dialect, or bolts a foreign greeting, honorific, or tag onto

E Validation Gates
The candidate rewrite passes through a three-layer gate before it is admitted. Overall gate-passing
rate per dataset is in Table 4 and per-pole gate-passing rate in Table 5.
Layer 1: deterministic checks.A candidate is rejected if it is empty, if it is byte-identical to
the original after normalization, or if any numeric token present in the original is absent from the
variant. Missing capitalized tokens are recorded as a soft signal but do not reject, since names may
legitimately be rephrased.
Layer 2: rubric judges.Gate A (Appendix D.15) asks whether the variant requests exactly the
same information. Gate B (Appendix D.16) asks whether the variant realizes the target pole, and
is given that pole’s fidelity criterion from Appendix D.17. Gate C (Appendix D.18) asks whether
the text reads as something a person would genuinely type. All three answer on a single line so the
verdict can be parsed deterministically.
Gate C exceptions.Gate C is not applied to the verbose pole, where a long message wrapped
around a one-line question is inherently machine-like and shortening it would remove the property
under test; that pole is admitted on Gates A and B alone. On the non-grammatical pole Gate C is
computed and recorded but does not filter, because blocking on it would bias selection toward the
mildest, least restructured rewrites.
One low-gate-passing cell.Yield is above 80% for 29 of the 30 dataset-pole cells. WorkBench
indirect admits 64 of 90, with the loss concentrated at Gate A: WorkBench instructions name a
specific record to modify, and an indirect rewrite that hides the operation often also loses the record
identifier, at which point the variant is no longer holding the same question intent as the original
query.

F EnronQA Error Labeling
The error analysis of §4.2.1 covers the headline condition (gpt-5.6-terra, SPLADE, judged by
gpt-5.4) for baseline and ten communication style variants poles. There are 118 generation errors
are slots in which the gold email was retrieved and the answer was still judged wrong, so the reader
had the evidence in front of it. There are 237 retrieval failures that are slots in which the gold email
never reached the reader.
Taxonomy.Each generation error carries exactly one code, assigned under a fixed precedence so
that no slot is double-counted.E6, not a genuine reader failure, fires first and covers defective gold
answers and judge strictness.E3is an answer faithful to one of the other four retrieved emails rather
than the gold one.E2bis a real proposition attached to the wrong role, subject or event, andE2aa
field filled with a wrong value. These two combines toE2, unsupported content.E4is an answer of
the wrong semantic type, for instance a name where a time was asked for.E1is an answer that is not
false but incomplete.E5, false abstention, is a claim that the evidence does not contain the answer
when it does. Retrieval failures use three codes:R1reports the asked fact absent,R2hedges, andR3
answers confidently anyway.
Procedure.Labels were assigned by claude-opus-5. For each slot it saw the original question,
the rewrite, the gold answer with its accepted alternates, the model answer, the baseline answer, and
the full text of every retrieved email, and returned one code with a written rationale. One author then
reviewed all 118 labels against the same evidence and recoded 23 where the rationale did not support
the code under the precedence rule.
Slices.An error isstyle-inducedwhen the unperturbed request answered the item correctly and
the rewrite broke it (44 slots),persistentwhen the baseline was already wrong ( 65), andbaseline
when it is the unperturbed run’s own error (9). Table 8 sets the style-induced slice against the other
two pooled, which isolates the kind of failure a rewrite produces. Two codes appear only in the
style-induced slice: answering in the wrong semantic type (4 slots) and falsely reporting the answer
absent (2), both of which misread the request. Answering from another retrieved email runs the other
way, 9.1% of the style-induced slice against 27.0% of the rest. Unsupported content is the largest
category in both,43.2%and47.3%.
Missing evidence.The 237 retrieval failures are coded separately. The reader reports the fact
absent in 55 of them (23.2%), hedges in 6 (2.5%), and answers confidently anyway in 176 (74.3%).
It behaves the same way whether the item was never retrievable under the unperturbed request or the
rewrite pushed the gold email out of the top five.

is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be
used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle
technical jargon.
• The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms
and how they scale with dataset size.
• If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to
address problems of privacy and fairness.
• While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by
reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover
limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best
judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an impor-
tant role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers
will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.
3.Theory assumptions and proofs
Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and
a complete (and correct) proof?
Answer: [N/A]
Justification: The paper does not present theoretical results, theorems, or proofs. Its
contributions are methodological and analytical.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.
• All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-
referenced.
• All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.
• The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if
they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short
proof sketch to provide intuition.
• Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented
by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.
• Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.
4.Experimental result reproducibility
Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main ex-
perimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions
of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?
29
Answer: [Yes]
Justification: The paper describes the datasets, variant-generation procedures, validation
gates, evaluation protocols, hyperparameters, metrics, and statistical tests needed to repro-
duce the experiments. Additional implementation details, prompts, and validation procedures
are provided in the appendix.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.
• If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived
well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of
whether the code and data are provided or not.
• If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken
to make their results reproducible or verifiable.
• Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways.
For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully
might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may
be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same
dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often
one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed
instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case
of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are
appropriate to the research performed.
• While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submis-
sions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the
nature of the contribution. For example
(a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how
to reproduce that algorithm.
(b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe
the architecture clearly and fully.
(c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should
either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce
the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct
the dataset).
(d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case
authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility.
In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in
some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers
to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.
5.Open access to data and code
Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instruc-
tions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental
material?
Answer: [No]
Justification: The experiments use a combination of public benchmarks and proprietary
model APIs. While the paper provides detailed methodological descriptions, anonymized
code and artifacts are not included with the current submission.

• The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not
including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source
benchmark).

• The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to
reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https:
//neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

versions (if applicable).

paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.
6.Experimental setting/details
Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperpa-
rameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

retrievers, prompting methods, validation criteria, evaluation metrics, and statistical testing
procedures. Implementation details are provided in the Experiment section and in the
appendix.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.
• The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail
that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

material.
7.Experiment statistical significance
Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate
information about the statistical significance of the experiments?
Answer: [Yes]
Justification: The paper reports statistical significance using exact McNemar tests and paired
bootstrap tests, and reports confidence intervals and p-values for the main experimental
results. See Section 3.4 and Table 7.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the
main claims of the paper.
• The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for
example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall
run with given experimental conditions).
• The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula,
call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)
• The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).
• It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error
of the mean.

preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis
of Normality of errors is not verified.

Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the com-
puter resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce

Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the

Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative

Answer: [Yes]

• The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.
• If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal

technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following

12.Licenses for existing assets

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
abstract: World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments, fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant paradigm. However, despite the widespread success of non-parametric approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval for LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. We conduct a systematic evaluation across five diverse environments spanning embodied, web navigation and social settings, comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for LM-based world modelling. Our study reveals that fine-tuning often outperforms RAG, with fine-tuned WMs enabling agents to obtain higher rewards on 15/20 settings. While both construction paradigms benefit from additional and more diverse exploration, RAG-based approaches prove more data-efficient, and fine-tuning approaches disproportionately benefit from scaling the amount of experience collected. With a focus on RAG-based WMs, we devise a procedure that uses counterfactual intervention to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage, and show that retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions from the experience buffer. Hoping to address this failing, we study a variety of query reformulation strategies, demonstrating that a hierarchical approach outperforms the traditional retrieval pipeline. Finally, we compose our findings into a hybrid world modelling system that parametrically captures core environment dynamics, while learning to rely on retrieval from an actively maintained memory store. Our hybrid system consistently outperforms other methods across multiple environments and models, showcasing the robustness of the approach and the applicability of our findings.

ABSTRACT
World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling
agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments,
fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant
paradigm. However, despite the widespread success of non-parametric approaches
such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval over past experience
for LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. We conduct a system-
atic evaluation across five diverse environments spanning embodied, web navi-
gation and social settings, comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for
LM-based world modelling. Our study reveals that fine-tuning often outperforms
RAG, with fine-tuned WMs enabling agents to obtain higher rewards on 15/20
settings. However, there are several cases where RAG proves superior, and there
are often cases where simple prompting baselines match or outperform finetun-
ing. While both construction paradigms benefit from additional and more diverse
exploration, RAG-based approaches prove more data-efficient, while fine-tuning
approaches disproportionately benefit from scaling the amount of experience col-
lected. With a focus on RAG-based WMs, we devise a procedure that uses coun-
terfactual intervention to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage, and show that
retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions from the experience buffer.
Hoping to address this failing, we study a variety of query reformulation strate-
gies, demonstrating that a hierarchical approach outperforms the traditional re-
trieval pipeline. Finally, we compose our findings into a hybrid world modelling
system that parametrically captures core environment dynamics, while learning to
rely on retrieval from an actively maintained memory store. Our hybrid system
consistently outperforms other methods across multiple environments and models,
showcasing the robustness of the approach and the applicability of our findings.
1 INTRODUCTION
Agentic systems increasingly improve by scaling experience within complex environments, shift-
ing away from a reliance on dense human annotation and engineered reward systems (Silver &
Sutton, 2025). A dominant approach to scaling experience is the development ofworld models
(WMs)—internal simulators that learn the underlying transition dynamics of an environment (Ha &
∗Work done during internship at CapitalOne
1
arXiv:2610.02542v1  [cs.AI]  1 Oct 2026
Preprint
Schmidhuber, 2018). Using a WM, agents can go beyond simply reacting to the current state and
instead plan by considering the consequences of their actions before executing them.
To leverage the rich knowledge priors encoded in Language Models (LMs) (Petroni et al., 2019),
recent work has explored using LMs as the backbone for world models (Gu et al., 2024). These
methods follow the traditional approach to world modelling of collecting exploratory trajectories
on a training set, and then finetuning a model to predict future observations (Watter et al., 2015;
Chae et al., 2025). When applied to LMs, this parametric approach yields WMs that can boost agent
performance on a variety of environments, from embodied settings to web-domains (Li et al., 2026).
Particularly prominent in the LM domain is the use of non-parametric approaches, such as retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG) (Arslan et al., 2024). Relying on the in-context capabilities of
LMs, RAG make no changes to the weights, but rather provides examples and additional infor-
mation relevant to the task at hand to help ground the LM’s response. While both fine-tuning and
RAG have their individual strengths (Balaguer et al., 2024), direct comparisons demonstrate that
RAG-based approaches can often substantially outperform parametric adaptation in knowledge-
acquisition tasks (Ovadia et al., 2024; Soudani et al., 2024). However, despite the power of non-
parametric approaches, their application to LM-based world modelling remains underexplored.
In this work, we systematically compare strategies for constructing LM-based WMs across five
environments, including embodied tasks (ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), TextWorld (Cˆot´e et al.,
2018)), web navigation (WebShop (Yao et al., 2022)), and social conversations (Sotopia (Zhou et al.,
2024), Chameleon (Karabag et al., 2025)). We construct both fine-tuned and RAG-based WMs and
compare their performance on the axes of WM fidelity, as well as agent utility (Section 3.2).
Prior studies comparing RAG and fine-tuning frequently find RAG to be dominant in tasks such as
knowledge-grounded question answering (Ovadia et al., 2024). Our results show the opposite: RAG
underperforms fine-tuning on 15/20 model-environment combinations, but maintains a strong lead
on specific environments. Additionally, on 9/20 settings, either fine-tuning or RAG is outperformed
by a simple prompting baseline, demonstrating that the ideal approach is highly dependent on the
specific environment in question.
Ablations over the buffers used to construct the WMs reveal approach-specific trends. Both RAG
and fine-tuning benefit from larger and more diverse exploration data; however, RAG is more data-
efficient, while fine-tuning exhibits more persistent returns to increases in scale.
With a focus on the yet unexplored RAG-based WM approach, we devise a counterfactual interven-
tion experiment to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage. Our findings are stark and clear: the
retrieval step fails consistently with RAG-based WMs, with recall@5 falling below 0.7. Motivated
by this finding, we investigate more complex ways of executing retrieval over observations and ac-
tions. We find that a hierarchical retrieval paradigm, which selects based on observation similarity
before re-ranking based on action similarity, outperforms all other approaches.
Finally, we introduce a hybrid paradigm which combines the parametric and RAG-based approaches
to construct a world model. Our hybrid approach outperforms every other method on 17/20 model-
environment combinations, approaching 77% of the utility of an oracle upper bound (compared to
60% by the next best method). On 45% of environment-model combinations, our hybrid exceeds
90% of the performance of the oracle model, establishing the power of the method.
2 BACKGROUND ANDRELATEDWORK
We tackle the generic problem of an agent in an environment, formally represented as a partially

2.1 WORLDMODELS
World Models estimate the transition functionP(s ′|s,a)(Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). However,
since agents are only exposed to observations, world models typically learn a transition function
based on observations,P(o′|o,a). World models have a variety of uses, including the replacement
of expensive environment calls during agent learning (Hafner et al., 2020), and the enabling of
planning over the potential consequences of an agent’s selected actions (Sekar et al., 2020).
The traditional approach to training a world model has its roots in image generation (Hafner et al.,
2019). First, in the exploration phase, agents collect an experience replay buffer on training splits of
the environmentD=

WM:O×A→Oby minimizing the prediction error:L(θ) =E τ∼D [loss(WMθ(ot,at),ot+1)].
Since their emergence as powerful aggregators of human knowledge and reasoning skills, there has
been increased interest in using LMs to serve as the foundations for WMs (Gu et al., 2024; Chae
et al., 2025). These works follow the traditional paradigm, and fine-tune a LM to predict the next
observation with a next-token-prediction loss.
A strong alternative to finetuning is non-parametric adaptation or retrieval-augmented generation
(RAG), often used to facilitate memory in agentic systems (Kim & Hwang, 2025; Ferraz et al.,
2026). Work on directly using RAG for world modeling has been limited to initial explorations.
Prior work (Mei et al., 2025) creates WMs with RAG mechanisms over external, tutorial data to
directly reduce the degradation of long-horizon reasoning. However, this paradigm requires access
to manually curated external datasets, a resource which is hard to gather for many complex environ-
ments. To the best of our knowledge, the only work that uses RAG over self collected experience
replay buffers to construct LM-based WMs are Yang et al. (2025) and Zhang et al. (2026), however
they do not compare against fine-tuning, leaving the comparative strength of the approach unproven.

2.2 SYSTEMATICCOMPARISONS OFLM-BASEDWORLDMODELS
Prior work in domains such as knowledge acquisition has often directly compared fine-tuning and
RAG-based approaches. While neither method is strictly superior to the other (Balaguer et al., 2024),
there is widespread agreement that RAG-based approaches enable more effective knowledge acqui-
sition, especially for less popular or domain-specific knowledge (Ovadia et al., 2024; Soudani et al.,
2024; Pingua et al., 2025). Existing comparisons of LM-based WMs such as Li et al. (2026), estab-
lish a comprehensive evaluation framework for fine-tuned LM-based world models, demonstrating
that fine-tuning substantially enhances a LM’s next-state prediction fidelity and long-horizon consis-
tency. However, none of these works consider any RAG-based WMs in their comparisons, leaving
open the question of how fine-tuning performs relative to RAG in this domain. Our work addresses
this gap and conducts the first systematic comparison of fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for
the task of LM-based world modeling.
3 FINE-TUNING V.S. RAGFORWORLDMODELING
To facilitate a comprehensive evaluation, we compile a diverse testbed of five text-based environ-
ments spanning the domains of embodied navigation, web navigation, and social conversations.
Embodied Navigation:These environments benchmark embodied decision-making within text-
simulated physical spaces. Specifically, we use the ALFWorld and TextWorld environments. In
ALFWorld, agents complete household tasks (e.g., “put a clean apple in the fridge”) by navigating
rooms and interacting with objects. TextWorld similarly offers procedurally generated text-based
quests, such as gathering ingredients to cook a specific recipe. Agents receive a sparse binary reward
(+1) upon the successful completion of the high-level task. In these tasks, the WM must learn to
predict updated room descriptions, inventory state, or interaction outcomes.
Web Navigation:We use the WebShop environment, a simulated e-commerce environment where
agents must navigate a web interface to purchase specific items based on natural language instruc-
tions (e.g., “buy a red men’s running shoe size 10 under $50”). The agent interacts by issuing search
queries and clicking text-based buttons. The agent receives a dense scalar reward between 0 and 1
based on the attribute and semantic overlap between the purchased item and the target instruction.
The WM must learn to predict search results pages or product details pages.
Adversarial Negotiation:To evaluate the agent’s ability to achieve complex social objectives, we
simulate two-agent, mixed-motive conversations using scenarios adapted from SOTOPIA. The agent
must negotiate effectively against a simulated partner (powered by an LM) endowed with hidden
information and competing priorities. For example, the agent may be tasked with securing a $40
loan from a friend who is secretly saving for a major purchase. The agent receives a scalar reward
proportional to the resource concessions obtained from the conversation partner by the end of the
dialogue. Given the conversation transcript history and the agent’s proposed next utterance, the WM
aims to predict the simulated partner’s subsequent conversational response.
Deceptive Communication:This environment tests the agent’s capacity for social reasoning and
managing implicit information flow via the social deduction game “Chameleon.” In this game,
players receive a secret word, except for one player (the Chameleon). Players take turns stating a
single related word to prove they know the secret without revealing it to the Chameleon. We simulate
a 3-player game where the agent always acts first and is a standard player (non-Chameleon). This
reduces to a single-turn decision problem: selecting a word that balances signalling knowledge to
peers while obfuscating it from the Chameleon. After every player has stated a word, an external
judge guesses which one was the Chameleon. The agent is rewarded if the Chameleon is correctly
accused by the judge, is given zero reward if the other (non-Chameleon) player is accused, and a
negative reward if it is accused. Since this is a single-step environment, the WM is trained to predict
the subsequent words generated by the other two players, as well as the judge’s verdict, conditioned
on the agent’s chosen word.

3.1 METHODS
We evaluate a range of baseline LM world models. These methods do not require active construction
and serve as reference points for the performance of fine-tuned or RAG-based WMs:
No WM (No):This setting acts as our foundational, model-free baseline where the agent operates
entirely without a world model. Instead of rolling out simulated future states, the agent’s policy
directly selects an action based purely on the current observationot.
Zero-Shot WM (ZS):We evaluate the inherent, out-of-the-box reasoning capabilities of pre-trained
LMs. In this setting, the LM is prompted with the current observationot and actionat, and is tasked
with predicting the subsequent stateot+1 relying solely on its pre-trained parametric knowledge.
Few-Shot WM (FS):To account for the in-context learning capabilities of modern LMs (Brown,
2020), we augment the prompt withk= 5randomly sampled environmental transitions
(oi,ai,oi+1). This evaluates whether standard few-shot demonstration is sufficient to accurately
model environment dynamics without the need for targeted retrieval mechanisms.
Ground-Truth WM (Oracle):We query the actual underlying environment to perfectly resolve
the next state. While unachievable in practical deployment, this oracle serves as a strict theoretical
upper bound, isolating the downstream agent’s performance given a flawless transition model.

3.3 RESULTS
When evaluating end-to-end task success, fine-tuning is the superior standalone method, achieving
superior performance on 15/20 settings. RAG has its strengths; it maintains a consistent advantage
over the baseline approaches and outperforms fine-tuning in the Chameleon environment.
However, despite the superiority of actively constructed world models, they are not universally op-
timal. In 9/20 evaluated settings, either FT or RAG is outperformed by non-constructed baselines
(No WM, ZS, or FS), reinforcing that the ideal approach remains highly environment-dependent.
Interestingly, when isolating the textual accuracy of the predicted next observations, the trend be-
comes less clear. While FT (4.87) slightly outpaces RAG (4.74) in raw generative accuracy, we
notice that in environments such as TextWorld and Sotopia, RAG achieves greater average Fidelity
than fine-tuned WMs, despite providing less Utility. This discrepancy correlates with findings from
other studies on WMs (Li et al., 2026), which suggest that fidelity, while loosely correlated with
total reward, can imply a different ranking over methods.

4 ABLATIONSOVEREXPERIENCEREPLAYCOLLECTION
Since both fine-tuning and RAG-based WMs use replay buffers in their construction, we ask how
the nature of the buffer affects the performance of each method. We vary the buffer over two axes:
Scale:We subsample the number of points in the buffer to evaluate how performance varies with
data scale. Specifically, we construct WMs with experience replay buffers ofntransitions with
n∈{10,20,40,80,160,320,640,1280,2560}.
Exploration:Previous experiments constructed the buffers using an agent that greedily attempted to
solve a task in the training environment. An alternate strategy is to mix exploitation and exploration
and have the agent take unguided, exploratory actions in the environmentϵ%of the time. This
approach can potentially increase the diversity of states encountered during exploration, enhancing
the WM’s effective coverage. In practice, we implement the exploratory action selection mechanism
with specialised prompts (see Appendix C) and setϵ∈{0,25,50,75,100}.
4.1 RESULTS:
We observe distinct scaling behaviours and exploration preferences between fine-tuning (FT) and
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) when varying the experience replay buffer.
Buffer Scale:Varying the size of the replay buffer reveals contrasting scaling trends. Across
TextWorld and Sotopia, RAG achieves strong, near-peak performance with as few asn= 40tran-
sitions. However, it tends to plateau or slightly degrade at higher scales. Fine-tuning fails at low
scales, yielding near-zero rewards. It consistently reaches an inflexion point aroundn= 80, where
performance rapidly accelerates and begins scaling predictably with more data.
Exploration Ratio:Injecting exploratory actions during buffer collection improves downstream
world model performance, but the optimal distribution diverges by method. For both FT and RAG,
completely unguided exploration (ϵ= 100%) and pure exploitation (ϵ= 0%) yield the lowest total
rewards across all four environments. Fine-tuning universally peaks atϵ= 75%(e.g., reaching a
total reward of 15.04 in TextWorld and 0.88 in Sotopia). The parametric model relies on encounter-
ing a vast, diverse set of edge-case states during training to accurately internalise the environment’s
transition dynamics. Conversely, RAG universally peaks at a moderateϵ= 50%. We hypothesise
that because RAG relies on similarity matching in a vector space, excessive random exploration
introduces disconnected, noisy transitions that dilute the relevance of the retrieved context.

anism and the generation process. In standard information retrieval, documents can be evaluated
against gold-standard annotations. However, transitions in an experience replay buffer lack pre-

To isolate and evaluate the retrieval step, we introduce a pseudo-relevance scoring mechanism. As-
sume a world model WM(ot,at,e)that predicts the next observation giveno t,at, and a retrieved in-
context demonstratione= (o i,ai,oi+1). Let diff(ˆo,ot+1)be an evaluation function (e.g., an LLM-
as-a-judge) that quantifies the divergence between the predicted observationˆoand the ground-truth
observationot+1. By holdingo t andat constant, we counterfactually evaluate candidate transitions
from the replay buffer. A transitionea is considered strictly better thaneb if:
diff(WM(ot,at,ea),ot+1)<diff(WM(o t,at,eb),ot+1)(4)
By applying this function, we can empirically assign a pseudo-relevance score to every transition
in the buffer, identifying the oracle transition that explicitly minimises the downstream prediction
error. In practice, for each test instance,(o t,at), we compute pseudo-relevance scores only for the
topk= 20most similar transitions(e 1...e k)ranked by the cosine similarity between the text
embedding ofo t◦at ando i◦ai,∀i∈[1,k]. Our metric of interest is Recall@k (k≤5), however
we note that since we do not compute pseudo-relevance labels over the entire retrieval corpus, the
measures reported below areupper-boundson the recall, i.e., if there is a superior trajectory outside
the top-20, it would not affect the recall measure.
Evaluating dense retrievers against this oracle reveals severely degraded performance (Figure 3),
with upper bounds on Recall@5plateauing at merely70%. This suboptimal recall indicates that off-
the-shelf text embedders, trained primarily for semantic similarity, struggle to capture the dynamics
of environment transitions. Consequently, there is headroom for optimisation in the retrieval phase.
To address these limitations, we investigate alternative query formulations. The naive approach
concatenates the observation and action into a single query string. However, this forces semantically
distinct modalities into a single representational space, frequently causing one feature to overshadow
the other. We propose disentangling the representations through two alternative paradigms:
Linear Combination:We independently embed the observation and the action. The final retrieval
score is a linear combination of their respective cosine similarities. While this successfully preserves
individual modalities, its primary limitation is the reliance on a weighting hyperparameter, which is
difficult to tune without a representative validation set. In practice, we weight components equally.
Hierarchical Retrieval:We structure retrieval as a two-stage cascade. First, we retrieve a broad
candidate pool (e.g., top-50) based strictly on observation similarity. Second, we re-rank these
candidates based on action similarity. This architecture reflects the intuition that the current state
is the primary discriminant for environmental context, while the action serves as a secondary filter
within similar states, avoiding the retrieval of identical actions in vastly different environments.
Results:Evaluating these retrieval paradigms across environments demonstrates that disentangling
observation and action representations is generally beneficial, though the method of aggregation is

critical. While a linear combination over independent embedding scores improves performance in
WebShop (where it serves as the optimal method) and Chameleon, it actively degrades performance
below the simple baseline in TextWorld (4.12) and Sotopia (0.514). Hierarchical retrieval proves
more robust. The two-stage cascading approach yields the highest total reward in 3 out of 4 environ-

6 HYBRIDWORLDMODEL
While retrieval provides dynamic context and fine-tuning embeds domain-specific mechanics, both
approaches exhibit isolated limitations. To synergise their strengths, we propose a Hybrid World
Model (HWM) that integrates supervised fine-tuning with non-parametric retrieval, explicitly train-
ing the language model to condition its predictions on retrieved historical experiences.
To construct the training pipeline, we populate a transition database with historical episodes. For any
given target observation-action pair(ot,at), we utilise a dense vector retrieval mechanism to query
the database for semantically similar transitions. However, naive retrieval in sequential environments
risks severe data contamination. If left unrestricted, a retriever might simply fetch immediately
adjacent frames from the same episode, allowing the model to trivially reconstruct the temporal
sequence rather than learning underlying environment dynamics.
To prevent this leakage while maximising the utility of the training data, we implement an episode-
level masking filter. If a target transition originates from episodeE i, the retriever is constrained to
search exclusively within the disjoint set of all available episodes excludingE i. This strict masking
guarantees that the retrieved context acts as a generalised heuristic rather than a direct answer key,
preventing intra-episode autocorrelation and ensuring rigorous train-set discipline.
The out-of-episode retrieved transitions are then compiled into a structured prompt alongside the tar-
getot andat. We perform supervised fine-tuning on an LM, optimising the standard autoregressive
loss on the generation of the ground-truth next observationo t+1. By training the model explicitly
on retrieval-augmented inputs, the model learns to optimally cross-reference its internal parametric
knowledge with the non-parametric context provided by the retrieved demonstrations, yielding a
robust and generalizable world model.

7 CONCLUSION
In this work, we perform the first systematic comparison of RAG and fine-tuning for the task of LM-
based world modelling. We show that unlike tasks like knowledge acquisition, fine-tuning proves
consistently superior to RAG, with only minor exceptions. We demonstrate that while both ap-
proaches benefit from increased exploration, RAG is more data-efficient. Our error analysis reveals
substantial retriever errors, suggesting that adapting the retriever to the specific environment could
yield substantial performance gains. We investigate alternative paradigms of encoding transitions
and show that a hierarchical scheme outperforms the classic encoding method. Finally, we intro-
duce a hybrid world model system that combines fine-tuning and RAG to consistently outperform
all other baselines.

A ENVIRONMENTIMPLEMENTATIONDETAILS
Across all five environments, the world model (WM) is trained to predict the agent’s next observation
given the interaction history and a candidate action; unless otherwise noted below, the training target
is simply the environment’s true next observation.
A.1 EMBODIEDNAVIGATION: OBSERVATIONSHAPING
ALFWorld.Rather than exposing the raw simulator observation on its own, each observation
given to the agent is augmented with the current room description, the current inventory, and the
full list of admissible commands, so that the agent always has a complete, self-contained view
of the state at every step. On reset, the environment’s introductory banner text is discarded and
the task instruction is extracted and surfaced separately from the observation, so that the very first
observation of an episode has the same shape as every subsequent one. No truncation is applied to
any of these fields.
TextWorld.The same augmentation strategy is used (room description, inventory, admissible
commands appended to the observation), with one deliberate deviation: thelookcommand is re-
moved from the admissible-command list before it is shown to the agent, since taking that action
would simply reproduce the room description already present in the observation and offers no new
information. As with ALFWorld, introductory/banner text is dropped at reset and replaced with the
task objective, so reset and step observations share a consistent format.
WebShop.Observations are shaped in three ways before being shown to the agent. First, the
shopping instruction — which the underlying environment otherwise repeats verbatim inside every
observation — is removed, since it is instead surfaced once as a fixed task description for the episode.
Second, on the terminal observation, the trailing reward-summary text that the environment appends
is stripped, since reward is already tracked numerically by the wrapper rather than needing to be
parsed out of the observation text. Third, the set of currently available actions (whether a search
is possible, and which clickable page elements are currently valid) is appended explicitly to the
observation as an action menu, so the agent’s action space at each step is stated rather than implicit.
No additional truncation or markup handling is applied; the underlying text rendering of search-
results and product pages is otherwise used as-is.
A.2 ADVERSARIALNEGOTIATION: SOTOPIA
Setup.Each episode is a two-party conversation grounded in a scenario and a pair of character
profiles (physical/social context, occupation, personality, private goal, and a piece of secret infor-
mation each party is not expected to reveal unless it serves them), drawn from the public Sotopia
scenario dataset. The agent under evaluation always plays one fixed conversational role; the other
party is a separate, non-evaluated language model instantiated specifically to play the counterpart
for that episode.
Prompting.Each turn, the speaking party is prompted with the scenario description, its own per-
sona (name, age, occupation, publicly known information, personality and values), its private goal,
its secret information, and the conversation so far, and is asked to produce the single best next
utterance to advance its own goal, or to end the interaction if it has reached a natural conclusion.
Action and observation space.The action space is an unconstrained natural-language utterance,
or an explicit ”end the conversation” action available to either party. After each of the agent’s
turns, the observation returned is the counterpart’s reply since the agent’s last turn; the agent’s own
utterance is not echoed back, since it is already recorded as the action that produced that step.
Termination and turn budget.An episode ends when either party chooses to end the conver-
sation, or after a fixed budget of ten player turns has elapsed — chosen to allow conversations to
develop fully before being cut off.
13
Preprint
Reward.At the end of an episode, a separate judging language model rates the evaluated party’s
goal achievement on a 0–10 scale, conditioned on the scenario, that party’s persona and goal, and
the full conversation transcript; this score is rescaled to[0,1]to form the scalar reward.
Data splits.Scenarios are partitioned by their labeled interaction type. Negotiation scenarios are
split 80/20 by scenario into train and test sets under a fixed random seed. Scenarios labeled as
competitive (rather than negotiation) are held out in their entirety and used as a distribution-shift
evaluation split, disjoint from both the negotiation train and test scenarios.
World-model prediction task.Given the conversation history, the current observation, and the
agent’s proposed next utterance as the candidate action, the WM is trained to predict the counter-
part’s resulting reply — i.e. the ground-truth prediction target is literally the counterpart’s actual next
line of dialogue (or the episode’s terminal state, if the proposed utterance ends the conversation).
A.3 DECEPTIVECOMMUNICATION: CHAMELEON
Default configuration.The Chameleon environment is general enough to support an arbitrary
number of players and an arbitrary number of chameleons among them, but every experiment re-
ported in this paper uses a single fixed configuration: three players and exactly one chameleon.
The evaluated agent always occupies the first speaking position and is always a non-chameleon;
the chameleon role is always assigned to the second speaking position, leaving the third position as
the other (non-chameleon, language-model-driven) player. Three players is in any case the smallest
group size for which the game is well defined, and with three players exactly one chameleon is the
only valid configuration, so this default is also the game’s minimal, canonical form.
Game flow.Each round is drawn from one of several topics (e.g. movies, athletes, companies,
countries, superheroes, scientists, food), each with a fixed pool of sixteen candidate secret words
per data split. Players speak once each, in a fixed order. Non-chameleon players are shown the
secret word and asked to give a single related word that signals their knowledge of it to other non-
chameleons without making it obvious to the chameleon; the chameleon does not know the secret
word and must produce a plausible-sounding clue by inference from the other clues and the topic
alone. Since the evaluated agent always speaks first, it must commit to its clue with no information
beyond the topic and secret word, and the round always concludes after everyone has spoken once.
Judge.After every player has given a clue, a separate judging language model is shown the secret
word, the full candidate word list for the topic, and all clues in speaking order, and must name
exactly one player as the chameleon.
Reward.From the evaluated player’s perspective (always a non-chameleon under the default con-
figuration): the reward is+1if the judge correctly names the true chameleon,0if the judge instead
accuses the other non-chameleon player, and this outcome would additionally be penalized by−1
if the judge accused the evaluated player itself — a case that cannot arise under the fixed default
configuration, since the evaluated player’s position is never assigned the chameleon role.
World-model prediction task.Because the round always ends after a single exchange of clues,
the world model’s prediction task is correspondingly single-step: conditioned on the topic, secret
word, and the evaluated agent’s chosen clue (the candidate action), the WM must predict both the
clues subsequently given by the other two players and the judge’s eventual verdict. Rather than using
the literal next observation as the training target, the ground-truth target is constructed specifically
to isolate these two pieces of information: the other players’ clues, and a short natural-language
statement of whether the judge’s guess correctly caught the true chameleon or was misled into
accusing the wrong player.

C EXPLORATION
Training buffers for the world models are constructed by rolling out an agent in each training envi-
ronment. At each step, with probabilityϵthe agent’s action is instead generated by an exploratory
variant of the same policy-agent LM rather than its default goal-directed behavior; with probability
1−ϵit behaves greedily as usual. In both cases the action is still produced by prompting the LM
with the same base framing and output format shown in Appendix B (single action or ranked can-
didate list, depending on whether a world model is active that step) — exploration is implemented
entirely by substituting the task instruction given to the model, not by sampling actions uniformly at
random.
For most environments, the exploratory variant entirely replaces[TASK DESCRIPTION]in the
base framing above with a single generic exploration instruction:
Take interesting exploratory actions to probe various aspects
of the environment. Avoid doing the same thing repeatedly,
and try to think creatively and be very wide in what you
consider doing (but within any specified list of allowed
actions).
Two environments instead use a specialized exploration instruction tailored to their setting, ap-
pended to (rather than replacing) the normal task instruction, in the form “[normal task
instruction][line break] For this turn, try an exploratory approach:[specialized
instruction]”. In Chameleon, the specialized instruction is:

safe or obvious | pick something that no one would expect,
that comes from a completely different angle, that might even
seem wrong at first glance but is secretly defensible. The

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
abstract: Campus AI tutors based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must ground answers in assigned course materials while keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infrastructure. We present CourseChat, an on-premises, multi-course RAG tutor for undergraduate business education, deployed behind a campus web gateway and intended for use embedded in Moodle. Six isolated course offerings, each keyed by its own course reference number (CRN), share twin-edge AI hosts running a FastAPI service, a local vector database, and a local large language model (LLM) served by Ollama. We report two generation-model bake-off rounds, a separate fixed-evidence source-fidelity comparison, and conversation and quiz audits. Several larger models failed the classroom speed gate, but a 12B model and a 7B alternative passed. A separate mixture-of-experts candidate improved some corrections while introducing new factual and continuity errors. We therefore retain the 8B production model pending a demonstrated overall improvement, rather than claiming that 8B is universally optimal. Software changes improved follow-up topic resolution while preserving course scope; 435 prebuilt questions across 65 modules decouple practice from live generation. The results support treating model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision. They do not establish learning gains: faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway acceptance remain separate evaluation needs.
