On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education:
Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
Sidney Shapiro ∗ Joshua Lindemann
Dhillon School of Business, University of Lethbridge
Abstract
Campus AI tutors based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must ground answers in
assigned course materials while keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infras-
tructure. We present CourseChat, an on-premises, multi-course RAG tutor for undergraduate
business education, deployed behind a campus web gateway and intended for Moodle-embedded
use. Six isolated course offerings—each keyed by its own course reference number (CRN)—share
twin edge AI hosts running a FastAPI service, a local vector database, and a local large language
model (LLM) served by Ollama. We report two generation-model bake-off rounds, a separate
fixed-evidence source-fidelity comparison, and conversation and quiz audits. Several larger models
failed a classroom speed gate, but a 12B model and a 7B alternative passed it. A separate
mixture-of-experts candidate improved some corrections while introducing new factual and
continuity errors. We therefore retain the 8B production model pending a demonstrated overall
improvement, rather than claiming that 8B is universally optimal. Software changes improved
follow-up topic resolution while preserving course scope; 435 prebuilt questions across 65 modules
decouple practice from live generation. The results support treating model choice, evidence
selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision. They do
not establish learning gains: faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway
acceptance remain separate evaluation needs.
Keywords:retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); on-premises large language models; campus AI
tutoring; business education; Moodle; course isolation; source fidelity; hardware–software co-design;
educational technology
1 Introduction
Campus AI tutors promise grounded help on assigned materials without sending copyrighted
textbooks or student dialogue to external APIs. Realizing that promise under institutional constraints
is a systems problem: limited GPU memory, concurrent classroom use, LMS embeds, and a hard
requirement that CourseAnever answer from CourseB’s corpus.
This paper documents CourseChat, a multi-course RAG tutor deployed for a business school.
Students interact through a Moodle-embeddable chat that supports (i) conversation grounded in
the selected offering’s indexed materials and (ii) module-scoped practice quizzes with answer keys,
hints, and source excerpts. Six offerings (anonymized here as Courses 1–6) share one application
binary while remaining isolated at the data and routing layers.
Our central claim is that building such a tutor requires an explicit hardware–software trade-off
strategy: choose models and pipelines that fit the host memory and concurrency envelope; push
∗ORCID:https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4193-1154
1
arXiv:2610.02510v1  [cs.AI]  1 Oct 2026
quality into retrieval, scoping, and evaluation rather than into ever-larger generators; and keep
product surfaces (conversation vs. quiz) aligned with what the stack can guarantee.
The practical question is which component should change when a tutor gives a poor answer.
An unhelpful follow-up can originate in lost conversational context, a missing passage, a relevance
filter that rejects a useful passage, or a generator that misstates correctly retrieved evidence. A
larger model addresses only some of these failures, and its benefits must be weighed against response
time and serving compatibility. We use this distinction to organize both the architecture and the
evaluation.
The paper makes three contributions. First, it describes a replicated local RAG architecture
and its course-scoping and artifact-management boundaries. Second, it reports a generation-model
comparison with fixed retrieval and token limits, alongside a deliberately separate model-and-
response-contract experiment. Third, it connects observed failures to concrete design choices:
retrieval-topic resolution, bounded evidence selection, and prebuilt practice banks. Together these
provide an evidence-based account of why the current release retains an 8B model despite having
enough memory to trial larger ones.
CourseChat began as a pilot project at the Dhillon School of Business to explore how a locally
developed AI tutor could add value to students’ learning. The university already provides students
with access to Copilot and Gemini, and students also use ChatGPT and other generative AI tools.
The pilot’s purpose was therefore to complement these existing options with support tailored to
local courses, teaching materials, and learning expectations. Rather than replicate general-purpose
AI assistance, CourseChat was designed to help students engage with their assigned material and
develop the confidence to work independently. Course-grounded explanations, practice questions,
hints, and feedback were intended to encourage students to attempt problems themselves, examine
their reasoning, and return to the course sources. The intended educational value lay in supporting
students’ own effort and understanding, with AI serving as a guide within that process.
2 Related work and positioning
CourseChat brings together three research concerns: how tutoring supports learning, how generated
explanations remain faithful to course evidence, and how an institution can serve those interactions
reliably. The relevant literature therefore extends beyond comparisons of language-model capability.
It also provides reasons to distinguish successful task completion, useful instructional interaction,
and learning that persists after assistance is removed.
2.1 Tutoring, practice, and self-regulated learning
Research on intelligent tutoring systems predates conversational language models and emphasizes
the organization of instructional support. VanLehn’s review distinguishes systems by the granularity
of their interaction, including whether feedback addresses a final answer or intermediate problem-
solving steps [2]. Kulik and Fletcher’s meta-analysis of fifty controlled evaluations found generally
positive learning effects for intelligent tutoring systems, while also showing that outcomes depend on
the comparison condition, assessment, and implementation [ 3]. These findings support studying the
instructional process around a response rather than treating fluent dialogue as sufficient evidence of
tutoring effectiveness. They do not imply that a language-model chatbot inherits the benefits of a
validated tutor.
Practice and feedback provide a more specific rationale for the pilot’s student controls. In
experiments using prose passages, Roediger and Karpicke found that retrieval practice improved
2
delayed retention relative to repeated study, even when restudy produced better immediate per-
formance [4]. The result motivates opportunities to attempt a question before viewing its answer,
although it does not establish the effectiveness of CourseChat’s multiple-choice banks. Nicol and
Macfarlane-Dick’s account of formative feedback links useful feedback to students’ ability to judge
their work and regulate subsequent learning [ 5]. In this framing, a hint or explanation should help a
learner identify a gap and decide what to do next. CourseChat adopts practice attempts, optional
hints, and explanatory feedback as design choices informed by this literature; whether they improve
study habits or retention in this setting remains an empirical question.
2.2 Generative AI assistance and independent learning
Recent experiments show why the manner of providing AI assistance matters. Bastani et al.
studied generative AI support in high-school mathematics, comparing a relatively unrestricted
assistant with a tutor configured to provide teacher-informed instructional support [ 6]. Access to
AI improved performance during assisted practice, but students using the relatively unrestricted
version subsequently performed worse than the no-AI control group on an unassisted exam. The
tutoring safeguards mitigated that reduction; this should not be interpreted as evidence that the
guarded condition produced a positive unassisted learning gain. The study distinguishes help with
the current exercise from developing the ability to solve another exercise independently. That
distinction is directly relevant to a pilot intended to encourage students’ own work rather than
merely make answers easier to obtain.
Kestin et al. report a complementary result from a randomized crossover study in undergraduate
physics: a deliberately designed AI tutor produced higher immediate learning gains than the
comparison active-learning class sessions [ 7]. The intervention embedded pedagogical guidance
and structured content, so it was more specific than access to a general chat interface. Its short
instructional scope also limits conclusions about long-term retention, other disciplines, or semester-
long use. Read together, these studies suggest that the instructional design and help policy are part
of the intervention being evaluated. They do not support either a universal claim that AI tutoring
improves learning or a universal claim that it undermines it.
For the Dhillon pilot, this evidence shifts the design question toward the additional educational
value of a local service. Students already have other ways to obtain generated text. CourseChat’s
intended contribution is to connect that help to the selected course and give students a practical
route between attempting a question, requesting limited assistance, checking an explanation, and
returning to the assigned material. This is a rationale for the design, not a claim that the pilot has
reproduced either study’s learning outcomes.
2.3 Course grounding and source fidelity
Retrieval-augmented generation provides a technical basis for connecting that help to local materials.
Lewis et al. combined a generative model with an external document index, demonstrating
improvements on knowledge-intensive tasks and a mechanism for updating accessible evidence
separately from model parameters [ 1]. CourseChat uses the broader retrieval-conditioned generation
pattern rather than reproducing that paper’s training procedure. Its course collections and module
filters determine which teaching materials are eligible to support a response. The resulting benefit is
control over the evidence supplied to generation; it does not make the generated answer automatically
correct.
Gao et al.’s ALCE benchmark evaluates generated answers along separate dimensions of correct-
ness, fluency, and citation quality [ 8]. Their results show that even citation-producing systems can
3
leave claims without adequate support. This distinction matters in education because a valid link
to a textbook passage can coexist with an incorrect interpretation of its conditions. CourseChat
therefore treats source selection, citation resolution, and fidelity of the explanation as distinct checks.
Source cards make evidence inspectable, while answer review must still establish whether the cited
passage supports the claim.
Increasing the context window is also an incomplete response to grounding failures. Liu et al.
found that the position of relevant information affected performance on document question answering
and key-value retrieval, with information in the middle of long contexts often used less effectively [ 9].
Their experiments concern particular models and tasks, not the present classroom deployment.
Nevertheless, they motivate testing evidence selection and organization instead of assuming that
supplying more textbook content will improve an answer. Bounded context, explicit scope, and a
fixed retrieval configuration make CourseChat’s model comparisons more interpretable.
2.4 Evaluation and serving constraints
RAG evaluation frameworks reinforce the need to assess components separately. RAGAs proposes
reference-free measures for retrieved context, faithfulness, and answer quality [ 10]. ARES uses
trained judges to evaluate context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, together
with human annotations to account for judge error [ 11]. These approaches provide useful models
for diagnosis, but their scores are not measures of student understanding. CourseChat’s reported
evaluation does not claim to implement either framework. It follows the same separation of questions:
whether the intended evidence was found, whether the response was supported, and whether the
interaction was useful. Faculty assessment and unassisted learning measures address additional
questions that automated retrieval or citation checks cannot settle.
Serving research also shows why the suitability of a model cannot be inferred from parameter
count alone. Kwon et al.’s work on PagedAttention demonstrates that managing the memory used
by active generation requests affects batching and throughput [ 12]. Their vLLM results do not
predict the performance of CourseChat’s Ollama stack or establish that this deployment would
benefit from a particular serving migration. They do establish a relevant systems concern: model
weights are only part of the resource demand during concurrent use. CourseChat accordingly treats
latency, request overlap, context limits, and client compatibility as evaluation criteria alongside
answer quality, while acknowledging that its serial trials do not measure classroom capacity.
2.5 Position of the CourseChat pilot
Related course-specific tutors combine retrieval with explicit instructional control. CourseAssist
uses course-grounded retrieval, user intent classification, and question decomposition to support
computer science students [ 13]. KITE combines multimodal retrieval from course materials with an
intent-aware Socratic strategy that provides hints, guiding questions, and progressive scaffolding for
algorithmic problem-solving [14]. CourseChat shares their emphasis on course-aligned assistance
and develops the operational side of that design: replicated on-premises serving across segregated
offerings, model-selection trials under a fixed latency allowance, and prebuilt quiz banks with source
bindings and item-review records. Its contribution is evidence about these deployment choices and
their observed failure modes in business education.
The pilot’s contribution is the integration and evaluation of these concerns within a local business-
school setting. It combines course-specific evidence, conversation continuity, prebuilt practice, and a
shared local generator across six separately scoped offerings. The paper contributes an account of
the resulting tradeoffs and failure modes, including why a working 8B configuration was retained
4
despite credible alternatives. It does not propose a new retrieval algorithm, demonstrate superiority
over institutionally available AI services, or report a controlled learning-outcome comparison.
This position also shapes the next evaluation. A useful local tutor should be assessed for its
ability to support appropriate independent effort as well as produce accurate explanations. Measures
of unaided problem solving, retention, source use, and patterns of hint requests would connect
the engineering results reported here to the educational aims established in the tutoring literature.
The present study supplies the implementation and diagnostic evidence needed to design that
evaluation.
3 System overview
3.1 Student experience
The student experience is organized around the material assigned in a particular course offering. In
the intended Moodle integration, students enter through an instructor-provided link embedded in the
LMS. CourseChat is meant to sit inside that Moodle course context rather than as a public textbook
or tutoring destination: the embed is the intended entry path, and the course slug is not advertised
to students as a standalone bookmark, although slug secrecy and enrollment checks are not claimed
as proven access controls. That link establishes the full-course, module, or named-activity scope;
the header displays the course, instructor, course reference number (CRN), and selected material.
This visible context helps students understand which materials the tutor can use and connects the
interaction to their immediate coursework. Conversation and quiz functions are implemented in
the course pages, while complete acceptance of the public gateway remains a separate deployment
task. The design seeks local value through this connection to assigned materials and practice,
complementing students’ access to general-purpose AI services.
In Conversation mode, students ask questions in ordinary language and receive explanations
accompanied by citations to passages from the selected offering. Inline citations open source
cards containing excerpts and available chapter, section, or page information. Keeping these cards
collapsed initially gives the explanation room while preserving a route back to the original material.
Students can request a shorter answer, more detail, or another explanation, and can adjust the
explanation level. These controls are intended to support checking and revisiting a concept rather
than treating the first generated answer as the endpoint of study. The interface also distinguishes
source relevance from answer correctness: its relevance score describes the match between a passage
and a query, not the probability that an explanation is correct. Course-configured relevance floors
set a trusted lower bound; students may raise but not lower that floor.
Conversational continuity matters because students need not restate a complete question at
every turn. After an explanation of net present value, for example, “Can you show me that with
numbers?” should preserve that topic and the selected module. A brief social aside should not erase
it. The router uses recent dialogue to resolve the reference, then retrieves current course evidence;
earlier assistant text does not become an authoritative source. Where several referents are plausible,
it asks a short clarification question. Social replies do not acquire artificial course citations. When
retrieval finds no qualifying passage within the selected module, a reported fallback may broaden
the explanation using the model’s current conversational context and material from the same course
offering. It does not retrieve material or conversation history from another segregated course. If
qualifying course evidence remains unavailable, the system reports the evidence gap. The presence
of a qualifying passage cannot by itself guarantee a faithful explanation.
Quiz mode provides a different form of participation. Selecting Quiz starts a practice session
from a prepared bank and presents one multiple-choice item at a time. The student can attempt the

The interface also provides progress messages and incremental answer text through server-

3.3 Deployment topology
Figure 2 summarizes the campus deployment architecture. The IIS gateway is assigned TLS
termination, course-slug rewrites, and routing to two AI nodes (Node A and Node B). Each node
runs the full stack locally: FastAPI, Qdrant, sentence-transformer embeddings, a cross-encoder

Hardware envelope (classroom hosts).Each node is a DGX Spark-class appliance with

and memory use. These are independent local serving stacks, not a pooled GPU model spread
across both machines. This envelope frames the model trials in Section 6; worker count alone does
not establish classroom capacity.
4 Hardware–software trade-off strategy
We treat model selection as a constrained operating decision. The desired outcome is a useful
explanation supported by the selected offering’s materials, delivered within a tolerable classroom
wait. The bake-off makes one performance constraint explicit: median complete-answer latency
must be no more than 30% above the production 8B baseline measured in the same round. Other
promotion criteria require usable overlapping requests, preservation of course scope, and a meaningful
improvement in reviewed answers. These are promotion requirements; a listed requirement is not
evidence that the corresponding experiment was completed.
7
Several design choices act on different parts of this objective. Model family and size affect
answer generation, whereas retrieval depth, context limits, and reranking affect which evidence
reaches the model and how soon generation can begin. Server-wide application profiles package these
performance settings; they do not select a course or change the collection boundary. A separate
product decision moves quiz authoring out of the request path. A separate deployment decision
moves document extraction and review to a workstation, leaving the serving hosts responsible for
indexing and inference.
Changing these components together would obscure why a candidate succeeded or failed. We
therefore keep the serving retrieval stack fixed during the model bake-off, and identify the separate
structured-answer experiment as a different comparison. Course content remains local, quiz questions
are prepared before practice, and reasoning-capable models must deliver student-visible output
within the configured budget before they are considered deployable. These choices trade some
flexibility for traceable failures and a bounded release process.
Table 1 brings together the main interventions, their observed outcomes, and the resulting design
decisions. It distinguishes generator comparisons from changes to retrieval and practice delivery;
Section 6 gives the model-by-model measurements. This overview makes explicit why the project
retained some components, changed others, and deferred alternatives that had not established an
overall advantage.
5 Design choices
5.1 Isolation without six fine-tuned LLMs
Isolation is enforced byseparate course ids,separate on-disk trees,separate Qdrant collections,
and ?course= routing. A shared Ollama generator receives passages from the routed collection.
Optional per-course embedding fine-tunes are a potential retrieval-quality intervention; they are
not required for isolation and were not changed in the model trials. The collection and request
boundaries determine which indexed materials can be selected, while source-faithful generation
remains a separate requirement.
Each uploaded offering is keyed by its own course reference number (CRN). Instructors can
therefore maintain different versions of the same catalog course—for example, distinct sections or
successive terms—and control which materials enter that offering’s retrieval collection. Uploading
documents updates the evidence available to that CRN; it does not retrain the shared language
model or merge corpora across offerings. Two offerings may share a catalog code (e.g., two sections
of the same strategic management course) yet must keep distinct corpora when instructors and
materials differ. The same principle applies to conversation history and quiz state: carrying a
previous course’s session into a newly selected offering would defeat collection-level separation.
Scope therefore belongs to request handling and session validation as well as storage. Passing the
reported scope checks supports these specific paths, rather than proving that a shared pretrained
model can never produce an unsupported statement.
5.2 RAG for content; prompts for pedagogy
Course knowledge is indexed, not baked into LLM weights. Tutoring tone and Socratic instructions
come from system prompts and optional bot-profile YAML. Chapter scope is applied through request
validation and retrieval metadata filters; any reported fallback remains within the selected course
offering. Content updates are re-ingest + replicate, not a training job. This allows revisions to
textbooks and decks to be associated with explicit source artifacts and ingestion receipts. A weight

5.3 Prebuilt quizzes
Early demos showed that generating a multiple-choice item at chat time is insufficient for a reliable
practice session. The platform therefore prebuilds banks containing source-backed items, keys,
explanations, hints, and evidence ledgers. Automatic generation is gated by index and answer
evaluation. A separate publication path accepts independently reviewed items bound to the exact
current source and question hashes; that path requires the author and reviewer identities to differ,
and that item-level review does not clear a failed free-form chat audit. Serving quiz turns is
deterministic grading against the bank (warm medians on the order of milliseconds server-local),
while conversation retains the generative path. Answer keys remain server-side until an attempt or
reveal, so the bank is not exposed as a downloadable key file in the student UI.
Across Courses 1–6 the deployed banks total 435 questions over 65 modules. Structural audits
and live API grading checks pass on both nodes; instructor pedagogical review remains an explicit
separate gate (instructor reviewed: falseuntil faculty sign-off).
This choice makes practice behavior reproducible: the hint, key, explanation, and supporting
excerpt can all be inspected before use. It also makes content maintenance explicit. When source
material changes, a bank must be checked against the new corpus rather than silently continuing
to cite stale evidence. The cost is a finite pool of questions and less spontaneous adaptation to a
student’s wording, which is why open-ended explanation remains a separate conversation mode.
5.4 Conversational turns over shared course evidence
Conversation gives students a way to work through the meaning of course material, including
questions that cannot be anticipated in a prepared quiz. The design combines three resources
with different roles: a pretrained model provides language generation, indexed passages provide
current teaching evidence, and prebuilt quiz items provide stable questions, hints, and grading
keys. Ingesting a professor’s materials updates the evidence collection; it does not retrain the
language model. Conversation can therefore extend the uses of the same corpus while preserving
the distinction between an open-ended explanation and a stored practice item.
A conversational turn carries more than a new search phrase. If a student asks whether a
different assumption would change a worked example, the tutor must retain the example’s setting,
identify the changed assumption, and find the course evidence needed to explain its effect. An
exchange about net present value might move from a definition to a numerical illustration and then
to the student’s own account of why a higher discount rate changes the result. This illustrates the
intended interaction: the student can test an interpretation and request a targeted explanation.
The model’s hypothetical numbers must remain clearly distinguished from facts attributed to course
sources, and a change of topic must still respect the selected module.
The implemented path resolves dependent turns against recent dialogue while passing the
student’s actual wording to generation. Recent dialogue is held in the browser and submitted with
each request rather than stored as a durable server session: history must match the selected course,
is bounded in length, and does not require sticky affinity between the twin nodes. The shared
resolver raised intended-topic follow-up rates to 90–100% across the five-course replay, without
changing the generator (Section 8). The conversation router handles social, course, mixed, follow-up,
and clarification turns, using deterministic rules first and a short classification call for ambiguity.
A casual aside can preserve the course topic; subsequent content questions retrieve fresh evidence.
10
Earlier assistant text helps interpret a reference but is not promoted into authoritative teaching
material. Only designated meta or policy FAQ entries short-circuit retrieval; content FAQs remain
in the course vector index and compete with other evidence.
LangChain components already provide model, prompt, document, and vector-store interfaces
in the retrieval application. They offer a basis for extending the conversation workflow around
the existing corpus: assemble the learning instructions and bounded dialogue, retrieve material
for the resolved turn, and generate an explanation with source references. LangChain’s memory
facilities support thread-level history and strategies for limiting its size; durable conversation state
would additionally require shared persistence and course isolation [ 18]. The current router uses
explicit Python control flow and browser-supplied history. A more extensive LangChain workflow,
or LangGraph orchestration for resumable multi-step activities, would be a future implementation
choice, evaluated against this simpler baseline.
This separation creates room for additional instructional modes without building another
knowledge base for each one. A future case-discussion mode could ask students to justify an
interpretation using a professor’s supplementary case; a guided-practice mode could focus on the
next reasoning step; and a revision mode could revisit a misconception exposed by a quiz. Each
would use an explicit interaction policy over the same scoped evidence and keep factual support
checks in place. Their local value would come from the instructor’s selected material and teaching
expectations, combined with opportunities for student reasoning. These are proposed extensions to
the deployed conversation and quiz modes, to be tested for usefulness and appropriate independent
effort.
5.5 Streaming vs. raw latency
Non-streaming live eval reports full-answer wall times (often ∼6–10 s on 8B). Perceived speed
is dominated by time-to-first-token through the gateway. The UI requests SSE, and gateway
configuration must preserve incremental delivery. The first metadata event, the first visible text,
and completed answer time are different measurements. The bake-off below measures the last of
these on the node itself; it does not quantify browser-perceived waiting time through IIS. Streaming
can expose an answer earlier without reducing total inference work, so it complements rather than
replaces model-latency evaluation.
5.6 Workstation / Node A / Node B pipeline
Scanned textbook OCR and page review run on a Mac workstation (Docling, Apple Vision, optional
on-device formula assistance). Reviewed corpora are prepared offline, ingested on Node A with the
same encoder the API uses, then snapshot-replicated to Node B. This split keeps OCR engines off
the classroom hosts and keeps A/B parity enforceable (parity-checkon git SHA and health).

6.3 Separate fixed-evidence fidelity comparison
A separate diagnostic compared the production 8B path with a qwen3.6:35b-a3b-q4 K M candidate
on twelve frozen cases. The fixture preserved the current question, earlier dialogue, selected source
passages, and source checksums. It included corrections after an incorrect assistant answer, numerical
illustrations, missing facts, topic switching, format constraints, and references to a previous example.
Unlike the generator-only bake-off, the final candidate changed the model, prompt, structured
response contract, validation, and transport together. Its results therefore evaluate that complete
configuration, not an isolated model-size effect.
The candidate returned an evidence list of source identifiers and exact quotations followed
by an answer. Validation checked structure, current source identity, quotation text, and cited
source numbers; rejected drafts were replaced by a fixed conversational gap response. Thinking was
explicitly disabled. Direct requests to the generation endpoint produced twelve valid JSON objects,
resolving a format-handling problem observed with the installed chat route. Nine answers passed
structural checks, including one materially wrong claim. Three were withheld: two appropriately
lacked evidence, whereas one was an answerable follow-up.
The independent comparison recorded three substantial improvements, two modest improvements,
three ties, one mixed result, and three regressions. The larger candidate corrected earlier accounting
and pricing mistakes, but also turned a qualified benefit of holding cash into a guarantee and lost
continuity on a reference to a prior example. Warm serial medians were 3.469 s for the production
path and 2.997 s for the candidate. A separate cold candidate request took 25.417 s, including 23.269 s
loading. With only twelve warm observations, the reported nearest-rank p95 is the maximum, not a
reliable estimate of classroom tail latency. The candidate occupied approximately 26.4 GB on the
GPU with the configured context, demonstrating that memory fit was not the decisive obstacle in
this trial.
The configuration was not activated. Its warm speed and correction gains were promising, but new
factual and continuity regressions prevented an overall quality win. Production streaming, dynamic
instructor instructions, and the broader interaction settings were also outside this diagnostic’s
validated contract. Section 9 uses these results to explain why retaining 8B is a conditional release
decision.

8 Evaluation
8.1 Multi-turn conversation
Frozen fixtures contain 20 dialogues and 80 turns per course, including 60 follow-ups. They cover
numerical examples, misconceptions, topic changes, brevity requests, locked-module boundaries,
and transitions between quiz and conversation. The harness records the resolved retrieval query,
scope, selected passages, model-visible context, reply, and latency. Topic-hit scores measure whether
a dependent question retains its intended subject; they do not measure whether every resulting
explanation is correct.
Course 1 was evaluated separately, and Courses 2–6 were replayed serially on Node B with the
production 8B generator. Table 4 reports the documented before/after topic checks. Course 1 has
two live replays; the Courses 2–6 baseline scores come from a resolver-only preflight with the prior
production resolver, followed by live evaluation of the update. In the five-course run, all 400 scope
checks passed with zero API errors, and each course reached the 90% follow-up target. Median
per-turn latency ranged from 3.24 to 6.19 s. The separate Course 1 replay improved from 31 to 60
successful follow-ups, while its median increased from 4.92 to 5.81 s. This is consistent with treating
quality and speed as distinct outcomes rather than assuming that every resolver improvement also
reduces latency.
The five-course run still contained 93 no match turns. Twelve were intentional locked-module
refusals, fifteen were quiz follow-ups whose wording did not retrieve a qualifying passage, and 66
involved other requests spanning 24 topics. Cleaner concept probes found evidence for nineteen of
those topics; five still required content or index investigation. A bounded facet expansion recovered
eleven of the 24 original questions without lowering the relevance floor. These diagnostics identify
recoverable retrieval failures; they are not an overall answer-accuracy score. Faculty ratings remain
pending, so neither the proposed 4/5 usefulness target nor the 95% supported-claim target is claimed
as achieved.

8.2 Source fidelity and routing checks
A targeted, agent-reviewed ten-request live textbook audit gives a complementary view of quality.
It found three supported replies, four retrieval misses despite available evidence, two source contra-
dictions, and one partly grounded answer. Every returned citation resolved to its source. Thus,
citation integrity coexisted with substantive error: locating a real passage did not ensure that the
answer preserved its meaning. The requests were selected diagnostics, not a representative sample
from which to estimate a population error rate.
The 20 September router extension has a different evaluation scope. Its frozen contract contains
32 crossover cases, supplemented by focused checks and live probes for social, mixed, course, follow-
up, and ambiguous turns. Both nodes passed 306 focused Python tests and the documented live
probes before activation. This supports the routing implementation; it does not retroactively turn
the earlier conversation runs into tests of that extension, or establish faculty-rated usefulness.
8.3 Quizzes
Both nodes passed full artifact and grading audits for all 65 modules. The artifact audit bound
each question to its current source excerpt and original file hashes, then exercised all 435 questions,
including deliberately wrong answers. It checked that hints do not reveal keys or advance progress,
and that requests cannot carry another course’s quiz state into the selected offering. These checks
establish reproducible practice behavior.
A separate 166-request live API audit included all 65 module starts on each node, plus warm
repeats, hints, and graded answers. Warm medians were 4.8 ms on Node A and 5.8 ms on Node B,
measured server-local. They describe stored quiz operations and must not be compared as if they
were generative tutoring latencies or browser response times. Instructor review of answer correctness,
distractors, difficulty, and instructional coverage remains incomplete.
9 Discussion
9.1 Why retain the 8B classroom generator?
Retaining llama3.1:8b is a deployment decision under incomplete quality evidence, rather than
a claim that eight billion parameters is an optimal model size. The first bake-off established that
several plausible upgrades increased full-answer latency substantially under the same retrieval and
output budget. The second round qualified that result: Qwen 7B ran at almost the baseline speed,
and Mistral Nemo 12B stayed inside the prescribed 30% latency allowance. Consequently, “larger
models are too slow” does not adequately explain the final choice. The production policy requires a
clear grounded-tutoring benefit in addition to acceptable speed. Passing twelve keyword-and-citation
checks, or producing slightly more complete answers on that set, does not establish that benefit.
The documented decision is to keep the existing generator while faculty compare the alternatives on
the quality of their actual explanations.
This choice preserves a known serving configuration while acknowledging its material weaknesses.
The fidelity diagnostic reproduced incorrect accounting claims, failure to correct an earlier pricing
error, and attribution of an equation to an exercise that did not state it. Those failures preclude
treating continued deployment as evidence that the 8B model has passed the proposed claim-support
target. The defensible rationale is narrower: no evaluated replacement has yet demonstrated the
complete combination of quality, continuity, integration, and operational readiness required for
promotion. A reviewed Qwen 7B or Nemo 12B improvement could change that decision without
changing the architecture.
16
9.2 A model is evaluated through its serving contract
The separate structured-response experiment illustrates why parameter count alone is a poor
predictor of either speed or usefulness. With thinking disabled, the 35B-A3B mixture-of-experts
candidate had a lower warm median than the 8B baseline on the twelve fixed-source cases. It
corrected important misconceptions that persisted in the baseline, but also overstated the protection
provided by holding cash and refused an answerable reference to a previous example. These are
consequential tutoring regressions: a student needs an explanation to preserve both the source’s
conditions and the setting established in the conversation.
That comparison held the evidence and dialogue fixed but changed the model, prompt, output
schema, validation, and transport together. Its gains therefore belong to the complete candidate
configuration; they cannot be attributed solely to model scale. Conversely, an empty response in
the original production-client bake-off does not show that the underlying model lacks knowledge.
The installed serving stack did not consistently apply the structured format to thinking-capable
chat requests when thinking was disabled. A direct generation request resolved the observed
JSON-formatting problem, while factual and continuity failures remained. Runtime compatibility
thus belongs in the experimental specification alongside model tag, quantization, context length,
and sampling options. The experimental answer contract also left production streaming and
instructor-specific instructions uncertified, providing another reason to withhold activation.
9.3 Grounding requires useful answers and appropriate abstention
The evidence suggests that stricter output validation trades some unsupported answers for refusals,
without eliminating semantic error. In the final candidate, all twelve outputs were valid JSON and
nine passed the quotation and citation checks. An accepted answer nevertheless strengthened a
conditional financial benefit into a guarantee. Of the three withheld answers, two lacked sufficient
evidence and one was an answerable follow-up. Exact quotation verifies a textual relationship with
a source; it does not verify that the explanation preserves the source’s meaning.
The separate entailment experiment reinforces this distinction. Its proposed contradiction
threshold missed both original production errors, even though the classifier detected simplified
versions of some errors. A hypothetical teaching example also received a neutral label, showing
why rejecting all non-entailed prose would suppress legitimate instruction. A useful tutor must
distinguish course-supported concepts, explicitly invented example values, unavailable facts, and
unjustified real-world guarantees. Evaluation should therefore report unnecessary abstention and loss
of explanatory context alongside unsupported claims. The proposed bounded revision experiment
addresses these failure modes, but it remains future work; neither a runtime factual guard nor a
reliable semantic repair mechanism has been demonstrated.
9.4 Retrieval and conversation control are complementary to generation
The multi-course resolver results identify a substantial source of improvement outside the generator.
Resolving a short follow-up into its intended retrieval topic allows the existing model to receive
relevant teaching material while still answering the student’s actual wording. Course and module
boundaries remain enforceable in this step. However, a correct topic does not ensure that an
adequate passage will be retrieved, and an adequate passage does not ensure that the model will
explain it faithfully. The five-course audit’s remaining retrieval misses, and the fixed-evidence fidelity
failures, demonstrate these distinct failure layers.
This decomposition helps allocate engineering effort. Clean-concept probes recovered evidence
for nineteen of twenty-four affected topics, indicating that many misses arose from query formula-
17
tion. Five topics still failed under that favorable probe and required corpus, index, or threshold
investigation. A bounded expansion using only words in the student question recovered eleven of the
original queries without lowering the relevance floor. These findings support targeted retrieval work;
they do not imply that query processing can repair missing material or generation errors. Preserving
each turn’s resolved query, selected passages, and displayed answer makes that distinction auditable
and reduces the temptation to attribute every poor answer to model size.
The subsequent conversation router, activated on both nodes on 20 September, extends this
separation to social, course, mixed, follow-up, and clarification turns. Obvious cases use deterministic
rules; ambiguous cases use a short structured classification request to the same 8B model. Sharing
the resident model avoids introducing a second model and a possible model-loading penalty while
routing is evaluated. Its validated intent schema is a deployed control mechanism, distinct from the
experimental evidence-first answer contract discussed above. The implementation also illustrates
a deliberate complexity trade-off: bounded browser-supplied history and a small Python router
meet the current requirements, while durable cross-device conversations would require additional
persistence. LangGraph remains an option for that future requirement, rather than a dependency
needed to obtain the reported improvements.
9.5 On-premises control carries operational obligations
Local inference and separate offering collections give the institution control over where course
materials and student dialogue are processed and which evidence enters an answer. Dialogue is
handled on the campus hosts rather than sent to an external generation API. Each offering is keyed
by its own CRN, so instructors can maintain different versions of the same catalog course and decide
which materials that version may retrieve. Sharing one generator across offerings avoids maintaining
six content-specific language models, while separate collections, data trees, browser-held histories,
and request routing keep those CRN boundaries in place. Uploaded materials update the retrieval
collection for the selected offering; they are not used to fine-tune a shared model on faculty or
student content. Access is organized around the LMS course context and course routing rather than
an application- level enrollment check in CourseChat itself. These mechanisms support reproducible
content updates and instructor-controlled corpora. Their evaluation demonstrates scoped behavior
on the recorded probes, rather than a general proof of security, privacy compliance, or enrollment
enforcement.
The two complete local stacks provide an operational alternative when one node is under
maintenance, but duplicate state introduces explicit maintenance work. Updating the primary
index is insufficient: the replica must receive the corresponding snapshots, and quiz banks and
evidence ledgers must be copied separately. Code, model configuration, and course artifacts also
need consistent versions. This is the cost of retaining local ownership and independently serviceable
hosts. The reported work does not measure capital amortization, electricity, administration time, or
cost per student; it therefore supports no claim that this deployment is cheaper than a cloud service.
Its demonstrated motivation is control under the institution’s chosen deployment constraints.
9.6 Prebuilt practice moves uncertainty into a reviewable build stage
Prebuilding quizzes changes both the computational and educational trade-off. Serving a stored
question and grading against its key avoids a generation request for each practice turn, while making
hints and explanations stable across sessions. It also makes evidence and arithmetic review possible
before an item reaches a student. In exchange, the bank offers finite variation and requires rebuilding
or re-review when course material changes. Six or seven questions per module establish availability
18
across the module map, rather than exhaustive coverage of each learning objective.
The distinction between artifact integrity and teaching quality remains essential. Successful
grading and exact source bindings demonstrate that practice behaves consistently, but they cannot
establish suitable difficulty, plausible distractors, or a single pedagogically defensible answer. All
banks still record instructor review as incomplete. Similarly, a module with limited source material
can offer bounded, supported practice without claiming comprehensive coverage. This explicit
limitation is preferable to letting live generation silently supply missing instructional content.
9.7 Faculty review, student uptake, and educational value
The next pilot stage should connect content maintenance to teaching practice. Instructors could
identify recurring misconceptions, contribute supplementary cases or worked examples, and review
the questions generated from those materials. A useful approval workflow would present each
question alongside its answer, distractors, hint, explanation, and supporting excerpts, allowing
the instructor to edit, approve, or return it for revision. The existing source bindings and item-
review records provide an artifact foundation for this workflow; a streamlined faculty interface
and completed instructor approval remain future work. Preserving approved edits and requesting
renewed review when their supporting material changes would make this feedback loop part of
maintaining a course, rather than a one-time inspection of generated content.
Student uptake should be evaluated over a teaching period. Initial visits would show reach,
while return visits and continued use across later modules would help distinguish sustained use
from novelty. Reporting use separately for explanation, conversational follow-up, and quiz practice
would reveal which activities students find valuable. Course coverage also matters: a service used
intensively in one offering may fit that instructor’s materials without transferring to other courses.
These observations should be paired with student feedback on usefulness, ease of use, trust in
source-supported answers, and reasons for abandoning an interaction. Acceptance cannot be inferred
from usage counts alone, particularly where an instructor explicitly encourages participation.
Educational evaluation should examine what students can do after assistance. A future study
could combine interaction measures, such as attempts before revealing answers and responses to
hints, with delayed assessments and new problems completed without the tutor. Appropriate
comparisons include the existing course resources and the general-purpose AI tools students already
use. Comparing equivalent learning tasks would help establish whether access to instructor-selected
evidence and reviewed practice adds value beyond convenient text generation. Perceived usefulness,
assisted task performance, and independent learning should remain separate outcomes.
Faculty acceptance is equally consequential. The pilot should record the time needed to prepare
materials, review questions, resolve reported errors, and update a course between offerings. A
proposed feedback mechanism could let students flag an unclear explanation or disputed answer for
instructor review, with confirmed issues feeding into corpus corrections and regression cases. This
would connect observed difficulties to concrete revisions while making the teaching workload visible.
Together, student and faculty evidence would guide which interaction modes to extend and which
content gaps deserve attention first.
9.8 Limits of the evidence and next evaluation priorities
The reported latency measurements are predominantly serial and server-local. Two API workers
permit overlapping requests, but worker count and available memory do not establish usable
classroom throughput. Warm model timings also exclude the substantial cold-load delay observed
for the larger candidate. The two-request overlap gate remains a requirement for promotion; the
19
presented results do not constitute a completed load study. Gateway time-to-first-token requires
separate measurement because proxy buffering can delay visible output without changing generation
time. SSE support is implemented, whereas public gateway readiness and verification for every
course slug remained open in the documented deployment snapshot.
The evaluation sets are engineering regressions rather than a representative sample of student
use. Repeated development on frozen fixtures can improve those cases without transferring to
unseen misconceptions or question forms. Faculty ratings for usefulness and factual support remain
pending, and no learning-outcome or controlled classroom study is reported. The next evidence
needed is therefore paired faculty review on held-out dialogues, explicit measurement of false refusals
and source-condition errors, and concurrent browser-to-gateway timing under representative load.
These checks would make a future model change defensible while preserving the current distinction
between an implemented system, measured engineering behavior, and demonstrated educational
benefit.
10 Conclusion
CourseChat began as a Dhillon School of Business pilot to provide useful local learning support
alongside the generative AI services already available to students. Its contribution rests on the design
of the whole teaching system: separate CRN-scoped collections preserve instructional context and let
instructors control which materials each offering may retrieve, a traceable ingestion pipeline connects
responses to supplied materials, conversation controls support follow-up questions, and prebuilt
quizzes make practice and feedback inspectable. These choices allow one shared generator to serve
different offerings while giving course content and instructional interaction their own development
and review processes. They also expose practical trade-offs, including preparation effort, finite
question-bank variety, and the need to keep replicated course artifacts consistent.
The model trials inform one part of this design. We retain llama3.1:8b because the evaluated
alternatives have not yet demonstrated an overall advantage across grounded explanation, conver-
sational continuity, latency, and serving compatibility. Credible 7B and 12B candidates remain
available for further assessment. The choice is therefore conditional on evidence and can change
without rebuilding the course architecture. The observed retrieval and fidelity failures also show
why improving a tutor requires attention to evidence preparation and dialogue handling alongside
model capability.
The next development stage should extend the course ingestion pipeline with relevant, reviewed
material supplied by instructors: supplementary cases, worked examples, lecture explanations, and
contextual material beyond the core assigned text. Better coverage can address missing evidence,
but adding documents alone does not ensure better answers; extraction quality, module mapping,
retrieval, and explanation fidelity must be evaluated together. A shared, versioned corpus can
support several interaction modes, including course discussion, guided examples, concept comparison,
and quiz practice, without maintaining a separate knowledge base for each mode. These modes
would complement general-purpose assistants such as ChatGPT by centering the instructor’s selected
context, expectations, and review of teaching materials. The local service’s purpose is to help
students reason within that context and apply it themselves.
Faculty participation should shape that development. A review workflow can allow professors
to inspect, revise, and approve quiz items and their supporting evidence, while student reports of
unclear or incorrect explanations can inform subsequent content and evaluation updates. Existing
review artifacts provide a starting point; instructor approval of the current banks is still pending. The
next pilot should assess sustained student uptake, acceptance of different interaction modes, and the
20
workload this process creates for faculty. Delayed and unassisted assessments, alongside comparisons
with existing resources and general-purpose assistants, would establish whether the system supports
independent learning. These findings should guide its expansion toward an instructor-informed
learning environment whose value comes from local context, useful feedback, and students’ own
effort.

title: Mapping the RAG Landscape: A Four Axis Taxonomy of Efficiency, Defense, Interactivity, and Reasoning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency across many tasks but remain limited by their static, parameter bound knowledge and their susceptibility to hallucinating information. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these issues by incorporating external retrieval into the generation process, grounding model outputs in verifiable and up to date sources. While prior surveys primarily focus on core RAG architectures and standard pipelines, recent research explores broader challenges and capabilities that extend beyond these foundational designs. This survey provides a consolidated and structured examination of contemporary RAG developments, organizing the field into a four axis taxonomy: improving retrieval efficiency, strengthening robustness and security, supporting user driven and interactive workflows, and enabling multi step or complex reasoning. We formalize key components of the RAG framework and review methods spanning dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies, embedding optimizations, and reinforcement learning based retrieval policies, highlighting how these advances influence practical deployment and system design. We also synthesize evaluation practices, domain specific applications, and architectural variants such as Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG. Finally, we outline persistent challenges related to retrieval quality, reliability, domain adaptation, scalability, and explainability, and identify opportunities for building RAG systems that are more reliable, adaptable, and transparent.

broader challenges and capabilities that extend beyond these foundational designs. This survey provides a consolidated and structured
examination of contemporary RAG developments, organizing the field into a four-axis taxonomy: improving retrieval efficiency,
strengthening robustness and security, supporting user-driven and interactive workflows, and enabling multi-step or complex reasoning.
We formalize key components of the RAG framework and review methods spanning dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies,
embedding optimizations, and reinforcement-learning–based retrieval policies, highlighting how these advances influence practical
deployment and system design. We also synthesize evaluation practices, domain-specific applications, and architectural variants such

1 Introduction
L
argeLanguage Models (LLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
have achieved remarkable progress in natural language
generation, supporting applications ranging from conversa-
tional systems to complex summarization and question an-
swering [7, 8]. Despite this progress, a longstanding limitation
of these models lies in their reliance on static, pre-trained
parameters, which restricts their ability to incorporate new or
domain-specific information. As a result, LLMs may produce
inaccurate or hallucinated content, particularly in settings
involving sparse inputs or attribute-heavy queries [9]. These
issues pose significant challenges in knowledge-intensive tasks
such as review generation [10, 11, 12, 13], dialogue systems
[14, 15, 16, 17], and data-to-text (D2T) generation [18,
19, 20], where factual correctness and contextual relevance
are essential [21]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
addresses these challenges by coupling LLMs with external
retrieval systems that provide access to relevant, verifiable
information at inference time [22, 23, 24]. Instead of depend-
ing solely on internal parametric knowledge, RAG models
dynamicallyretrievesemanticallyrelevantcontentfromstruc-
tured or unstructured corpora such as relational databases,
RDF graphs, or large-scale text collections [25, 26, 27]. This
retrieval-grounded formulation enables more accurate gen-

This retrieval-capable architecture also allows RAG sys-
tems to support personalized or user-specific workflows [28,
29, 30], such as product reviews, recommendation systems,
and user-facing assistants, as well as high-stakes domains
such as medical diagnosis [31, 32, 33], education [34], and
customer support where factual grounding is critical [35].
Reinforcement learning for LLMs [36, 37, 38] has further been
used to optimize retrieval strategies dynamically, improving
relevance and efficiency in real-world deployments [39]. We
review the formal structure of RAG and its architectural
variants-Naïve, Advanced, and Modular RAG-together with
their evaluation practices in §3.1.
Figure 1 summarizes the four core dimensions emphasized
in recent RAG research-efficiency, security, interactivity, and
complex reasoning-which reflect emerging priorities as RAG
transitions from experimental prototypes to widely deployed
systems and is increasingly integrated into training pipelines
and domain-adapted workflows [40]. This survey organizes
recent advancements along these four themes-compression
and efficiency [41], defensive RAG [40, 39], interactive and
user-centric RAG [27, 26], and complex reasoning [42, 21, 43]-
each tied to a central research question (RQ1-RQ4 below)
and characterized by representative contributions in retrieval
scoring, context construction, safety-aware filtering, personal-
ization, and multi-step reasoning.
These axes were selected because they represent emerg-
ing, orthogonal, and under-reviewed dimensions of the RAG
ecosystem-dimensions that extend beyond traditional tax-
onomies centered solely on retrieval or generation pipelines.
Previous surveys have primarily focused on dense-versus-
sparse retrieval comparisons, broad architectural overviews,

than treating RAG as a monolithic augmentation strategy,
we highlight concerns such as retrieval–generation coupling,

yet remain dispersed across the literature. By consolidating
these developments into four coherent axes, this survey of-

retrieval-augmented systems are evolving and where they
diverge from traditional LLM enhancement strategies.
To provide a concrete and answerable structure, we orga-
nize this review around four research questions that reflect
central, unresolved tensions in the RAG literature:
RQ1 (Efficiency):How can RAG systems maintain high
factualaccuracywhileoperatingundertheinference-time
constraints imposed by large-scale and heterogeneous
corpora-and which retrieval and compression strategies
most effectively navigate the accuracy–cost trade-off?
RQ2 (Defense):What principal vulnerabilities does exter-
nal retrieval introduce into LLM pipelines-including cor-
pus poisoning, demographic bias amplification, and pri-
vacy leakage-and how effectively do current defensive
architectures mitigate them?
RQ3 (Interactivity):To what extent can RAG systems
adapt to evolving user intent, interaction history, and
preference signals-and what mechanisms best balance
personalization with factual precision?
RQ4 (Reasoning):How does integrating retrieval into iter-
ative, step-conditioned reasoning pipelines improve per-
formance on multi-hop and knowledge-intensive tasks
compared to single-pass retrieval-and what architectural
properties prevent error accumulation across reasoning
steps?
These questions are neither fully solved nor fully open: §3
surveys what the literature has achieved on each, §5 maps
where each question remains unresolved, and §6 identifies the
research directions most likely to produce progress. Together,
they provide a lens for evaluating whether a given system

2 Survey Methodology
To ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility,
we adopt a structured literature review protocol inspired
by Snyder’s framework for systematic and semi-systematic
reviews [44] and aligned with the PRISMA 2020 principles.1
Our goal was to capture developments in RAG across the
rapid expansion period from January 2020 to January 2025.
We queried three major scholarly repositories-Google Scholar,
Semantic Scholar, and arXiv-using both broad and domain-
targeted keywords such as “retrieval-augmented genera-
tion”, “RAG LLM”, “RAG pipeline”, “RAG benchmark”,
“RAG evaluation”, “RAG defense”, “RAG fairness”, “multi-
hop retrieval LLM”, “RAG hallucination”, and “knowledge-
grounded generation”. These searches yielded approximately
780 records across peer-reviewed venues, preprints, and work-
shop papers, forming the identification stage of our PRISMA-
inspired workflow.
Screeningproceededunderexplicitinclusionandexclusion
criteria designed to ensure consistency across the surveyed
literature. We included works that (i) integrate retrieval and
generation within a unified pipeline, (ii) introduce method-
ological, architectural, or empirical innovations relevant to
RAG, (iii) propose RAG-specific benchmarks or evaluation
frameworks, or (iv) investigate security, robustness, fairness,
or safety aspects of retrieval-augmented LLMs. We excluded
works that (i) lack a retrieval component, (ii) describe stan-
dalone retrievers or standalone LLMs without integration, or
(iii) offer no technical or empirical contribution. The resulting
corpus forms the evidence base synthesized throughout this
survey and directly supports the four-axis taxonomy intro-
duced in later sections. This ensures that the review reflects
both breadth and depth, provides balanced coverage across
research directions, and maintains alignment with established
systematic review standards.
To further control for completeness, we supplemented the
keyword-based search with a targeted citation-snowballing
pass. Starting from one representative paper per taxonomy
axis plus the foundational RAG paper (Lewis et al., 2020 [45],
for the field as a whole; RAPTOR [46] for compression and
efficiency; SELF-RAG [47] for defensive RAG; Chat-REC [48]
for interactive, user-centric RAG; and GenGround [49] for
complex multi-step reasoning), we traced citations in both
directions, examining each seed paper’s own references (back-
ward) and the works that cite it (forward). This pass was
scoped as a targeted completeness check on the four axes
rather than a re-execution of the full identification stage,

3 Taxonomy of RAG-LLM Architectures
3.1 Conceptual Overview
RAG is a hybrid framework that enhances the capabilities
of Large Language Models (LLMs) by integrating real-time
information retrieval into the text generation process. Unlike
conventional LLMs that rely entirely on static, paramet-
ric knowledge learned during pre-training, RAG introduces
an external retrieval step that surfaces relevant, up-to-date
information from knowledge bases, databases, or document
repositories. This augmentation allows the model to pro-
duce more reliable and contextually grounded outputs while
mitigating hallucinations that arise when the model lacks
sufficient internal knowledge. The dynamic nature of retrieval
enables RAG systems to remain responsive in domains where
information evolves rapidly, making them especially effective
in knowledge-intensive or time-sensitive applications.
The RAG framework operates in two principal stages.
During the retrieval stage, the system identifies documents
or passages that are relevant to an input query using methods
such as Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR), which leverages neu-
ral embeddings for semantic matching, or sparse techniques
like BM25, which use term-frequency and inverse-document-
frequency scoring. Following retrieval, the generation stage
conditions a pre-trained language model, such as GPT or T5,
on the combined query and retrieved content to synthesize
a coherent and factually grounded response. This fusion step
ensuresthatgeneratedtextreflectsboththemodel’sparamet-
ric knowledge and the contextual evidence provided through
retrieval.
A key advantage of RAG lies in its adaptability. Tra-
ditional LLMs require costly retraining to incorporate new
information, whereas RAG systems can integrate updates at
inference time simply by retrieving from refreshed or domain-
specific corpora, improving factual accuracy in domains with
frequent updates (e.g., medicine, finance, law). This design
also improves interpretability, as users can trace generated
statementsbacktosupportingevidenceratherthananopaque
parametric prior, creating a more transparent generation
processwellsuitedtoknowledge-intensive,time-sensitive,and
high-stakes applications.
3.2 Theoretical Background
By separating knowledge retrieval from parametric genera-
tion, RAG systems overcome constraints imposed by static
training pipelines, remaining responsive in fields such as
healthcare, legal reasoning, and technical support where ac-
curacy and specificity are critical. This conceptual shift lays
the groundwork for hybrid systems that match the fluency
of LLMs with the factual grounding of information retrieval,
formalized below.
The retrieval component in RAG plays a central role in
enabling this hybrid functionality. Rather than generating

This hybridization of parametric and non-parametric

particularly their inability to access or incorporate new in-

systems overcome this rigidity by retrieving new informa-

and relevance offered by retrieval-based augmentation. These
methods create a more flexible and adaptive architecture that
supports dynamic reasoning, domain-aware responses, and

3.3 Historical Development
Early retrieval systems such as TF-IDF and BM25 enabled
large-scale lexical document search but were limited by
surface-level term matching, which hindered semantic flex-
ibility. This motivated the development of neural retrieval
methods-and eventually the tight coupling of retrieval with
generative language models-that provide deeper semantic
alignment and more flexible knowledge integration.
The introduction of neural retrieval models in the late
2010s marked a transformative shift toward more expressive
retrieval mechanisms. Dense retrieval systems such as DPR
employeddeepneuralnetworkstomapqueriesanddocuments
into a shared embedding space, enabling semantic similarity
computation via vector distance rather than relying solely
on lexical overlap. This innovation significantly improved
retrieval quality and made it possible to integrate external
evidence more effectively into downstream language genera-
tion tasks. The formalization of the RAG framework in 2020
by researchers at Facebook AI and OpenAI further advanced
this trajectory by unifying dense retrieval with generative
LLMs into a tightly coupled inference workflow. Unlike earlier
pipeline-style approaches, this unified architecture allowed
models to generate responses that were contextually coher-
ent and grounded in verifiable external knowledge, resulting
in substantial improvements on knowledge-intensive bench-
marks. More recently, long-context retrieval systems have ex-
tended this trajectory to entire documents and heterogeneous
knowledge sources, supporting multi-hop inference, dynamic
knowledge adaptation, and domain-specific reasoning.
3.4 Positioning Relative to Prior RAG Surveys
Recent surveys have examined RAG systems from a variety
of perspectives, yet each tends to focus on a specific subset
of challenges rather than providing a unified methodological
analysis. Brehme et al. [55] focus on evaluation methodolo-
gies, particularly the reliability of LLM-based judges and the
challenges associated with automated assessment of gener-
ated content. Hindi et al. [56] emphasize precision and in-
terpretability within legal-domain RAG, offering application-
specific insights but lacking generalizable evaluation frame-
works that extend beyond legal settings. Ni et al. [57] ap-
proach RAG from the standpoint of trustworthiness, dis-
cussing robustness, safety, and fairness but not addressing
dataset construction, indexing behavior, or generator-side
evaluation. Zheng et al. [58] extend RAG analysis into the
multimodal space by examining retrieval-augmented vision-
language systems, while Oche et al. [59] provide a broad sys-
tematic review that highlights year-wise progress and indus-
trial adoption trends. Finally, Singh et al. [26] survey agentic
RAG, emphasizing planning, tool use, and autonomous work-
flows in retrieval-augmented agents. However, none of these
surveys synthesize a unified evaluation perspective that spans
the core components of RAG pipelines, including datasets,
retrievers, indexing strategies, and generation modules.
Table 1 summarizes the distinctions between these prior
works and the focus of this survey. Existing literature pri-
marily centers on trust, domain specificity, multimodal rea-
soning, or agentic behavior, each typically treated as an
isolated concern rather than part of a broader organizing
structure. By contrast, this survey organizes RAG research
along four orthogonal axes-compression and efficiency, de-
fensive and safety-aware design, interactive and user-centric
personalization, and complex multi-step reasoning-each for-
malized through a dedicated objective, reference algorithm,
and synthesis of representative contributions. This structure
addresses practical needs for system builders who must jointly
reason about retrieval cost, safety, personalization, and rea-
soning depth rather than treating these as disconnected de-

3.6 Compression and Efficiency-Driven RAG
The compression and efficiency axis is included in the taxon-
omy because a large portion of recent RAG research explicitly
examines the computational bottlenecks introduced by re-
trieval at scale [46,60, 61, 62]. Asexternal corpora continue to
grow and RAG systems increasingly integrate heterogeneous
sources, a consistent theme across the literature is the need to
reduce retrieval latency, limit token overhead, and improve
the relevance–cost trade-off when selecting context. These
concerns are especially salient in production systems, where
inference cost and throughput place tight constraints on how
much context can be retrieved and processed. Many works
therefore treat retrieval as an optimization problem that
balances the benefits of additional evidence against the cost
of longer input sequences and slower decoding. This pattern
recurs across studies published from 2020-2025 and motivates
treating compression- and efficiency-oriented approaches as
a distinct dimension within the broader RAG landscape. In
practice, this axis captures methods that rethink how much
to retrieve, how to compress it, and how to allocate scarce
context budget without sacrificing model performance.

A complementary line of work made clear why cost-aware
selection matters.LLMs Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrel-

so that compression and pruning do not discard useful ev-

ways. Augmentation-aware retrievers explicitly model the
interaction between retrieved context and generative objec-
tives, encouraging retrieval policies that better align with the
downstream use of evidence and treating the retriever and
generator as co-adaptive modules rather than disjoint com-

idea to non-knowledge-intensive tasks such as classification
and text generation, using prompt reranking to better align
retrieved context with task-specific requirements [78]. Query-

strategies across multiple domains argued that one-size-fits-
all retrieval policies fail to generalize and advocated adaptive
mechanisms informed by dataset characteristics and task ob-

explicit by adopting utility-maximization formulations that
guide retrieval based on expected generation quality, directly
instantiating the utility termU(q,d i)that the efficiency ob-

3.1.2 Structural Compression and Hierarchical Retrieval
A second family of methods targets the compression cost
Cϕ(di)directly, reducing the token and computational foot-
print of retrieved evidence through structural means. On the
model side, structured pruning methods compress generative
backbones without significant loss in performance, offering a
lightweight alternative for latency-sensitive applications [79].
On the representation side, SANTA pretrains language mod-
els with an inductive bias toward structured data formats,
improving dense retrieval from semi-structured corpora such
as tables or knowledge graphs [80]. Rather than retrieving
flat sets of passages, RAPTOR organizes information into
recursive tree-based abstractions that can be traversed or
summarized,enablingmoreefficientreasoningovermulti-level
content;in effect,it implements theSelectTopDocuments step
of Algorithm 2 over a hierarchy of higher-level units rather
than a flat candidate set [46]. Compression itself was pushed
to an extreme by xRAG, which distills relevant information
into minimal tokens without compromising response quality-
an approach that directly minimizes the compression-cost
termC ϕ(di)in the efficiency objective [60]. Superposition
prompting complements these methods by exploring parallel
retrieval streams that reduce inference latency and filter noisy
documents [73].

3.1.3 Domain-Adaptive and Low-Supervision Retrieval
Athirdthemeconcernsadaptingretrievaltonewdomainsand

than tokens alone. The challenge of handling diverse retrieval
sources was tackled inRAG across Heterogeneous Knowl-

corpora with varying formats, quality, and domain alignment
through multi-source retrieval and fusion. To reduce the cost
of labeled supervision, PROMPTAGATOR proposed a few-
shot dense retrieval pipeline that required as few as eight
examples, using LLMs to synthesize training queries in data-
scarce settings and lowering the entry barrier for new retrieval
systems [82]. Retrieval was also used as a form of implicit
supervision in model synthesis for domain-specific languages
(DSLs), where in-domain exemplars guide generation and
help systems cope with out-of-distribution generalization [83].
Generalization to unseen tasks was advanced by UPRISE,
a universal prompt retrieval system for zero-shot evaluation
that leverages retrieval to design effective prompts without
task-specifictuning[84],whileintherecommendationdomain
RAG techniques were adapted for open-world personalization
by incorporating retrieval-augmented knowledge into recom-
mender pipelines [85].
As RAG expanded into specialized domains, structure-
and language-aware retrieval became central. Chunking
strategies tailored to financial documents were proposed to
improve retrieval granularity in dense, highly technical cor-
pora [86], and benchmarks such as LegalBench-RAG [87]
