5. Discussion
One of the core hypotheses of MatRAG is that the semantic hierarchy of
a clustering structure can be exploited through the nested MRL structure.
This means that coarser levels can be indexed at shorter prefix dimensions
without a significant loss of discriminative power. The retrieval results sup-
port this hypothesis; in fact, MatRAG outperforms the baselines on most
metrics while operating with a lower dimensionality of the embeddings at the
upper levels of the DAG. The largest improvements are seen in MuSiQue,
which may suggest that hierarchical traversal is most beneficial when single-
document similarity is insufficient to identify the relevant evidence chain.
Another core component of MatRAG is the entity-Jaccard re-ranking
signal. Hyperparameter analysis (Table 3) shows that the entity score com-
plements semantic similarity. Removing it entirely (α= 1.00) reduces per-
formance, particularly on 2Wiki, where compositional reasoning chains tend
to introduce numerous named entities across hops. Conversely, relying ex-
clusively on the entity signal (α= 0.00) also results in poor performance,
as entity overlap alone cannot capture semantic relevance. The optimal bal-
ance is achieved atα= 0.50across all datasets, indicating that the two
signals complement each other. Furthermore, the adaptive anchoring sched-
ule shows that neither anchoring the search exclusively to the original query
nor expanding it without control is sufficient. This is because the interpo-
lation guided byβt is necessary to exploit the retrieved context and, at the
same time, prevent semantic drift. This tension cannot be solved by static
scoring strategies.
The clustering analysis provided further evidence in support of the cen-
tral hypothesis of MatRAG. As shown in Table 9, the clusters obtained from
truncated Matryoshka prefixes are competitive with those obtained from
full-dimensional embeddings and tend to produce slightly better clustering
24
quality. This is refelected in lower DB indices and higher Silhouette scores
in several configurations. This suggests that, at the coarser levels of the hi-
erarchy, the additional dimensions of the full embedding contain redundant
information for forming well-separated clusters, which is removed by trun-
cation. Consequently, the Matryoshka indexing scheme reduces the cost of
similarity computations without compromising the quality of the hierarchy.
After verifying that MRL maintains the quality of the hierarchy, a com-
plementary question is whether this also applies to end-to-end retrieval, in
which truncated representations are used to traverse the DAG and rank doc-
uments. Tables10and11addressthisissuebycomparingMatryoshka’strun-
cated and full-dimensional embeddings during retrieval. Across all bench-
marks, the Matryoshka configuration achieves better performance consis-
tently in terms of both QA metrics and retrieval recall while reducing re-
sponse time. These results suggest that truncating embeddings to a lower-
dimensional subspace, as enabled by MRL, does not degrade retrieval qual-
ity. This behavior can be attributed to the way Matryoshka embeddings are
trained, as the most semantically relevant information is encoded in the lead-
ing dimensions. This effectively concentrates the signal and reduces noise in
the higher-dimensional components. Consequently, using only the truncated
embedding prefixes acts as a form of implicit regularization, as it discards di-
mensions that provide little discriminative information and could introduce
spurious similarity signals. The observed efficiency gains in response time
further reinforce the practical appeal of this design choice, as operating on
lower-dimensional vectors makes the retrieval step computationally cheaper
without sacrificing the quality of the retrieved documents or the downstream
answers.
The results obtained in our tests have several important implications
for the design of retrieval systems. First, coupling the embedding dimen-
sion with the index depth is a productive inductive bias because it exploits
the multi-scale structure of existing MRL models without requiring addi-
tional trainable parameters or training. Second, lightweight, entity-based
signals can effectively proxy the reasoning and planning typically performed
by LLMs, substantially reducing query time without a corresponding loss
in answer quality. Third, a performance comparable to that of graph-based
pipelines can be achieved with structured retrieval, without the need for
explicit KGs, entity linking and LLM-based summarization. This makes
MatRAG’s approach applicable to a broad range of corpora without requir-
ing explicit KG construction, eliminating the need for the preprocessing that
theseoperationsrequire. Together, thesefindingssuggestthatthedichotomy
between cheap, flat retrieval and expensive, structured retrieval can be par-
25
tially bridged by carefully co-designing the embedding strategy and the index
structure.
As for the MatRAG’s limitations, we observe that the entity extraction
step of MatRAG relies on GLiNER [41], which can fail to identify domain-
specific entities or produce inaccurate extractions on corpora with unusual
terminology. Errors in this step propagate into the budget control mecha-
nism and the re-ranking signal. Additionally, the quality of the hierarchical
index depends on the density of the embedding space. For instance, clusters
may be poorly defined on corpora with very uniform semantic distributions,
reducing the discriminative value of the DAG traversal. Finally, the greedy,
top-down traversal of the DAG selects the most similar cluster centroid at
each level, committing irrevocably to that branch without a backtracking
mechanism. An error at a coarse level, where shorter Matryoshka prefixes
provide less discriminative representations, propagates downward and may
exclude relevant documents from the candidate set, regardless of their simi-
larity at finer levels. The nearest overlapping assignment mitigates this risk
by ensuring that each node is reachable frompparent clusters, thus provid-
ing redundant paths through the hierarchy. However, if the correct branch
is not among the selected parents of a relevant node, the traversal offers no
recovery mechanism.
6. Conclusion
Inthispaper, wehavepresentedMatRAG,ahierarchicalRAGframework
for multi-hop Question Answering that leverages the structural alignment
between density-based clustering and MRL. MatRAG organizes a document
corpus into a DAG of clusters, associating each level with a correspond-
ingly shorter MRL prefix dimension. This enables top-down retrieval that is
dimensionality-aware and semantically structured. Unlike the multi-hop ap-
proach used by many KG-based RAGs, MatRAG employs an entity-driven
iterative mechanism that controls the retrieval budget through entity counts
and re-ranks candidates based on entity overlap. Furthermore, an adap-
tive anchoring schedule mitigates query drift by progressively increasing the
weight of the original query as the budget is consumed.
Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, designed
to compare MatRAG with seven representative baselines, demonstrate that
MatRAG consistently delivers superior retrieval and answer quality across
a wide range of settings. Additionally, it reduces indexing time by orders
of magnitude compared to graph-based methods and reduces query-time
latency by over35.14%compared to NaiveRAG.
26
Future work will explore three main directions. The first is predicting
a query-dependent retrieval budget, which adjusts the number of retrieved
documents based on the query complexity. The second direction involves
learning adaptive cluster connectivity, which replaces a fixed number of par-
entassignmentswithahierarchythatbetterreflectsthesemanticstructureof
the corpus. The third direction involves a query-dependent anchoring sched-
ule that balances the original and expanded queries dynamically, enabling
more effective exploration while preserving alignment with the question.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
abstract: Context. Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality. However, existing research remains fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting our understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle. Aim. We consolidate the state of the art on architectural degradation by examining how researchers measure it, which metrics and tools support its assessment, and how existing approaches address remediation. Method. We conducted a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies. We supported screening, data extraction, and classification with a locally executed LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication. We then analyzed the resulting taxonomies and their cross-dimensional relationships. Results and Conclusions. We identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. In contrast, remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions and shows substantially less consolidation. Overall, the field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. Our results provide a structured view of the available techniques and identify the diagnosis-remediation gap as a key direction for future research.

1 Introduction
Software architecture underpins the long-term maintainability, modifiability, scalability, and evolvability of a sys-
tem [10]. Yet as systems evolve to meet new requirements, technologies, and business constraints, their implementation
inevitably drifts away from the intended design. This phenomenon,architectural degradationorerosion, gradually
erodes architectural integrity and threatens sustainability [11, 21].
Degradation is rarely the result of a single poor decision. It accumulates through continuous evolution, undocumented
changes, architectural violations, growing dependency complexity, and routine maintenance. Over time, systems become
harder to understand, maintain, and extend, while organizations face rising costs and mounting architectural technical
debt [16]. Understanding how to identify, measure, and remediate architectural degradation has therefore become a
pressing research and industrial challenge.
Over the past two decades, researchers have proposed a broad spectrum of techniques to tackle this challenge,
including architecture conformance checking, architectural smell detection, dependency analysis, architecture recovery,
software metrics, static and dynamic analysis, and, more recently, AI-assisted approaches [17, 23]. Numerous tools
support degradation assessment, and remediation strategies have been proposed at the code, architectural, organizational,
and runtime levels. Despite this substantial body of work, the knowledge remains fragmented. Existing secondary
studies typically examine only isolated aspects, metrics, recovery, or erosion detection, making it difficult to see how
measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies relate to one another. Consequently, researchers
and practitioners still lack a unified view of the architectural degradation landscape and the connections among its
fundamental building blocks.
To fill this gap, we conducted a Multivocal Literature Review (MLR) [9] that synthesizes evidence from both peer-
reviewed and grey literature. To handle the large-scale analysis, we employed an LLM-assisted pipeline based on
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), multi-model validation, and human adjudication. Beyond independently
classifying the existing literature, we connect the resulting taxonomies through cross-dimensional and maturity
analyses, providing an integrated perspective of the architectural degradation ecosystem. This study makes the
following contributions:
•a comprehensive multivocal literature review on architectural degradation;
•four evidence-based taxonomies;
•an integrated and maturity analysis of the research landscape.
Our synthesis reveals a striking convergence: the community has built a mature, structurally focused diagnostic
apparatus, static analysis, structural design metrics, and detection-oriented tooling dominate the field. In contrast,
remediation remains fragmented across code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions, and the transition
from detecting degradation to acting on it is still comparatively immature. These findings offer researchers a structured
agenda for closing the diagnosis–remediation gap and give practitioners an evidence-based map of the techniques
available for assessing and managing architectural degradation.
Paper structure:Section 2 describes the background and the related works, while Section 3 the design of this study.
Section 4 presents the obtained results and Section 5 discusses them. Section 6 identifies some threats to validity while
Section 7 draws the conclusion.
2 Background and Related Works
In this section, we review existing studies and present a detailed comparison with our own research.

The evolution of software architecture topic over time has been extensively investigated in the software engineering
literature. This section summarizes the most relevant contributions in this area, covering a variety of approaches
and findings. The existing work addresses both conceptual frameworks and practical solutions, with a particular
focus on improving recovery techniques and mitigating associated risks. However, a comprehensive understanding of
architectural degradation requires examining not only how it is detected and measured, but also the tools that support
its assessment and the strategies proposed for its remediation. In this regard, there remains a need for a comprehensive
investigation integrating these complementary dimensions of architectural degradation.
To show how research in this area has evolved, we present the selected studies in chronological order. The earliest
review was conducted by De Silva and Balasubramaniam [23], while the most recent, to the best of our knowledge, is
by Baabad et al. [3]. The primary objective of each study is summarized in Table 1.
The study by De Silva and Balasubramaniam [23] provides structured overviews of architectural erosion, classifying
existing techniques into prevention, minimization, and repair. The authors analyze the methodologies, tools, and
processes associated with each category, emphasizing that architectural erosion cannot be effectively addressed through
a single strategy. Instead, they advocate for a combined approach that integrates multiple techniques to manage the
problem more comprehensively.
Herold et al. [10] conducted a literature review focusing on empirical studies related to architectural degradation
and consistency checking. The objective was to assess the current state of research and identify areas that have been
underexplored. Their findings indicate that many proposed solutions to remediate architectural degradation rely on case
studies with limited generalizability. As a result, the authors highlight the need for more rigorous empirical validation,
including controlled experiments and large-scale studies, to better understand the effectiveness of these approaches.
These insights were later reinforced in their subsequent work, where they outlined a roadmap for future research [10].
The work by [30] examines the evolution of architecture recovery techniques, particularly the transition from manual
to automated approaches. The study reflects the growing influence of industry demands for faster development cycles,
which has driven the need for more efficient recovery methods. The authors emphasize the importance of maintaining
architectural integrity in rapidly evolving systems and suggest that future research should focus on automated and
semi-automated solutions.

4 Noman Ahmad, Ruoyu Su, Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, and Davide Taibi
Sinkala et al. [24] carried out a mapping study investigating the application of architecture recovery techniques in
software product lines (SPLs). The study highlights the challenges of adapting approaches designed for single systems to
the more complex SPL context. In particular, it identifies limitations in the handling of shared assets and the management
of variability. The findings suggest that existing techniques do not adequately address architectural degradation in
SPLs, especially in systems that evolve from cloned or ad hoc codebases and accumulate technical debt over time.
Baabad et al. [2] reviewed the architectural degradation in open-source software, identifying key contributing factors
such as frequent modifications, rapid system evolution, and limited architectural awareness among developers. The
study also highlights common indicators of degradation, including code smells and architectural smells, and emphasizes
the need for more research to better understand these causes and improve remediation strategies.
Li et al. [17] conducted a survey to explore architectural erosion from a practitioner’s perspective. The study aims to
understand how developers perceive, identify, and manage erosion in practice. The results indicate that architectural
erosion is viewed as a structural issue affecting software quality, driven by both technical and organizational factors.
Practitioners typically recognize erosion through its symptoms and attempt to mitigate its impact, although the study
highlights the need for stronger empirical support for existing tools and techniques.
Finally, Baabad et al. [3] presented a mapping study focusing on metrics for architectural degradation. The study
categorizes existing metrics and demonstrates their role in identifying architectural decay. However, it also highlights
the need for further investigation into how these metrics function and how effectively they capture different aspects of
degradation.
Although previous secondary studies have examined architectural erosion, recovery techniques, degradation metrics,
and practitioner perceptions, they generally address these dimensions separately. None provides an integrated syn-
thesis connecting measurement approaches, metrics, tool support, and remediation strategies across the architectural
degradation lifecycle. Our work addresses this gap through a multivocal literature review that combines academic and
practitioner evidence and analyzes both the individual dimensions and their cross-dimensional relationships.
In summary, existing secondary studies provide valuable but largely dimension-specific views of architectural
degradation. What remains missing is a synthesis that jointly examines how degradation is measured, which metrics
operationalize it, which tools support its assessment, and which strategies are available for remediation. Our study
addresses this gap by integrating these four dimensions and examining their relationships across the architectural
degradation lifecycle.
3 Methodology
This section addresses methodology. we defined the research goal and the search process such as inclusion and exclusion
criteria.
3.1 Goal and Research Questions
The purpose of this study is to investigate the phenomenon of architectural degradation and identify the approaches to
measure and remediate architectural degradation. Therefore, we conducted a multivocal literature review supported by
Large Language Models. Based on the objectives of our study, we defined the following Research Questions (RQs).
RQ1 Which approaches have been proposed for measuring architectural degradation?
Manuscript submitted to ACM
Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate 5
The purpose of RQ1 is to explore the different methods that have been proposed or developed to measure software
architectural degradation. Architectural degradation has been investigated through a broad range of approaches,
including metric-based analyses, architecture conformance checking, smell detection, dependency analysis, graph-based
techniques, and machine learning methods. However, these approaches have been proposed independently, making
it difficult to obtain a comprehensive view of the available solutions and their characteristics. This analysis provides
researchers and practitioners with a consolidated overview of the current state of the art and reveals areas requiring
further methodological advances.
RQ2 Which metrics have been considered for measuring architectural degradation?
RQ2 addresses the metrics used to assess software architectural degradation. Architectural degradation cannot be
directly observed or quantified. Instead, existing studies rely on a variety of proxy metrics that capture structural
properties, architectural symptoms, software evolution, and quality-related consequences. Despite the extensive body
of research, there is currently no consolidated understanding of which metrics are adopted, which architectural dimen-
sions they capture, or whether a common measurement framework has emerged. RQ2 therefore aims to systematically
identify and classify the metrics used to assess architectural degradation, providing a comprehensive overview of the
architectural properties they measure and highlighting opportunities for more standardized measurement frameworks.
RQ2 aims to systematically identify and classify the metrics used to assess architectural degradation, providing a compre-
hensive overview of the architectural properties they measure. This analysis highlights inconsistencies, underexplored
dimensions, and opportunities for developing more standardized and comprehensive measurement frameworks.
RQ3 Which tools have been proposed to support architectural degradation analysis?
The research question RQ3 aims to find several tools and approaches by concentrating on these solutions, which
can assist in measuring software architectural degradation and understanding how they address different aspects of
architectural degradation. Although numerous techniques for detecting architectural degradation have been proposed,
their practical adoption largely depends on the availability of supporting tools. Existing tools differ substantially in
terms of supported analyses, automation capabilities, integration with development environments, scalability, and
maintenance support. However, there is currently no comprehensive overview of the available tool ecosystem. RQ3
aims to identify and classify the tools proposed for assessing architectural degradation, analyzing their supported
functionalities, underlying approaches, and level of automation. This provides practitioners with an overview of existing
tool support while highlighting research opportunities for more integrated and continuously operating solutions.
RQ4 Which approaches and techniques have been proposed for remediating architectural degradation?
We need to systematically understand the approaches and techniques proposed in the literature that can help to
remediate architectural degradation. Identifying and classifying approaches in RQ4 can provide insights to solve the
concern of architectural degradation. Moreover, by uncovering the gaps in current techniques and approaches, this
research RQ4 aims to direct future architectural sustainability research and development. Detecting architectural
degradation represents only the first step toward preserving software architecture. Long-term software sustainability
Manuscript submitted to ACM
6 Noman Ahmad, Ruoyu Su, Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, and Davide Taibi
requires effective remediation strategies capable of preventing, mitigating, or repairing architectural degradation
throughout the software lifecycle. Although numerous studies focus on degradation detection, considerably less
attention has been devoted to remediation. RQ4 aims to systematically identify and classify the approaches proposed
to remediate architectural degradation, including preventive, corrective, and continuous remediation techniques. By
synthesizing existing solutions, this research question highlights current limitations and identifies research gaps toward
proactive and automated architectural sustainability.
3.2 Search Strategy
Our search methodology included the following steps: selection of bibliographic sources, definition of inclusion and
exclusion criteria, selection of search terms, data extraction, and data classification (Figure 1).
We used the LRM/LLM configuration (rules and steps) described in Section 3.3 for the search and selection, data
extraction, and data classification processes (Figure 1) and carried out two execution rounds: one for the comprehensive
reading and another for the title and abstract selection. Additionally, we provided a full description of the outcomes
produced by LRM/LLM for each stage in Table 9.
All the steps were performed within a secure environment of the university’s supercomputer locally. We didn’t use
any cloud services or external API’s. PDFs documents were utilized only for inference and were not used to fine-tune
or train any model. In addition, all downloaded PDFs were removed after processing, and each job was operated in an
isolated environment without persistent storage, guaranteeing that no data remained on the system after completion.
3.2.1 Search String.To provide complete coverage of the literature, multiple terms associated with software architecture
degradation were utilized in the search strategy, including degradation, aging, erosion, decay, drift, deterioration,
degeneration, consistency, adherence, and conformance. Since several of these terms are used interchangeably in prior
studies, they were included as alternative keywords. Furthermore, wildcard characters (*) were applied (e.g., software
architec and degrad‘) to capture different lexical forms of the terms, such as singular and plural nouns, verb forms, and
other word variations. Accordingly, the following search string was defined:
Search String
“software architec*”AND(degrad* OR aging* OR erosion* OR decay* OR drift* OR deteriorat* OR degenerat* OR
consisten* OR adher* OR conform*)
3.2.2 Bibliographic Sources.To identify peer-reviewed studies, we selected a set of well-established bibliographic
databases based on the guidelines proposed by Kitchenham and Charters [ 13]. These sources are widely regarded
as representative of the software engineering research community and have been extensively utilized in previous
secondary studies. Accordingly, the selected databases includedScopus,Springer Nature,Web of Science (WoS),IEEE
Xplore, and theACM Digital Library. To complement the academic literature with gray literature, data were collected
from several web-based sources, includingYahoo,Bing,Google,Google Scholar(for non-peer-reviewed publications),
andStack Overflow. These platforms were chosen because they provide access to practitioner knowledge, industrial
experiences, technical reports, blogs, and other forms of gray literature that may not be indexed in traditional academic
databases. Their use is consistent with established guidelines for conducting Multivocal Literature Reviews (MLRs) [9].
For example, Janes et al. [12] employed general-purpose search engines and practitioner-oriented platforms such as
Stack Overflowto supplement academic evidence in their systematic gray literature review on microservices.

Traditional NLP methods can also do this task, but they needed feature engineering that was specific to the job,
training data, and a lot of tweaking for each classification dimension. However, LLMs enabled us to:
• Extract multi-label, semantically rich data from brief sentences without the need for custom pipeline engineering;
•Use similar prompt logic throughout dimensions;
•Evaluate results at scale using model agreement and sampling.
The recent studies performed by [5], [22], [25] show that LLMs can help practitioners and researchers with encour-
aging levels of dependability across a wide range of software engineering tasks, such as classification, summarization,
and decision-making.
Previous studies synthesizing evidence [?] on architectural degradation have predominantly relied on manual coding,
keyword-based techniques, or predefined taxonomies, approaches that can become increasingly resource-intensive
when applied to large and heterogeneous bodies of literature [17? ?].
In contrast, our approach, successfully applied in similar tasks [22, 25, 26] integrates LLM-based semantic extraction
with multi-model cross-validation and human adjudication, enabling the systematic analysis of a large and heterogeneous
corpus of academic and gray literature. This pipeline supports the extraction and classification of measurement
approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies at scale while preserving human oversight throughout the process.
Importantly, our aim is not to replace established empirical review methods, but to support their application at a larger
scale while maintaining methodological rigor and traceability.
In our study, we analyzed peer-reviewed and grey literature on software architectural degradation and extracted
information on measurement approaches, metrics, supporting tools, and remediation strategies. Our methodology
followed five main steps:
(1) Using a large reasoning model to make a decision about papers inclusion and data extraction;
(2) Validation of the output with three LLMs and human validation;
(3) Clean and unify the extracted data;

3.4 LRM/LLMIntegration, Experimental Design and Validation
LRM/LLM Model Roles:We assigned a unique role to each model based on its responsibility in the data analysis
pipeline as follows (Table 7):
• Large Reasoning Model (LRM):Marco-o1 is responsible to extract the required information. For each prompt,
it receives input data (e.g., title/abstract, full paper), it makes decision first of all about title and abstract selection
and then full read the selected papers and later on classifies the data into categories, and provides information.
Its output formed the basis for further verification and was referred to as LRM responses throughout the study.
• Validation Models (V1/V2/V3):Llama, Mistral-NeMo, and Qwen are used for validation task. They receive the
similar input as the LRM and used to evaluate against the LRM’s reasoning and output.
Prompting Techniques:We applied prompt engineering strategies to steer LRM/LLM in classifying approaches
to measure and remediate software architectural degradation. Prior research indicates that in-context learning via
chat-based prompting can achieve performance comparable to or exceeding that of fine-tuning, while avoiding its
higher computational cost [6]. In our setup, each prompt comprised two elements: asystem message, which defined the
assistant’s role and specified the required output structure, and auser message, which supplied the contextual input (e.g
title/abstract). The model was instructed to produce a structured JSON output including:
•The predicted category;
•A briefdescription;
•The correspondingreasoning.
We employed a few-shot learning approach combined with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [28] to encourage
more transparent and accurate classification.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG):.We implemented a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism into
our pipeline for both full-document processing. RAG enhances the model’s input with relevant external knowledge by
retrieving semantically similar, previously labeled instances from the dataset using embedding-based similarity search.
In our case, scientific PDFs exceed typical model context limits, each document was first converted into text, segmented
into overlapping chunks, and indexed using embedding-based similarity search (FAISS). The model was then instructed
to generate a structured JSON output containing one concise answer per category. This approach enables efficient
processing of long documents while ensuring that classification decisions are evidence-based, context-aware, and less
prone to hallucination.
Running LRM/LLM:.For executing this big scale analysis, we CSC’s Mahti supercomputer, using vLLM to serve the
LRM/LLM for large-scale inference1. Mahti is a high-performance computing platform intended for computationally
and data-intensive research, providing more than 180,000 CPU cores connected through a fast interconnect network.
Our jobs leveraged up to four NVIDIA A100 GPUs, ensuring high-speed and memory-efficient inference to process
large volumes of data effectively. We employed deterministic decoding (temperature = 0, max_tokens = 1900) with a

Human Validation:Since no previous study reported findings on the accuracy of LLMs for the task at hand, we
designed a validation involving three human experts mimicking the LLM validator’s roles. The goal was to assess the
quality and correctness of the model-generated outputs and to determine whether the validation models provided
consistent judgments. Our validation followed a three-step protocol.
• One expert independently reviewed the same input provided to the LRM and the three validation models (V1–V3),
and manually evaluated the correctness of each model’s motivation. For each case, the expert indicated whether
they agreed or disagreed with the LRM’s motivation, noted the majority decision among the validation models,
and identified the models they considered correct.
• A second expert repeated the same evaluation independently and documented their level of agreement with the
first expert’s judgments.
• In cases of disagreement between the first two reviewers, a third expert was brought in to independently assess
the same outputs. Final decisions were made through majority voting among the three validators.

progress has not been uniform across the architectural degradation lifecycle. The literature has advanced considerably
in understanding how degradation can be identified, whereas substantially less agreement exists on how it should be
prevented, remediated, and continuously managed.
This imbalance appears consistently across all four research questions. Measurement approaches, metric families, and
tooling exhibit a high degree of convergence, indicating that the community largely shares a common understanding of
how architectural degradation should be assessed. In contrast, remediation strategies remain fragmented across technical,
architectural, and organizational interventions, with no comparable consensus emerging. More than a decade ago, De
Silva and Balasubramaniam argued that effectively controlling architectural erosion requires combining prevention,
detection, and restoration strategies rather than relying on isolated technical solutions [23]. The evidence collected in
this review suggests that this objective has not yet been fully achieved. While the literature provides a mature ecosystem
of techniques for recognizing degradation, considerably less attention has been devoted to understanding how different
remediation strategies should be selected, coordinated, and sustained over time.

Perhaps the most consistent finding is the strongstructural biasthat characterizes the literature. Static & Structural
Analysis dominates the measurement approaches, while Structural Design Metrics appear in more than 90% of the
primary studies. This observation agrees with previous work showing that architectural degradation is primarily
identified through structural symptoms, architectural anomalies, and conformance violations rather than runtime
evidence [3, 19]. Our results indicate that this predominance extends beyond the choice of metrics. Structural reasoning
shapes the entire assessment process, influencing how degradation is measured, how evidence is collected, and how
supporting tools are designed.
By comparison, relatively few studies investigate degradation through system execution. Dynamic analysis, runtime
metrics, and runtime-aware remediation remain markedly underrepresented. This imbalance is understandable because
structural artifacts are easier to collect, deterministic to analyze, and supported by mature tooling. However, archi-
tectural degradation is inherently an evolutionary phenomenon. It emerges through continuous software evolution,
changing requirements, operational pressures, and accumulated design decisions rather than from static structure
alone. Consequently, assessment approaches centred primarily on structural evidence are likely to identify degradation
only after its effects have already materialized within the implemented architecture. This predominance of structural
assessment contrasts with the broader view that architectural quality should be continuously preserved throughout
software evolution rather than periodically evaluated [14].
This interpretation also complements the observations of Li et al. [?], who argue that architectural erosion should
not be viewed solely as a structural phenomenon but also as the result of organizational and evolutionary processes.
While the literature increasingly acknowledges these broader causes, the methods used to assess degradation remain
overwhelmingly centred on structural properties. The evidence therefore reveals a disconnect between how architectural
degradation is conceptualized and how it is empirically investigated.
The end-to-end paths reported in Figure 2 reinforce this interpretation. The most informative observation is not that
the dominant path represents only 18 studies, but that nearly all dominant paths follow the same sequence of static
analysis, structural metrics, and detection tools before diverging during remediation. This remarkable stability indicates
that methodological diversity is concentrated almost entirely after degradation has been identified. In other words, the
community has largely converged on how degradation should be observed, while substantially different views remain
on how corrective actions should be designed, prioritized, and combined.
This pattern also clarifies the conclusions of previous secondary studies. De Silva and Balasubramaniam organized
the literature into complementary prevention, detection, and restoration strategies [23], whereas Li et al. highlighted the
broad spectrum of techniques proposed to detect and address architectural erosion [18]. The evidence synthesized here
suggests that this diversity is not uniformly distributed across the degradation lifecycle. Instead, it emerges primarily after
degradation has been diagnosed. Before that point, the literature exhibits a remarkably stable methodological pipeline
centred on structural assessment. The principal challenge therefore appears to have shifted from improving degradation
detection toward understanding how different remediation strategies should interact to preserve architectural integrity
throughout software evolution.
1. Key Take Away.
Architectural degradation research has reached methodological maturity in diagnosis but not in reme-
diation.The literature consistently converges on static analysis, structural metrics, and detection tools to identify
degradation. In contrast, remediation remains fragmented across code-level, architectural, and organizational

5.1 Detection Without Action
A second concern emerging from the findings is the clearimbalance between diagnosis and intervention. The
literature provides a rich ecosystem of approaches for identifying architectural degradation, including structural
metrics, rule checking, smell detection, and dedicated analysis tools. By contrast, considerably fewer studies investigate
how degradation should be addressed once it has been detected. This imbalance is particularly evident in the tooling
landscape, where Detection & Analysis Tools largely outnumber Remediation-Support Tools. The evidence therefore
suggests that the community has invested substantially more effort in answering the question“Is the architecture
degrading?”than“What should be done next?”
The remediation landscape reveals an additional level of fragmentation. Code-Level Repair, Architecture-Level
Repair, and Process & Organizational Remediation all receive substantial attention, yet they are rarely investigated
as complementary components of the same intervention strategy. Most studies focus on one level of action while
treating the others as external concerns. However, architectural degradation rarely originates from a single cause. It
accumulates through design decisions, implementation shortcuts, evolving requirements, and organizational constraints
acting simultaneously. This observation closely resembles the challenges discussed in the Architectural Technical Debt
literature, where long-term architectural quality depends on continuously managing the consequences of local design
decisions rather than periodically correcting accumulated problems [15, 20].
The unexpectedly high presence of Recovery & Reverse-Engineering tools reinforces this interpretation. Rather
than preventing degradation during software evolution, a considerable portion of the literature concentrates on
reconstructing architectural knowledge after it has already been lost. Similar observations motivated previous work on
architecture-preserving refactorings, where architectural recovery is viewed as a prerequisite for restoring architectural
integrity rather than preventing degradation in the first place [27]. Together, these findings suggest that a significant
part of the literature remains inherently reactive, addressing degradation after architectural knowledge has already
deteriorated.
Another notable observation concerns predictive approaches. Despite the increasing availability of software reposi-
tories, architectural histories, and development analytics, Machine Learning and Prediction remain among the least
represented measurement approaches, while AI/ML-based tooling also occupies only a limited portion of the landscape.
Rather than indicating a lack of interest in artificial intelligence, these results suggest that predictive architectural degra-
dation remains an emerging research direction. Existing studies continue to rely predominantly on structural indicators
and threshold-based reasoning, whereas comparatively little attention has been devoted to forecasting degradation
trajectories before architectural symptoms become observable. This gap appears particularly significant considering
that architectural degradation is inherently progressive and cumulative, making early intervention substantially more
valuable than late diagnosis.

The concentration of approaches, metrics, and tools aroundstructural assessmentgives researchers several ways to
examine dependencies, modular boundaries, and architectural violations. Far fewer approaches explicitly investigate how
these properties change: the catalogue contains 78 static and structural approaches, compared with seven evolutionary
and historical approaches. This difference highlights an opportunity to connect structural observations across successive
versions and examine when architectural changes indicate deterioration. Static techniques can contribute to this
investigation, provided that their application and interpretation account for the system’s evolution.
Choosing among the available structural techniques requires understandingwhat additional evidence each
contributes. Techniques may examine similar properties while relying on different assumptions, inputs, or thresholds.
Combining them may broaden the assessment, but it may also reproduce the same information through several indicators.
Comparative evaluations would help distinguish complementary measurements from redundant ones and establish
whether their conclusions remain consistent across systems and stages of evolution.
The breadth of remediation extends across implementation, architecture, and development practices, with 66 code-

as immature and makesintervention selectiona more precise concern. An architectural violation, for example, may
require both a technical correction and changes to the practices that allowed it to recur. The catalogue identifies possible
responses, but does not establish which combinations are appropriate under particular conditions. Studies connecting
the diagnosed problem to the intervention rationale, implementation costs, and outcomes over subsequent releases
would provide stronger guidance for these decisions.

and neither alone establishes how degradation develops.
Comparative studies would make extensive catalogues easier to use by clarifying technique selection and applicability.

repair advocated by previous reviews [18, 23].
3. Key Take Away.
The breadth of available techniques makes their selection and integration a central research challenge.
Structural assessment and remediation offer extensive catalogues, but their size alone does not establish maturity
or effectiveness. Comparative evaluations are needed to clarify which techniques provide complementary evidence,
when particular interventions are appropriate, and whether their benefits persist over time. Shared benchmarks

5.3 Implications for Practice and Research
Our review brings together techniques for observing architectural degradation and strategies for addressing it, while
showing a stronger emphasis on structural assessment within measurement approaches and tooling. We therefore
identify a practical need to distinguisharchitectural anomalies from evidence of architectural degradation.
Although coupling, complexity, or a detected smell can identify a concern, establishing degradation requires examining
its relationship with architectural intent and its consequences for system evolution. Conformance checks and recovered
architectural views can support this interpretation; however, recovered views describe the implemented structure and
may reproduce the dependencies under investigation. We consequently recommend distinguishing recovered structure
from intended constraints before using it to guide corrective action.
Through RQ4, we identified strategies addressing both software structure and development practices, which motivates
connectingarchitectural repair with measures that prevent recurrence. While refactoring may remove an
unwanted dependency, architectural rules, decision documentation, and review responsibilities may help prevent its
reintroduction. We therefore recommend comparing technical repair alone with repair accompanied by changes to
architectural guidance or development practices. Such comparisons would establish whether organizational measures
reduce recurring violations sufficiently to justify their cost, thereby giving empirical substance to combined erosion-
control strategies [23].
Evaluating those interventions also requires distinguishingmeasurements of architectural deterioration from
descriptions of structural change. Although RQ 2 identifies a broad catalogue of structural metrics, changes in
coupling or complexity do not necessarily imply worsening maintainability or increasing change effort. We thus
propose examining when metric changes coincide with architectural violations, changes spreading across component
boundaries, or more costly modifications, while comparing cases in which similar structural changes support legitimate
evolution. The resulting evidence would help determine both when a measurement warrants intervention and whether
an observed improvement indicates successful remediation.
Across RQ3 and RQ4, we observed an emphasis on detection-oriented tooling alongside a broad range of remediation
strategies; we consequently identifyexplicit links between degradation symptoms and corrective actionsas
a research priority. While diagnostic evidence identifies the concern, selecting a repair also requires considering
architectural constraints and expected evolution costs. We therefore propose investigating how those factors justify
particular interventions, so that supporting tools can explain the rationale and trade-offs behind their recommenda-
tions. Evaluations could then establish whether the recommended actions address the diagnosed degradation without
transferring dependencies or maintenance burdens elsewhere [15].
 4. Architectural degradation should increasingly be managed as a continuous architectural governance
activity rather than a periodic assessment task.
Future research should prioritize runtime-aware assessment, decision-support for remediation, and predictive
architectural governance to complement the mature ecosystem of structural analysis and detection techniques.

6 Threats to Validity
This section discusses the potential threats to validity following the categories proposed by Wohlin et al. [29].
Construct Validity.Construct validity concerns whether the collected data accurately represents the phenomenon
under investigation [29]. We investigated approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation techniques related to architectural
degradation across both peer-reviewed and grey literature. However, architectural degradation lacks a universally
accepted terminology, and closely related concepts such as erosion, decay, drift, aging, technical debt, and architecture
conformance frequently overlap. In particular, several primary studies treat architecture conformance as evidence
or a proxy of architectural degradation, whereas others consider it a distinct research topic. Consequently, some
included studies may operationalize degradation differently, potentially affecting the resulting taxonomy. Moreover,
our LLM-supported extraction and classification pipeline may have interpreted ambiguous descriptions differently from
human experts, particularly in heterogeneous grey literature. Our manual validation also showed that one validation
model (Qwen) consistently achieved lower agreement than the other models for several extraction and classification
tasks. Rather than relying on a single model, we mitigated these threats by defining explicit inclusion criteria, grounding
model responses through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), validating every extraction using three independent
LLMs, identifying disagreements through model consensus, and resolving them through human adjudication and
majority voting.
Internal Validity.Internal validity concerns whether the reported findings originate from the analyzed evidence
rather than methodological artifacts [29]. Our study relied on LLMs to support study selection, information extraction,
and thematic classification. Different LLMs may encode different prior knowledge, reasoning strategies, or alignment
policies, potentially producing different classifications for ambiguous cases. Likewise, prompt formulation and category
consolidation may influence the final taxonomy. We reduced them by assigning specialized roles to the models, validating
every output through a multi-model consensus process, performing several rounds of iterative refinement before final
validation, and involving multiple independent human validators to resolve disagreements through majority voting.
External Validity.External validity concerns the generalizability of the findings beyond the analyzed dataset [ 29].
We analyzed 284 primary studies retrieved from multiple scientific databases together with grey literature, providing
broad coverage of both academic and industrial perspectives. Nevertheless, our dataset only includes English-language
publications indexed by the selected databases and search engines that were available at the time of the search.
Furthermore, grey literature varies substantially in reporting quality and methodological rigor. Although we applied
identical inclusion criteria, extraction procedures, and validation processes to both peer-reviewed and grey literature,
some industrial practices, non-English publications, or emerging trends may remain underrepresented. Future updates of
the multivocal literature review may therefore identify additional approaches, metrics, tools, or remediation techniques.
Conclusion Validity.Conclusion validity concerns whether the conclusions are adequately supported by the
available evidence [29]. Our study synthesizes recurring patterns across 284 primary studies rather than establishing
statistical or causal relationships. Therefore, frequently reported approaches, metrics, tools, or remediation strategies
should not be interpreted as evidence of superior effectiveness, but as the most consistently reported evidence in the
literature. The use of LLMs introduces additional threats due to the inherent variability and limited transparency of
their outputs. We mitigated these threats through local inference with fixed model versions, deterministic decoding
(temperature = 0), fixed parameters, RAG, and validation using three independent LLMs followed by human majority
voting. We also documented the complete pipeline and provide a replication package. Nevertheless, different models or
Manuscript submitted to ACM

execution environments may produce minor variations; reproducibility should therefore be considered at the level of
taxonomies, categories, and aggregate findings rather than exact outputs.
7 Conclusion
This paper presented a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 primary studies, delivering the first integrated view of
architectural degradation across four dimensions: measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies.
The resulting taxonomies and cross-dimensional analysis reveal a field that has matured impressively atdetecting
degradation, static analysis, structural metrics, and detection tools dominate the landscape, but remains fragmented
and comparatively immature when it comes toactingon what is detected. Remediation strategies are scattered across
code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions with no shared vision, and the tooling ecosystem offers
extensive support for diagnosis yet very little for deciding or executing corrective actions.
The central implication is clear: the next generation of research must shift from building yet more detec-
tion techniques toward closing the diagnosis–remediation gap.Priorities include decision-support frameworks
that help practitioners select and prioritize remediation strategies, runtime-aware and predictive approaches that
catch degradation before it solidifies, and continuous architectural governance that treats degradation management as
an ongoing process rather than a periodic assessment. For practitioners, the evidence synthesized here provides an
actionable map of what is available today and where the blind spots remain.
Architectural degradation is not a solved problem, but the path forward is now visible. We hope the taxonomies,
maturity analysis, and conceptual framework offered in this work serve both as a reference for future research and as a
practical foundation for building the next generation of intelligent, continuous, and automated degradation-management
solutions.

measured using Cohen’s Kappa (K) and Gwet’s AC1. The results showed moderate to substantial agreement across the
raters. For Cohen’s Kappa, the pairwise agreement values range from 0.46 to 0.71. The highest agreement is observed
between the LRM (Marco-o1) and V1 (Mistral) raters (K = 0.71), followed by V2 (Qwen) and V3 (Llama) (K = 0.66). In

title: Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes
abstract: Patient-specific clinical question answering requires locating the right evidence within long, heterogeneous longitudinal clinical records in which relevant facts may be scattered across encounters, repeated in copied-forward notes, or expressed using different clinical terminology. We evaluated whether biomedical reranking can improve evidence selection and downstream answer quality in a locally deployed retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for longitudinal clinical notes. The pipeline combines PubMedBERT dense retrieval, BM25 lexical retrieval, weighted reciprocal-rank fusion, and MedCPT cross-encoder reranking. Across 1,000 open- and closed-ended question-answer pairs from a cohort of 200 bariatric surgery patients, reranking increased exact source-chunk retrieval within the top 10 items, Hit@10 from 46.6% to 60.6% and mean reciprocal rank from 0.2371 to 0.3252. With Qwen3-8B generation, local judge-assessed answer correctness increased from 44.8% to 48.6%. These results show that biomedical reranking can improve the placement of relevant clinical evidence within a limited context window, although gains in retrieval do not translate proportionally into gains in answer correctness.

Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical 
Notes 
     Maryam Shahbaz Ali1, Laura B. Strachan1,2, Caitlin Sherman1, Mark Kovler1, Eleanor Mackey1,3, 
Syed Muhammad Anwar1,3 
 
1 Children’s National Hospital, Washington, DC, USA 
2 University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA 
3 George Washington University, Washington DC, USA 
 
ABSTRACT 
Patient-specific clinical question answering requires locating 
the right evidence within long, heterogeneous longitudinal 
clinical records in which relevant facts may be scattered 
across encounters, repeated in copied -forward notes, or 
expressed using different clinical terminology. We evaluated 
whether biomedical reranking can improve evidence 
selection and downstream answer quality in a loca lly 
deployed retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for 
longitudinal clinical notes. The pipeline combines 
PubMedBERT dense retrieval, BM25 lexical retrieval, 
weighted reciprocal-rank fusion, and MedCPT cross-encoder 
reranking. Across 1,000 open- and closed-ended question-
answer pairs from a cohort of 200 bariatric surgery patients, 
reranking increased exact source-chunk retrieval within the 
top 10 items, Hit@10 from 46.6% to 60.6% and mean 
reciprocal rank from 0.2371 to 0.3252. With Qwen3 -8B 
generation, local judge -assessed answer correctness 
increased from 44.8% to 48.6%. These results show that 
biomedical reranking can improve the placement of relevant 
clinical evidence within a limited context window, although 
gains in retrieval do not translate proportionally into gains in 
answer correctness. 
 
Index Terms- Clinical question answering, retrieval 
augmented generation, biomedical reranking, hybrid 
retrieval, local language models 
 
1. INTRODUCTION 
 
Patient-specific clinical question answering (QA) differs 
from general medical QA because the required evidence is 
often buried within a single patient’s longitudinal record 
rather than contained in model pretraining. Relevant facts 
may be distributed across encounters, repeated in copied-
forward notes, or expressed using different clinical 
terminology. This creates a retrieval problem in which the 
system must identify the most informative evidence from a 
large, redundant record while operating within a lim ited 
context window. 
   Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a 
mechanism for supplying patient-specific evidence to a 
language model, but the usefulness of the final answer 
depends heavily on which passages are retrieved and how 
they are ranked. Towards this goal, MIRAGE benchmark and 
MedRAG toolkit were introduced to systematically evaluate 
retrieval configurations for the medical QA [1]. In 
longitudinal clinical records, this distinction is particularly 
important because retrieving the relevant evidence and 
correctly interpreting that evidence are separate stages of the 
pipeline.  
Dense retrieval can capture semantically related text, 
whereas lexical retrieval rewards direct term overlap. These 
complementary signals can be combined using reciprocal-
rank fusion (RRF) [2], after which a cross encoder can jointly 
score the question and candidate passage. MedCPT provides 
a biomedical retrieval and reranking framework trained from 
PubMed search interactions [3]. Recent work has extended 
retrieval augmentation to electronic health record 
applications beyond general medical QA. RAG was applied 
to EHR summarization and clinical information extraction 
[4], while RAM-EHR was introduced to augment clinical 
prediction with retrieved medical knowledge [5]. Recent 
studies have further examined RAG for biomedical 
applications, longitudinal EHR reasoning, factual -aware 
medical QA, and evidence-grounded patient QA [8]-[12]. 
These studies demonstrate the broader value of retrieval 
augmentation, but do not directly evaluate whether 
biomedical cross-encoder reranking improves evidence of 
selection for patient-specific question answering over 
longitudinal clinical notes. 
 We evaluate this approach using a frozen set of 1,000 
QA pairs generated from 200 bariatric surgery patients, with 
retrieval restricted to each patient’s longitudinal record and 
clinical inference performed locally. This work makes three 
contributions: 1) evaluates biomedical cross -encoder 
reranking for longitudinal clinical QA, 2) quantifies the 
relationship between improved evidence retrieval and 
downstream answer correctness, including separate analysis 
of open- and closed-ended QA, and 3) demonstrates a fully 
   
 
   
 
local, patient-restricted RAG evaluation incorporating 
retrieval, generation, and identifier screening. 
 
2. METHODS 
An overview of the proposed method is presented in 
Figure 1, with details about each component in the following 
text. 
2.1. Dense and lexical candidate generation 
Questions and retrieval chunks were encoded using 
NeuML’s PubMedBERT base embeddings checkpoint 
through Sentence Transformers [6]. The 768-dimensional 
vectors are normalized to unit length. Dense retrieval used a 
FAISS inner-product index within each patient’s corpus, 
yielding cosine-similarity rankings. Cached corpus 
embeddings were verified against the corpus; both contained 
71,289 rows with matching source-identifier ordering. 
Lexical retrieval used the BM25Okapi implementation 
from the rank_bm25 Python package, based on the Okapi 
BM25 ranking function [13]. Text was lowercased and 
tokenized into alphanumeric sequences using the regular 
expression [a-z 0-9] +. Each retriever returned up to 30 
candidates, producing a union of at most 60 unique source 
chunks. 
For a candidate chunk c and query q, weighted reciprocal 
rank fusion is assigned as,

where Dq and Bq are the truncated dense and BM25 rankings, 
respectively, and ranks begin at one. The plus sign denotes 
the sum of the dense and BM25 reciprocal -rank 
contributions. The 0.30/0.70 weights were selected during 
development based on retrieval performance, with BM25 
weighted more heavily because it performed better on this 
cohort. The denominator constant 60 is the standard RRF 
offset. Candidates absent from a ranking receive zero 
contribution from that retriever. The coefficients are rank-
fusion weights rather than weights on raw PubMedBERT or 
BM25 scores.  
2.2. Biomedical reranking and generation 
The reranked condition uses the ncbi/MedCPT cross-
encoder [3] checkpoint to score the full union of up to 30 
dense and 30 BM25 candidates for each question. Question–
passage pairs were processed in batches of eight, with the 
question followed by the candidate passage. The combined 
input is limited to 512 tokens, with truncation applied only to 
the passage. Candidates are ordered by descending model 
score, and the ten highest-ranked chunks are selected. Tied 
scores retain the weighted reciprocal-rank fusion order. The 
reranker runs locally on the CPU using cached model files. 
This comparison uses the original cached PubMedBERT 
embeddings rather than the token-window variant. Because 
all candidates are reranked, the fusion weights affect the final 
ranking only when reranker scores are tied.  
Qwen3-8B [7] generates answers with either no retrieved 
context or the selected top ten chunks. Previously generated 
no-RAG answers were reused for the reranked experiment, 
while RAG answers were regenerated. The clinical 
generation was served through a local vLLM endpoint on an 
NVIDIA RTX A5000 with 24GB memory; reranking ran on 
CPU. Public reranker weights were downloaded before local 
clinical processing. The local execution is a deployment 
Fig. 1. Patient-specific clinical question answering using hybrid PubMedBERT and BM25 retrieval, weighted rank 
fusion, MedCPT reranking, and local Qwen 3-8B generation. Retrieval and answer quality are evaluated separately. 
 
   
 
   
 
property, not a guaranteed text containing no identifiers. The 
generation prompt instructs the model to answer only from 
the information provided and to return “Insufficient 
information”, when an answer is unsupported. Closed-ended 
answers are normally limited to 20 words, while open-ended 
answers are requested in one to three sentences. The prompt 
also instructs the model to omit reasoning and patient 
identifiers. Retrieved passages were numbered in rank order 
and separated by blank lines.  
   
3. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULT 
3.1. Dataset 
The retrieval corpus was constructed from longitudinal 
clinical note records belonging to the 200-patient evaluation 
cohort who underwent bariatric surgery at our clinical center. 
Data are collected under an approved IRB study. Clinical note 
text was cleaned by normalizing whitespace, removing 
records with empty text or invalid timestamps, and 
eliminating exact duplicates, yielding 40,197 cleaned note 
records. Each cleaned note was converted into one or more 
retrieval chunks, defined as contiguous segments of clinical 
text that serve as the searchable units of the retrieval system. 
Chunking was character-based with a target length of 
approximately 1,600 characters. Notes containing fewer than 
250 characters after cleaning were excluded as very short text 
fragments, while notes containing 250-2,200 characters were 
retained as single chunks. Longer notes were split at newline 
boundaries, while trailing text carried into subsequent chunks 
to preserve local context. Duplicate chunks were removed 
within each patient after lowercasing and whitespace 
normalization. After removal of 7,925 duplicate chunks, the 
final retrieval corpus contained 71,289 patient -linked 
retrieval chunks.  
Retrieval was patient restricted: each question searched 
only chunks belonging to the corresponding patient. Each 
chunk retained a source identifier linking it to the designated 
reference evidence used for evaluation; source identifiers 
were not used as retrieval features. This setting assumes that 
patient identity is already known and does not evaluate cross-
patient record discovery. 
3.2. Evaluation questions and reference evidence 
Patients were eligible if they had at least 20 non-empty 
note records with valid timestamps and at least five distinct 
encounters. The frozen cohort matched a random sample of 
200 eligible patients selected with seed 42.  The frozen 
evaluation set contains five questions per patient: 1,000 total, 
comprising 500 open-ended and 500 closed-ended questions. 
Each row contains a patient index, question, reference 
answer, and a designated source chunk.  
An initial automated quality check using Qwen3-8B [7] 
classified 993 questions as pass, four requiring reviews, and 
three as fail. Subsequent checks covered 117 repaired rows, 
and six corrected rows, all of which passed their rechecks. 
One initially review-flagged question was absent from both 
later checks; hence its resolution could not be established 
from the retained quality-check records. These automated 
checks do not establish independent human validation. 
Several configurations were examined on the same 200 
patient cohort. These findings therefore describe performance 
during development and not just the independently held-out 
generalizations. No independent held-out test split or manual 
validation is claimed in this study. 
3.3. Retrieval and answer metrics 
The exact source Hit@10 measures whether the 
designated source chunk occurs among the ten retrieved 
chunks. The reciprocal rank is 1/r at the first occurrence of 
that chunk and zero when absent from the searched candidate 
list. Reported mean reciprocal ran k (MRR) is therefore 
candidate-limited: the individual retrievers search up to 30 
items, while the fused and reranked lists can contain up to 60. 
An exact source miss therefore does not prove that all the 
retrieved passages are irrelevant; overlapping or r epeated 
notes may contain equivalent evidence.  
     Automated semantic correctness is the primary answer 
metric against the frozen reference answer. A local Qwen3-
8B [7] judge evaluates blinded candidate A/B answers, with 
candidate assignment determined by a SHA256 hash of the 
QA identifier. The judge receives the question, question type, 
reference answer, and both candidate answers. It is instructed 
to assess each candidate independently, allowing both to be 
correct and incorrect. Closed-ended answers must provide the 
requested fact, allowing equivalen t wording, standard 
abbreviations, and equivalent numerical values or units. 
Open-ended answers must contain the essential information 
without material errors or contradictions. Insufficient 
information is scored as incorrect when the reference 
provides an answer. Retrieved passages are not supplied to 
the judge, so this assessment measures agreement with the 
reference rather than grounding in the retrieved context. 
Answer performance was additionally evaluated separately 
for the 500 open-ended and 500 closed-ended questions. For 
the open-ended subset, BLEU-4 and ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, 
and ROUGE-L F1 scores were computed as complementary 
text-overlap metrics. Normalized exact match is a secondary 
metric. Candidate and reference answers are lowercased, 
characters other than letters, digits, periods, percent signs, 
plus signs, hyphens, and slashes are replaced with spaces, and 
whitespace is collapsed before comparison.

3.4. Evidence retrieval  
Table 1 summarizes retrieval performance. Weighted 
fusion achieved 46.6% Hit@10, compared with 37.9% for 
dense retrieval and 43.7% for BM25. MedCPT reranking 
increased Hit@10 to 60.6% and MRR to 0.3252. Relative to 
weighted fusion, 171 questions changed from miss to hit and 
31 from hit to miss. The net increase was 140 questions, or 
14.0 percentage points (95% patient-cluster CI, 11.4–16.6). 
   The union of the top 30 dense and top 30 BM25 candidates 
contained the designated chunk for 778 questions (77.8%). 
This is a candidate coverage bound for exact-source retrieval 
under this pool, not an answer-accuracy bound. Reranking 
placed 606 of these targets in the top ten; 172 remained below 
rank ten, while 222 were absent from the candidate pool. 
3.5. Downstream question answering 
MedCPT reranking increased automated answer 
correctness from 44.8% with weighted -hybrid RAG to 
48.6%, an absolute gain of 3.8 percentage points (95% 
patient-cluster CI, 1.1-6.5). Across the two judging runs, 123 
questions changed from incorrect to correct and 85 changed 
in the opposite direction.  
      When stratified by question type, correctness increased 
from 49.6% to 51.8% for open-ended questions and from 
40.0% to 45.4% for closed-ended questions. For open-ended 
QA, BLEU-4 increased from 0.1813 to 0.1883, ROUGE-1 F1 
from 0.4300 to 0.4545, ROUGE-2 F1 from 0.2702 to 0.2863, 
and ROUGE-L F1 from 0.3910 to 0.4093. In the reranked 
condition, correctness was 63.4% for questions in which the 
designated source was retrieved within the top ten and 25.9% 
for retrieval misses. However, 222 of 606 retrieval -hit 
questions were still judged incorre ct, indicating that 
successful evidence retrieval did not guarantee a correct 
generated answer. 
3.6. Window ablation and identifier screening 
Tokenization identified 5,528 of the 71,289 chunks 
(7.75%) above the embedding model’s 512-token limit. A 
448-token overlapping-window ablation achieved 46.5% 
hybrid Hit @10 and 0.2372 MRR, providing no improvement 
over the original hybrid (46.6%, 0.2371); therefore, it was not 
used for reranking.  The audit flagged any identifier in 44 
weighted-hybrid RAG answers and 40 reranked RAG 
answers. No-RAG had 15 flagged answers in both 
experiments. Condition flags decreased from 56 to 48 
questions. Among the 952 questions for which neither 
condition’s answer was flagged by the identifier screen in the 
reranked evaluation, RAG correctness was 49.1%. Different 
flagged subsets preclude interpreting these filtered accuracies 
as a matched comparison between RAG variants. The flagged 
outputs require review before any release.  
4. DISCUSSION 
    Biomedical reranking improved evidence selection by 
increasing Hit@10 by 14.0 percentage points, while 
automated answer correctness increased by 3.8 points overall. 
Stratified gains were 2.2 points for open-ended and 5.4 points 
for closed-ended QA. Remaining errors may reflect 
incomplete evidence, distracting context, generation errors, 
reference limitations, or judge errors.  
Several limitations constrain interpretation. The same 
Qwen3-8B family generated and judged answers, the 
development cohort was reused for configuration selection, 
exact-source labels may undercount equivalent evidence, and 
patient-restricted retrieval ass umes reliable patient 
association. Independent human evaluation and held -out 
validation are needed to establish generalization.  
 
5. CONCLUSION 
In a local patient -specific QA evaluation, MedCPT 
reranking improved exact source Hit@10 from 46.6% to 
60.6% and automated answer correctness from 44.8% to 
48.6%. The results support a distinction between evidence 
retrieval and downstream answer quality. Independent human 
evaluation and held-out validation are needed to establish 
generalization.

title: AGO AI Quality Gate: Evidence-First Release Decisions for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Enterprises adopting retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) face a recurring operational decision: promote, revise, or block a system version. The evidence is incomplete and the metrics come from fallible LLM judges. We report on AGO AI Quality Gate (AGO), an evidence-first quality-gate framework deployed in industrial RAG assessment engagements. AGO integrates four key components: a four-state decision model that treats missing data and judge errors as explicit outcomes; layered scoring combining deterministic checks, local guardrails, and structured LLM evaluation; a stratified beta-binomial gate that quantifies regression risk probabilistically; and a mandatory meta-evaluation protocol to validate the LLM judge before it influences decisions. Since engagement data is proprietary, we evaluate the judge layer on RAGBench, a public benchmark of 100k annotated RAG traces across 12 datasets. On identical stratified test samples (N=1200 per judge), a low-cost judge (gpt-4.1-nano) detects non-adherent answers barely above chance (AUROC 0.603 [0.570, 0.634]), despite producing flawless protocol output, while gpt-4o reaches 0.783 [0.756, 0.807] -- yet its per-domain performance still ranges from 0.62 to 0.88. A fixed-seed gate study spanning regression, no change, and improvement quantifies unsafe promotion, false-alarm cost, and improvement throughput. Under regression, the decision-grade profile reduces unsafe promotion to 22.2%-35.1%, against 29.3%-41.8% for a naive gate. These results support the design choices that judge quality must be measured per engagement and that point estimates alone are not a release decision.
